en: 1. Prakaraṇa: Vairāgya. Oṃ!
Constantly agitated by its own Mount Mandara of Will, impelled by the quality known as Sovereignty, [the intellect] is drawn from its essence-filled and eternally unshakable form.

Victorious is the wondrous Lord of the Supreme River, known as Awakening, who causes to appear within his own heart that jewel-mine of the essence of reality—which is composed of himself, yet distinct from and similar to himself. //1//

I bow to the primordial God, the stainless Śiva, who is called Awakening; who is pure like a crystal mirror, eternally made one with Himself by His own power because of its transparency, yet [seems] filled with various internal and external impurities arising from His own power; who, through that same power, always causes even these impurities to dissolve into Himself; and who is a forest fire to the six sheaths.

I constantly take refuge in that pervasive Lord for the sake of attaining true awakening—He who is the supreme manifestation of the distinction between awakening and non-awakening, who is awakened by those endowed with awakening, whose stainless form is devoid of both awakening and non-awakening, whose sole essence is awakening, and who conceals even that very awakening within Himself. (3)

Salutations to that one who is the abode of the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*), the eternal teacher by nature—to him who, by resorting to the state of being a mother through his own purity, attained the name "Vaiḍūrya" (the Lapis Lazuli-like Arhat), and having subsequently assumed the designation of "Anvavatāra," reached a state of utter clarity; and who, having made his own reality manifest, then returned to his very own true nature.

Skilled even in the discernment of the utterly transparent self-awareness, he who took recourse in the form known as Vaidūrya and subsequently entered into the state of an incarnation out of a desire to teach the reality;

having taught that reality to his disciples, he then returned to his own essential nature—to him, the illustrious treasure-store, the teacher Prakāśa, the bestower of true awakening, I pay homage. (5)

Salutations to those who, through the power of discernment (*vimarśa*), are constantly intent upon beholding the sun of unfolding consciousness (*unmeṣa*)—which removes dullness—from within the junction of the branches of temporal succession arising from the tree of the mind situated on the mountain of the body; and who perceive that state of absolute oneness within themselves as well as in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) which appears by virtue of its light. (Verse 6)

Victorious is this certain unprecedented power of the Blessed One, which is beyond the reach of the heart, transcending all determination, and preeminent in its lightness; for when even a mute person is possessed by it in this exceedingly great task called "explication"—a domain belonging to the Lord of Speech—they too attain the authority [of speech]. (7)

This unsurpassed, profound, and sufficient inner secret—which is self-established, obtained from my own father, and supreme—I have undertaken this effort here solely to reveal it to all, and not with the intention of proclaiming my own intellectual acumen. (8)
Some are blind by their very nature, while others, due to the darkness of anger, have no regard for the power of their own innate light.

Therefore, as if this work were unmanifest even in the lamp of [my] commentary, I have made this effort here for those who might wander in the delusion that "there is no one qualified for this," or "who could possibly be so? (9)
Bhāskarakaṇṭha, the son of Avatārakaṇṭha and grandson of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, composes this commentary as an ornament for the throats of the learned. *10*
Since I lack the requisite power and other qualities, I shall stumble at every step as I proceed; may the virtuous serve as my support. *11*
Having bowed to Gaṇeśa, who is worshipped by the lords of the gods; to the Goddess of Speech, whose nature is creative intuition;
and likewise to my gurus, beginning with Kaulanarottama, I compose this commentary, which is fit to be drunk from the vessel of the ears.
Having remembered the feet of my gurus and performed self-worship by myself,
I shall provide a concise commentary on the treatise titled *Mokṣopāya*.

In this world, there was indeed a certain great soul who, having himself attained the illumination known as perfect knowledge through the jewels of instruction from Śrī Vasiṣṭha— which produce the knowledge of Śrī Rāma found within the Bālakāṇḍa and other sections of the ocean-like *Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Śrī Vālmīki— then, out of compassion for others and desiring to extract those jewels from that ocean in order to reveal them to others, [worshipped] the Supreme Self, whose nature is the Supreme Deity, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of that extraction.
Salutation to that Self of the universe, the all-pervading Lord who shines as the very essence of light within me— in heaven, on earth, in the sky, and both outside and inside.

Salutation to Him who is well-known, the Self of All, because He exists as the essence of everything and is thus the Self of all; that is to say, salutation to the Supreme Self. Let there be a state of prostration, which consists in the subordination of one's own limited existence within His immeasurable existence. In other words, let me contemplate my own existence as merged into His very existence. To whom? To Him whose nature is light.

That which is the Self of the universe—the essence of the knowledge whose objects are the various external and internal multitudes of entities, whether they pertain to the external world or the internal—shines forth; it manifests as direct perception itself. For these various appearances, while manifesting directly, when subjected to inquiry, come to rest in the state of the Supreme Self alone, whose nature is ineffable. Therefore, through the manifestation of diverse appearances...

The sense is that it is the Supreme Self alone that appears. Of what nature is it? It is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), meaning omnipresent. Where? Outside—that is to say, in that external region which has been brought within the scope of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*)—of me, the limited subject (*parimitapramātṛ*). This is because I have fallen away from the state of the unlimited subject whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) by assuming the status of a limited knower, and have consequently become denotable by the limited expressive word "I" (*asmacchabda*). Thus, it is the Supreme Self alone that shines forth.

Furthermore, where? Internally, in that region which has been brought within the scope of non-egoity (*ahantā*); and externally, in what form? In heaven (*divi*), in the form of the celestial world (*svargaloka*) which serves as the support for all the gods;

likewise on earth (*bhūmi*), in the form of the terrestrial world (*bhūloka*) which serves as the support for all various beings such as humans; and similarly, in space (*ākāśa*), in the essential nature of the world of space (*ākāśaloka*) which serves as the support for mere emptiness. By this, the inclusion of the fourteen worlds (*caturdaśabhuvana*) should be understood.

And "within" (*antaḥ*) means in what form? In the form of the state of dreaming, which has the nature of mere luminosity in the sky (*divi*); in the form of the waking state on earth, due to the similarity of grossness; and likewise, in the form of the state of deep sleep in space (*ākāśe*), due to the similarity of being the substratum of mere emptiness. And here, the all-pervasiveness of the Supreme Self exists through its predominance as power by way of being the material cause (*upādānatayā*), and through its own predominance.

It should be understood that [the presence of the deity] is twofold, because [the deity] stands as a witness. Having thus performed the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) characterized by salutation to the chosen and appropriate deity, the author of this commentary— desiring to state the fourfold preliminary connection (*anubandha*) consisting of the qualified student (*adhikārin*) and so forth for this work which is about to be extracted— indicates the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) by implication, and proceeds to define the qualified student.
He realizes it directly.

He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am bound; may I become liberated," is neither one who knows that [reality] ultimately nor one who does not know it; he alone has the qualification for this scripture.

Of that person who has become the recipient of the compassionate glance of the Blessed Lord: "I," being of the nature of a limited subject, am bound; my mind is attached to the multitude of enjoyments pertaining to the body, which is determined as my own self—how is this so? (This is the implied question.
"How may I become one whose mind is not attached to the aforementioned multitude?"—in this way, such a resolve should be constantly present in the mind.

There may be an inquiry: that person would be qualified for this treatise which is about to be extracted, titled *Mokṣopāya* (The Means to Liberation). The meaning is that this scripture is to be investigated by him alone. Of what nature is he?
He is "not an absolute knower of that" (*nātyantatajjñaḥ*). The meaning is that, despite desiring liberation, he is devoid of perfect knowledge.

For one who possesses right knowledge (samyagjñānin) does not even desire liberation, because mere desire itself is bondage. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is "not ignorant of That" (nātajjñaḥ), because he is liberated from the desire for enjoyment (bhoga). Indeed, one who is ignorant of That is unable to abandon the desire for enjoyment. Since one who knows That perfectly has accomplished all that was to be done (kṛtakṛtya), there is no qualification for him in this scripture; whereas for one who is ignorant of That, it is due to unfitness—such is the distinction.

In this [text], the identity with the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*), because it is what is expressed at every step and because it accomplishes the supreme purpose called liberation (*mokṣa*) by means of the knowledge of its own object; for in all scriptures, it is observed that the subject matter itself is the accomplisher of the supreme purpose.

Right knowledge regarding that [subject] is the intermediate purpose (*avāntaraprayojana*). Otherwise, one who desires that [knowledge] would not possess the status of an intermediate qualified candidate (*adhikārin*) unless they were a fool.

It would not be so; for liberation is the ultimate purpose (*paramaprayojana*). Otherwise, one who desires that—that is, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*)—would not possess the status of a supreme qualified candidate (*paramādhikāritva*). The relationship between the intermediate purpose of the treatise and its ultimate purpose, as well as between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the ultimate purpose, is that of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). As for the qualified candidate, however, he has been stated explicitly by the author himself; thus, everything is consistent.
Having thus determined the subject matter and other preliminary elements, he begins the exposition of the scripture with the words "Vālmīki said.
Vālmīki refers to the sage named Vālmīki. "Said" means he spoke; the ellipsis to be supplied is "to Śrī Rāma. To address the question of what he said, he states:
Having first examined the means to worldly success, he who, being wise, then examines these means to liberation is not born again.

The means consisting of stories are "kathopāyas"; these [are the means]. It should be understood that even stories function as means because they incite one toward right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). These are those which will be described hereafter. Now, an objection might be raised: "How did the venerable Vālmīki speak the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa*, which consists of the life-story of the venerable Rāma, to the venerable Rāma himself? For it is indeed appropriate for one person to relate the life-story of another."

True. Some resolve this by saying that Śrī Vālmīki, who appeared in the present kalpa, spoke to Śrī Rāma—who also appeared in the present kalpa—the *Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa*, which consists of the ancient account of Śrī Rāma and was composed by Śrī Vālmīki of a previous kalpa. What is the use of our worrying over the validity or invalidity of such a theory, since we are merely engaged in providing an exposition? Moreover, there is something here [to consider].

Even a hidden seed of human effort is to be accepted, as indicated by the verse to be stated later; and that is to be understood by those possessed of intuition (*pratibhā*) on their own. For others, its explanation would be improper. Thus, enough with this disclosure of secrets.
O crusher of enemies, having previously composed these means for the story of Rāma—which yield great fruit—in this *Rāmāyaṇa*, I have placed them at the very beginning.
To this disciplined and wise disciple, Bharadvāja, he, with one-pointed mind, gave the beautiful jewels, just as the ocean gives them to a suppliant.

"Rāma" is the form of address, because he alone is the one to be instructed. "Having first seen these"—meaning, having accomplished [the task] at this very moment—[he spoke] to him who was standing before him. "One-pointed" means his mind was fixed upon him due to his disciplined conduct.
This is a pair of verses (yugalaka).
Then these methods of discourse were proclaimed by the wise Bharadvāja in the presence of Brahmā, in a certain thicket on Mount Meru.
They have been cited; that is, they have been explained.
Then the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being pleased with him, spoke thus: "O son of great resolve, choose a boon."
This is clear. (MT 1.1.7)
Bharadvāja said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, this boon pleases me today: please declare that by which these people may be liberated from sufferings."
"Lord of the past and future" means the knower of the past and the future; "speak," that is, tell.
Having heard the words of Bharadvāja, the venerable Brahmā said to his preceptor Vālmīki: "Request him here with diligence; by him this irreproachable Rāmāyaṇa has been commenced."
When that is known, a person shall cross over from all delusion by means of it, just as one crosses to the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge endowed with boundless virtues.

This is a pair of verses (*yugalaka*). The word "pāram" (the further shore) is also to be construed with the first half-verse. The ablative case in "ambudheḥ" (from the ocean) concludes the statement of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus to Bharadvāja, the Supreme Lord, the Creator of all beings, came to my hermitage together with that Bharadvāja.
He is Parameṣṭhin because he abides in the supreme, highest state called pure consciousness (cinmātra), owing to his nature as the pure mind.
Quickly honored by me with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites, that God, the Great Being who delights in the welfare of all creatures, spoke to me.
This is clear.
Brahmā said:
O blameless and excellent sage, because of this discourse on the true nature of Rāma, you must not abandon your effort until its completion.
"Until completion" means up to the very end of the completion.

"Now, why should I not abandon this effort? To this he replies: "By means of this knowledge, this world shall quickly cross over from the peril of this saṃsāra, just as one crosses the ocean by means of a boat. (MU 1.1.14)
The word "atha" (now/then) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
"I have come here specifically to tell you this very matter: for the sake of the welfare of the world, compose a scripture"—thus spoke the Unborn One.
This is clear. He concludes the statement of Brahmā with the words, "Thus he spoke."
Rāma vanished from that holy hermitage in an instant; in a moment he rose up high, like a wave of water.

From that holy hermitage, my own sacred retreat, at that time he was taken away; for sages indeed take up ever-new hermitages. Like Brahmā? Like a wave. Just as a wave rising from water has previously emerged, yet after a moment returns to disappearance—such is the meaning.
When that Blessed One had departed, I was filled with wonder; once again, with a clear mind, I questioned Bharadvāja on that matter.
In what state was Bharadvāja? He was characterized by a clear intellect; the implication is that otherwise, the very act of questioning would have been improper.
"What did you ask? To this he replied:
"O sinless Bharadvāja, tell me quickly what this was that was spoken by Brahmā. Thus addressed, Bharadvāja spoke again to me: MU 1.1.18.
O sinless one, O Rāma free from all faults!
Bharadvāja said:
"The Blessed One has spoken thus: 'Compose the Rāmāyaṇa quickly for the welfare of all the world—a boat for the ocean of saṃsāra.'"
It fulfills the expectation for this word, as shown by the phrase "yathā" (as).
"Now, what does that matter to you? To this he replies: "O Blessed One, tell me how Rāma and the high-minded Bharata conducted themselves even while caught in the straits of saṃsāra."
"Vyavahṛtaḥ" means he has engaged in worldly activity (*vyavahāram kṛtavān*). The particle "api" indicates improbability and is connected with the phrase "in the perils of *saṃsāra*. (MT 1.1.20)
Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as the illustrious Sītā, and those highly intelligent sons of ministers who were Rāma’s followers.
This is clear. (MT 1.1.21)
Tell me clearly how these beings have attained this state free from suffering; in that very way, I too shall cross over, together with the multitude of people.
These are Rāma and the others.
The venerable Vālmīki says to Śrī Rāma:
"O Indra among kings, when I was addressed with respect by Bharadvāja as to when [I might come], I then began to speak in order to carry out the command of the Lord."
"I am"—in the manner previously described—thus was he spoken, thus was he declared, by the Lord Brahmā.
He clarifies the very process of engagement:
"Listen, dear Bharadvāja; I shall tell you according to what was asked, by hearing which you will cast delusion far away. (MU 1.1.24)
"Enough with this excess"; he thus provides the introduction in order to fulfill his promise, "Listen."
O wise one, conduct yourself in such a way that you may live happily, just as the lotus-eyed Rāma did, with an intellect free from all attachments.
With complete non-attachment, being free from all clinging to results.
With the intention of showing that it was not only Rāma, but others as well, he says:
"Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata, and the high-minded Śatrughna;
Kausalyā and Sumitrā, Sītā, and likewise Daśaratha."
This is clear. (1.1.26)
Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, who were firm in their resolve, free from conflict, and had reached the perfection of awakening, as well as the other eight ministers, [were there].

*Kṛtāstha* and *Avirodha* were his names. There were eight ministers and eight counselors; likewise, there were another eight ministers. Thus, in reality, there were sixteen ministers. He clearly states the meaning of "the others" [as follows]:
"Ghṛṣṭi, Vikuṇṭha, Bhāma, and Satyavardhana, Vibhīṣaṇa, Suṣeṇa, Hanumān, and likewise Indrajit. (MU 1.1.28)
This is clear. (MT 1.1.28)
These twenty-eight are declared to be those whose minds are free from passion; they are great-souled ones liberated while living, who follow whatever state has naturally arisen for them.
This means they follow what has been attained, rather than reaching their goal through their own independent effort.
My son, if you conduct yourself exactly as they took, gave, grasped, stayed, and remembered, then you are indeed liberated from this peril.
By these, namely Rāma and the others.
In order to provide Bharadvāja with an opportunity to ask questions, he concludes his own discourse with this verse at the end of the chapter:

"Having attained supreme yoga, one who has plunged into the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra and possesses noble character does not fall into grief nor succumb to dejection; freed from fever, he remains eternally content. (MU 1.1.31)

The shoreless ocean of saṃsāra—into that he falls, being prone to falling. A noble being (*udārasattva*) is a person endowed with superior fortitude. Having attained the supreme (*parām*), most excellent reasoning (*yukti*)—the reasoning to be described hereafter, characterized by the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible—he does not undergo sorrow (*śoka*), which is characterized by longing; nor likewise does he undergo dejection (*dainya*), that is, a state of wretchedness, or lack of contentment (*atṛpti*).

...until [he reaches this state]. He does not "go" [to another state]; on the contrary, he remains free from fever—that is, devoid of the fever consisting of expectation—and for that very reason, he abides eternally satisfied. May there be auspiciousness! (MT 1.1.31)
Thus ends the first canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 1,1 //
Bharadvāja asks:
"O Brahmin, having first established the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) through the story of Rāghava, tell it to me in due order, so that I may become eternally happy."

"O Brahmin Śrī Vālmīki, you—having begun with Rāghava, the illustrious Rāma—tell me the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta-sthiti*) and the boundaries of one liberated while living; that is to say, tell me by way of the narrative of the illustrious Rāma. [The sage asks: "But for what purpose should I tell it? To this he replies: "I shall become... [meaning: "by which [narrative] of the state of one liberated while living, I may [become such]."
I shall become eternally happy, endowed with the great bliss known as liberation while living.
The venerable Vālmīki first offers general instruction in order to establish the eligibility for hearing the account of Śrī Rāma:
"O virtuous one, I consider the forgetting of this worldly delusion—which has arisen like the color of the sky—to be better than its repeated recollection."

O holy one! I [shall describe] the non-recollection—that is, the state of not bringing back into the range of memory again—of this delusion, which consists in the false cognition of the world's reality; which appears before me, belonging to the world (jagat), that is, having the world as its object; and which has arisen, having become manifest, like the color of the sky, that is, like the blueness of the sky. It is a false appearance, meaning a false cognition in the form of the knowledge of the world's existence. Non-recollection means not allowing it to become an object of memory once more.

"Upekṣām" means "indifference. "Varam" means "preferable" or "superior. "Vismaraṇam" means "forgetfulness. I consider that indifference alone is appropriate here, not forgetfulness; the implication is that the latter is pervaded by dullness (*jāḍya*). // MT 1.2.2 //
"Now, by what means will that non-recollection come about? To this he says:
"Without the cognition of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible, that [non-recollection] is not experienced; therefore, let that cognition be sought after by someone at some time. (MU 1.2.3)

The term *nāma* is used here in the sense of certainty. By a certain person, that non-recollection [of the Self]—which has the dense form of ignorance regarding the object of perception and is characterized by thick egoism—is called "impure latent impression" (*vāsanā*) by the wise, as it brings about rebirth. (MU 1.2.12)

The wise have stated that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are impure. Of what nature are they? They possess a very dense form due to ignorance (*ajñāna*). By "ignorance" is meant the lack of knowledge regarding pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); that [impurity] is that which has a very dense form. Indeed, it is through the ignorance of pure consciousness alone that latent impressions become solidified. Otherwise, if there were identity with pure consciousness, what would be the object of the latent impressions? Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are "dense," meaning uninterrupted.

That which is *ahaṅkāra* is the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*) having the body and so forth as its object. She is "possessed of that," for it is solely through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that the *ahaṅkāra* centered on the body and other such things becomes solidified. Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is "the cause of rebirth," bringing about existence once again, because she manifests in the form of objective entities.
He describes the nature of the Pure [state]:
"Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth, it remains like a parched seed; it persists until the end of the body, having known that which is to be known—it is called 'Pure'. (MU 1.2.13)

That latent impression (*vāsanā*) is called "pure" by the wise. What is it? It is that which persists only until the end of the body—that is, for as long as the body remains—and not even beyond that. Of what nature is it? It is one that has been abandoned by the sprout known as rebirth; because it remains like a parched seed, like a roasted seed. Just as a parched seed [does not sprout].
It remains as a mere appearance and is not capable of producing a sprout. Likewise, pure latent impression (*vāsanā*) also remains as a mere appearance;

the meaning is that it is not capable of producing the sprout of rebirth. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that by which the known object—the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*)—which exists as something necessarily to be known, becomes such [as it is]; that is, by means of that which takes the form of scriptural inquiry and so forth.
For it is indeed by means of pure latent impression alone that the reality of the Supreme Self is known.
He describes the specific nature of the substrate of the pure [state]:
"In embodied beings who are liberated while living, the pure latent impression (vāsanā) which effects the absence of rebirth exists within the body like the whirling of a wheel. (MU 1.2.14)

In embodied beings who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), a pure latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists within the body that prevents rebirth—that is, it does not cause rebirth—but it does not exist in the mind. What is it like? It is like an illusion (*bhrama*). Just as an illusion, which is the spinning in the form of a wheel, exists in the wheel, so too is the meaning here. For those who are liberated while living, the latent impression does not produce the pursuit of fruits and the like.
The meaning is that it exists in this very way.
He describes the characteristics of one liberated while living:

"Those whose mental impressions are purified so that they are no longer vessels for the miseries of rebirth, and who have known that which is to be known—they are called the high-minded ones liberated while living."
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanā) are pure—they are such as these.
Having given this general instruction, he begins the narrative of Śrī Rāma:
"I shall relate to you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living, for the sake of pacifying old age and death."

"Now, for what purpose do you speak of Śrī Rāma’s attainment of liberation while living? To this he replies with the word "jarā" (old age). The sense is that by hearing of Śrī Rāma’s attainment of the state of liberation while living, even for you there will be the pacification of old age and other such afflictions, in accordance with his own conduct.
[The opponent objects: "But for me, who desires many instructions, what is the point of speaking only of the sequence of Rāma? To this, [the author] says:
"O Bharadvāja of great intelligence, listen to this auspicious sequence of Rāma; I shall speak it, and by that alone you will know everything in every way. (MU 1.2.17)
By the word "in every respect" (*sarvathā*), the intended meaning is that you should have no further desire for anything beyond this.
He tells of that very thing:
having emerged from the house of learning, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home, free from fear and full of playful diversions.
For days, but not for months. "Akutobhaya" means one from whom no fear arises from any quarter; the sense is that he is fearless.
Then, as time passed while that king protected the earth, his subjects remained free from sorrow and devoid of all affliction.
At one time, the mind of the virtuous Rāma became intensely eager to behold the series of hermitages belonging to the sages at the sacred fords.
This is clear. [This concludes] the pair of verses.
Having reflected thus, Rāghava approached his father’s feet and grasped them, which were like two fresh lotuses with new filaments, as a swan might grasp two lotuses.
The meaning is that he performed a prostration at his feet.
Śrī Rāma says to his father:
"O Father, my mind is indeed intensely eager to behold sacred fords, temples, forests, and shrines."
For "hi" [is used] in the sense of certainty.
Therefore, you ought to fulfill this former purpose; for there is no supplicant in the world, dear son, who has ever been disregarded by you.
The intention of the previous [verse] is that "I have not yet made any request of you today."
He concludes Śrī Rāma’s prayer with these words:
"Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha, the king then deliberated and released this very Rāma, who was the first petitioner."
Only after having investigated, and not without having investigated; first the petitioner—that is, one who has become a petitioner prior to that [investigation].

On an auspicious day under a favorable constellation, Rāghava, his body adorned with auspicious ornaments and having had rites for well-being performed by the twice-born, set out together with his two brothers.
Accompanied by a few affectionate and excellent princes, as well as by Brahmins sent by Vasiṣṭha who were proficient in the sacred scriptures.
Having been adorned by his mothers with blessings and embraced again and again, he departed from that house, intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
By the repetition "embracing, embracing," an excess of affection is illuminated; *niragāt* means he went out.

He departed from his own city, accompanied by the citizens and cheered by the sound of musical instruments, while being gazed upon by the eyes of the city women, which were as curved as swarms of bees.
He was showered by the villagers with handfuls of parched grain offered from their lotus-like hands, appearing like the Himalaya mountain covered in snow.
Winning over the hosts of Brahmins, hearing the blessings for the people, and surveying the horizons of all directions, he wandered through the forest.
He traveled on foot; for in a pilgrimage, traveling on foot brings merit.
Then, starting from his own territory of Kosala, he proceeded in due order and beheld [the holy sites], preceded by ritual bathing, charity, austerity, and meditation.
The word "ha" is a particle.
In response to the expectation of an object for the verb "what did he see?", he says:
"Rivers, sacred bathing places, holy forests, and shrines; jungles at the edges of the woods, and the shores of oceans and mountains. (MU 1.2.32)
There were jungles situated at the edges of the forests and regions filled with water.
The Mandākinī, which resembles the moon; the Kālindī, with its stainless blue lotuses; the Sarasvatī, the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī.
This is clear. (MT 1.2.33)
The Veṇā and the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Nirvindhyā and likewise the Sarayū, the Carmaṇvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, and also the Bāhudā.
This is clear.
Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and likewise Gayā; Vārāṇasī, Śrīgiri, Kedāra, and likewise Puṣkara.
This is clear.
And Mānasa, Kramasaras, as well as Uttaramānasa, Vaḍavā, Maḍavā, and the multitude of Tīrthas together with their siblings.
Of what nature was the multitude of sacred fords (*tīrthavṛnda*)? It was accompanied by the *sodara* ford, that is, together with the ford known as *sodara*.
The great sacred ford Agnitīrtha, as well as Indradyumna-saras, the lakes and ponds, and likewise the series of tanks and wells.
This is clear.
[He saw] his master Kārttikeya, as well as the Sālagrāma Hari, and the sixty-four sacred sites of Hara, the lord of Girijā.
This is clear. (MT 1.2.38)
The shores of the four oceans, variegated with many wonders; the caves and groves of the Vindhya mountains, and the regions of the principal mountain ranges.
This is clear.
And [he saw] the auspicious hermitages, which purify, belonging to the great royal sages and likewise to the brahmin sages, as well as to the gods and the brahmins.
This is clear.
Again and again, that bestower of honor wandered with his two brothers across all the regions of the earth, reaching even the furthest ends of the four quarters.
This is clear.
With a verse at the end of the canto, he concludes the account of the wandering pilgrimage:

Honored by gods, kinnaras, and humans, and having beheld this entire earth, the joy of the Raghus returned to his own home, having traversed all directions like the Lord [Śiva] returning from the realm of Śiva.
In what manner is the Lord? He is one by whom the directions have been traversed—that is, made the objects of his movement. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the second canto in the section on detachment (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The glorious Śrī Rāma entered his home,
strewn with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city-dwellers, like Jayanta entering heaven.
Vikīrṇa means filled; Jayanta is the son of Indra.
Then Rāghava, having arrived first, bowed down to his father Vasiṣṭha, his maternal relatives, the brahmins, and the elders.
This is clear.
Then Rāghava could not contain himself amidst the repeated embraces and formal courtesies of his friends, mothers, father, and the assembly of brahmins.
Then Rāghava, filled with great joy, could not contain himself amidst the customary greetings of his friends and others, which took the form of embraces; such is the sense.
While that son of Daśaratha was firm [in his resolve], the quarters of the sky vibrated with mutual conversations of pleasant words, as if with the soft sounds of sweet flutes.
In that [city], the quarters—the cardinal directions—reeled, as it were, due to the mutual exchange of pleasant news concerning Śrī Rāma, the son of Daśaratha;

that is to say, by the mutual expressions of joy such as "Śrī Rāma has arrived home. This statement is made because of the occurrence of earthquakes that herald auspicious events. [This was] through those pleasant narrations.
In what manner? By means of [speech] that was firm, likewise sweet, pleasant to the ear, and consisting of endearing discourse. With what, as it were?
Like the sounds of soft flutes. The meaning is: just as men reel from those [sounds], so too [do they reel] from this.
Many days have passed here with the festival of Rāma’s arrival, which releases the people into great joy and is filled with the clamor of playful festivities.
In this city of Daśaratha, there was a festival—the arrival of Rāma—for how long? For many days;
the meaning is "until many days had passed. What was the festival doing? Releasing the people into great joy. The form *āsa* is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
From that time forward, Rāghava lived happily in his home, describing the various customs and regional practices found here and there.
Hither and thither, here and there.
Having risen in the morning and performed his twilight devotions according to the prescribed rites, Rāma then beheld his father seated in the assembly hall, equal to Indra.
This is clear.
Having spent a fourth part of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, he remained respectfully engaged in most wonderful conversations filled with the essence of knowledge.
Permitted by his father and surrounded by a vast army, he went to the forest teeming with boars and buffaloes, out of a desire for the hunt.
With the desire for hunting, that is, with the longing for the chase.
Then, having returned home and performed his ablutions and other rites in due order, he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night in the company of his companions.
This is clear.
Intending to convey that he did not perform such conduct on only a single day, but rather at all times, he says:
"Rāghava, whose daily conduct was of this nature, returned from his pilgrimage and dwelt with his two brothers in his father's house. (1.3.11)
This is clear.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:
That sinless king passed his days with such activity as was pleasing to the conduct of a ruler—a moonlight to the minds of the virtuous, and tender as the essence of the nectar of sacred learning.

That sinless one, Śrī Rāma, devoid of all faults, passed the days—meaning he spent them—in such a manner of conduct: by means of royal administration, such as the judicial inquiry into subjects; it was a conduct that was pleasing and heart-entrancing, and likewise like moonlight in the minds of the virtuous—that is to say, delighting the hearts of good people. And so it was.

Regarding "śrute" (in hearing) and "śravaṇe" (in listening): the sense is that if [the Lord] is so exquisite, like the essence of nectar, even when merely heard, then what need is there to speak of him when he is actually seen? Thus all is auspicious. MT 1.3.12.
Thus ends the third canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Then, while the sixteenth year was current, the descendant of Raghu [Rāma] remained there, as did Śatrughna, who followed Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa as well.
While Bharata remained constantly in his maternal grandfather’s house in happiness, the queen protected this entire earth according to the law.
And for the sake of his sons' welfare, King Daśaratha—highly wise, skilled in counsel, and knowledgeable in statecraft—conversed daily with his ministers.
When his pilgrimage was completed, Rāma, remaining in his own home, grew thinner day by day like a clear lake in autumn.
Likewise, "being less than sixteen years of age" is the meaning; "for the sake of procreation" means for the sake of marriage; "emaciation" means a state of depletion.
His large-eyed face gradually assumed a pallor that spoke only of emaciation, like a white lotus with petals blossoming from ripening, bearing rows of pale grains.
For when there is emaciation of the face, pallor arises.
With his hand resting upon the surface of his cheek, seated in the lotus posture, he became silent and inactive, overcome by deep reflection.
He is Śrī Rāma.
With emaciated limbs, filled with anxiety, exhausted, and deeply dejected, he said nothing to anyone, appearing as if he were fixed in a painting.
This is clear.
Being entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness, he performed his daily ritual with his lotus-like face withered.
This is clear.
Having thus beheld Rāma, that preeminent sage and mine of manifold virtues, his two brothers fell into that very same state.

The "eminent sage" refers to the most excellent sage because of his possession of dispassion (*vairāgya*); [the poet] refers to that very same state belonging to Rāma, characterized by emaciation and so forth.
Thus, as those sons became distressed and emaciated, the protector of the earth, together with his wife, fell into a state of helplessness due to anxiety.
This is clear.
"O son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours? Thus he questioned Rāma again and again with affectionate words, but Rāma did not tell him.
He is Rāma; [he is] of this father.
"Father, I have no sorrow at all," said Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals; having spoken thus, he sat upon his father's lap in silence.
This is clear.
Then King Daśaratha asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers and knower of all affairs, "Is Rāma distressed?"
The sense is that he knows all matters and is proficient in all tasks; otherwise, questioning him would indeed be improper.
"There is a reason for this, O illustrious one; let there be no sorrow for you, O King. Thus addressed by the sage Vasiṣṭha, the king was filled with anxiety.

Because it brings about the fruit known as glorious knowledge (*jñāna*), there is a certain cause known as detachment (*vairāgya*); the sense is that it is improper to speak of this at the present time.
Although the speech of Vasiṣṭha has been concluded, he states it once more with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"The virtuous do not harbor anger, dejection, or widespread joy except under the influence of a significant cause."
O King, in this world, beings do not bring about great transformations unless they possess creative impulse and the power of combination.

The virtuous and noble do not carry—do not harbor—an extensive anger, an extensive state of dejection, or an extensive joy, due to even a slight cause. The qualification "slight" is to be understood as being connected with the word "cause.
Here, he provides an illustrative example by way of contrast using the word "creation": "O King, the great elements..."

The great elements (*mahābhūtāni*), in this world (*jagatyām*) within the universe (*jagati*), without creation—that is, without a great emanation (*sargeṇa vinā mahāsṛṣṭim vinā*)—and likewise without the force of dissolution (*saṃhatijavena vinā*), which is the velocity called reabsorption (*saṃhārākhyavegena vinā*), do not undergo modification; that is, they do not become possessed of the modification called the arising of effects (*kāryotpattyākhyavikāra*), nor do they become possessed of the modification called destruction (*nāśākhyavikāra*). [The suffix] *ṇic* is used in the sense of "he does that" or "he describes that. Thus, [the text says] "they possess modification" (*vikāravantīti*).

Or this is the reading [of the text]. The meaning is that during the state of persistence (*sthiti*), they do not arise by means of a minor cause in the form of a collection of intermediate creations (*avāntarasarga*).
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the fourth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, King Daśaratha remained filled with doubt; overcome by distress, he maintained silence for some time, waiting expectantly.
While all the queens in the royal palaces were exhausted, remaining vigilant on every side regarding Rāma’s movements.
At that very time, however, a great seer known as Viśvāmitra arrived at Ayodhyā to see that lord of men.
He arrived; he was coming.
"Now, for what purpose did he come? To this, he says:
"At that time, the sacrifice of that wise man who desired righteousness was indeed plundered by Rākṣasas, who were intoxicated by their power of illusion, heroism, and strength. (MU 1.5.4)
For the sake of protecting that sacrifice, he desired to see the king; for that sage was not able to attain that sacrificial rite without obstacles.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose did he wish to see him for the sake of protection? To this, he says: "For not... (na hi).
Then, intent on their destruction, Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism and possessed of great splendor, set out for the city of Ayodhyā. "He set out" means he approached.

Desiring an audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers: "Quickly announce that I, Kauśika, the son of Gādhi, have arrived. The word *ha* is a particle (*nipāta*). When there is an expectation for the object of what was said, the second half of the verse provides that object by saying "quickly. "Announce" (*ākhyāta*) means "tell"; "you all" is the understood subject. Having heard those words of his, the gatekeepers went to the royal palace, their minds all agitated, impelled by that speech.
By that speech, by the speech uttered by Viśvāmitra.
Having gone to the royal palace, they then informed the lord of the gatekeepers that the seer Viśvāmitra had arrived. (The term *pratīhārapati* refers to the official in charge of the gatekeepers.)
Then, approaching the king who was seated in the royal assembly at an improper place, that staff-bearer, acting with haste, addressed him.
This is that Yāṣṭīka, the lord of the doorkeepers.
"What did he request? To this he replied:
"O King, a glorious man of great splendor, resembling the rising sun, with a mass of matted hair as red as flames, stands at the gate."
This is clear.
And he made that region rich with yak-tail banners, along with horses, elephants, men, and weapons, so that it was strewn with gold by their splendors.
This is clear.

The staff-bearer speaks to us quickly with a humble voice: "Announce to the King that the sage Viśvāmitra has arrived. The connection is: "That man speaks to us with a humble voice. "O staff-bearers" is the address; the word "you" is to be supplied.
Having heard these words of Yashthika, that best of kings, together with his ministers and vassal lords, rose from his golden seat.
From the golden seat, from the throne of gold.
On foot alone, he was protected by a great multitude of kings, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, and praised by the vassal lords.
This is clear.
He went to the place where the great sage Viśvāmitra was; there he saw that tiger among sages stationed at the gateway.
This is clear.
In response to the expectation of what kind [of being] he saw, he says:
"For some reason, [he saw one] who had arrived upon the surface of the earth like the sun, pervaded by Brahmanic splendor and by the great majesty of the Kṣatriya."
This is clear.
His shoulders were covered by a creeper-like mass of matted hair, perpetually withered by age and made coarse by the expansion of his ascetic penance, like a mountain shrouded in twilight clouds.
This is clear.
He bore a radiant body that was both tranquil and lovely, luminous yet non-resistant, serene and yet possessed of a majestic form.
It is non-resistant, having the aspect of non-obstruction; it is tranquil and soft.
With a splendor that was both charming and most formidable, serene yet restless, profound and overflowing, he delighted the people.
This is clear.
He held in his hand a single, smooth, and flawless lute—a companion to the state of infinite life—while his own mind remained unfading.
Smooth and elegant.
Because his mind was overcome with compassion, he seemed to drench these subjects with nectar through his glances, which were serene and sweet.
This is clear.
With white and dark corners of the eyes extending to the ends, and with bright, arched eyebrows, it bestows both bliss and fear within the beholder.
For one who observes or beholds it, it bestows bliss because of its extreme loveliness; it bestows fear because of its radiant splendor.
Beholding the sage from afar, the king, with his body bowed low, prostrated himself so that the ground was adorned by the garlands of jewels falling from his crest.
"Flowing," and so forth, are adverbs modifying the action.
There, the sage also greeted the lord of the earth with a sweet and noble voice, just as the sun greets Śatakratu.
This is clear.
Then all the twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha, respectfully honored him with the traditional rites beginning with a welcome.
This Viśvāmitra.
Daśaratha said:
"O virtuous one, we have been graced by your radiant appearance, which has come upon us unexpectedly; we are like beds of lotuses favored by the sun."
Unexpectedly brought about by Śaṃkara; [this was done] by him who had approached, that is, arrived.
O Sage, through seeing you today, we have attained that blissful joy which is beginningless, unshakable, and free from all states of woe.
The sense is that by the sight of you, we have attained the bliss of Brahman.
Today we truly stand at the forefront of those who act righteously, for by virtue of your arrival, we have come into the sight of the world.
"We exist" means "we abide. Let it be understood that this refers to the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*), which is to say, the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*).
Thus conversing there, the kings and the great seers took their seats within the assembly hall and sat down together.
They sat down; they were seated.

Seeing that the sage had arrived, blazing with splendor, the king was struck with awe; yet, with a joyful countenance, he personally offered him the guest-offering (*arghya*). (He "offered" means he presented it.)
Having accepted the *arghya* from the king according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, he honored the king by performing a circumambulation.
This is clear.
Honored by the king, he then, with a joyful countenance, inquired after the welfare and the inexhaustible well-being of the lord of men.
This is clear.
Having met with Vasiṣṭha and smiling, that bull among sages honored him as was fitting and then inquired after his well-being.
This is clear.
Having met together and honored one another for a moment as was appropriate, they all, with joyful minds, entered the residence of the great king.
This is clear.
Seated upon their respective appropriate seats, their splendor mutually increased as they all respectfully inquired after one another's well-being.
This is clear.
To that wise Viśvāmitra who was seated, he repeatedly offered water for his feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and cows.
[This is clear.]
Having worshipped Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites, the king, with palms joined in reverence, disciplined in mind, and joyful at heart, spoke these words.
This is clear.
Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain in a time of drought,
and just as the recovery of sight for one who is blind— such is your arrival.
This is clear.
The acquisition of wealth as desired, the birth of a son for one who was childless,
the attainment of an object seen in a dream— such is your arrival here.
This is clear.
Just as there is union with what is desired and the arrival of that which is wished for,
and just as there is the recovery of what has been lost, so too is your arrival.
This is clear.
Just as there is joy for one who has died because of returning through the path of the sky, so too, O Brahmin, is there joy from your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage!
Regarding the phrase "because of returning after death," the word "just as" (*yathā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "O great sage! Welcome be to you! (MU 1.5.42).
"To whom would dwelling in the world of Brahmā not bring joy? O Sage, your scripture is likewise; I tell you this as the very truth.
This is clear.
"And what is your supreme desire? And what may I do for you? You have arrived as a worthy recipient for me, O Brahmin, most righteous one.
(MU 1.5.44) "O Brahmin! You have arrived as a worthy recipient for me. (MT 1.5.44)

O Blessed One, formerly you were worthy of my veneration by the very title of *rājarṣi* (royal sage); subsequently, having illumined your progeny through asceticism (*tapas*), you attained the status of a *brahmarṣi* (divine sage), and thus you remain worthy of my veneration.

O Blessed One, previously you were indeed venerable by the designation of a royal sage; thereafter, having become one whose progeny was illuminated by asceticism, you attained the state of a divine sage; therefore, you are venerable to me.

Just as joy would arise in me from being sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, so too does the joy from seeing you cool my inner self, as it were. (5.46) *Antaḥ* means in the mind (*manasi*). (5.46)
Free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion and free from affliction—O Brahmin, it is most wonderful that you have come to me.
The sense is: "He approached me, though I am unworthy."
O best among those who know what is to be known, I perceive myself as having entered a pure field, free from defilement, like the orb of the moon emerged from the water.
"Unmagna" means risen.
I consider your arrival to be like that of Brahmā himself in person. O Sage, I am purified and I am graced by your visit.
(MU 1.5.49) [Rām I 555] This is clear. (MT 1.5.49)

O virtuous one, because my birth and my life have been colored by the merit arising from your arrival, they have become fruitful today; that life is truly well-lived. (MU 1.5.50) [By the merit produced from your arrival, my birth and my life—which have been colored, that is, made to be imbued with your presence—have become, for that reason, a fruitful birth for me and a well-lived life.]
Having seen you arrived here, having honored you and bowed down,
I bow within my very self, just as the ocean bows when it beholds the moon.
This is clear.
"O bull among sages, whatever task you have come for and for whatever purpose, know that it is already accomplished; for you are truly highly honored by me.
(This is clear.)
“O Kauśika, you ought to deliberate upon your own business; O Blessed One, there is indeed nothing that cannot be granted to you.

“O Kauśika, you ought to deliberate—that is, you ought to investigate—what my business might be, along with your own business. [The opponent asks: ‘But for what purpose should I deliberate upon it together with my own business?’”
Regarding this, he says, "O Blessed One. For, O Blessed One, whatever is requested of you or required for use, there is nothing that should not be given; the meaning is that I shall indeed give it.
And you ought to deliberate upon the matter in accordance with dharma; I am your agent for everything, and you are my supreme deity.
(This is clear.)
With a verse at the end of the canto, he describes the sage’s attainment of joy through the humble speech of Daśaratha:

Having heard these exceedingly sweet words, spoken with humility by one who knows the meaning and which are pleasing to the ear, the bull among sages, distinguished by his own renowned virtues, attained the highest joy. (Rāmāyaṇa I.17.39)

"Extremely sweet" means distinguished by the quality known as *utkṛṣṭamadhura* (exquisite sweetness). "Pleasant to the ear" means pleasant for the hearing. It was "spoken with humility"—that is, it was uttered or told in a manner characterized by modesty—by Daśaratha, who knew the meaning, that is, who understood the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, it was "distinguished by those qualities" which are renowned as the qualities of speech; thus, it is "distinguished by renowned qualities."

Thus it goes on. Having heard such words, that bull among sages, Kauśika—the best of ascetics—attained supreme joy. For great joy arises in supplicants through the humility of a donor. May there be auspiciousness! MT_1,5.55.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were so wonderfully extensive, the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke:
[This is clear.]
"O tiger among kings, this is worthy only of you upon this earth—you who are born of a great lineage and follow the tradition of Vasiṣṭha.
The meaning is: "This belongs to you alone, and not to anyone else."

"O tiger among kings, carry out the decision regarding that matter which is in my heart; uphold righteousness. The word *tu* (but/however) indicates that the task expressed by the speech is extremely difficult to accomplish. "The decision regarding that matter" means the decision regarding the task expressed by the speech residing in the heart. To the question, "Why should I do this?", he replies: "Righteousness (*dharma*)."
Thus, the sense is that by this means there will be the protection of the Dharma for you.
He makes manifest the speech within his heart:
"O bull among men, I observe this restraint for the sake of success; however, terrible Rākṣasas stand as obstacles to it. *Ātiṣṭhe* means "I resort to" or "I undertake."
But whenever I performed a sacrifice for the assembly of the gods, on each such occasion the night-stalkers would destroy that sacrifice of mine.
I sacrifice; I worship.
When that sacrifice had been performed many times, those leaders of the Rākṣasas strewed the earth with flesh and blood.
This is clear.
When that assembly of sacrifices had thus become desolate, I, having exerted myself in vain, lost my enthusiasm and departed from that place. "Apāgamam" means "I went away."
"O King, my mind does not incline toward releasing anger; for such was that deed, and no curse can affect it. The sense is that by the giving of a curse, that sacrifice would have been destroyed.
And such is my forbearance, O King, regarding that great sacrifice; through your favor, may I attain its great fruit without obstacle.

Therefore, O King, such is my forbearance toward him at that great sacrifice. Therefore, by your grace, may I cause that sacrifice of great fruit to be attained—may I attain it. [The form] *prāpayeyam* is used in the sense of the reflexive (*svārthe*), with the *ṇic* suffix being an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
You ought to protect me, who am afflicted and have come seeking refuge; for the hopelessness of those who seek help is indeed a defeat for the virtuous.
This is clear.
"Now, in what manner shall I provide you with protection? To this he replied:
"You have a glorious son, possessing the prowess of a proud tiger; a hero like the great Indra, Rāma, the destroyer of demons."
This is clear.
"Surely, what follows from that? To this he says:
"O tiger among kings, you ought to give me that son Rāma, whose prowess is truth, the heroic eldest one who still wears the side-locks of youth.
The sense is: "By him alone will my protection—which is synonymous with preservation—be secured."
"But how will he, being merely a child, protect your sacrifice from the Rākṣasas? To this he replied:
"For he is capable, protected by me, by his own divine splendor, in the subduing of the heads of those Rākṣasas who would do us harm.
This is clear.
"And in this matter, I shall perform manifold and infinite deeds of excellence, by which he will become worthy of worship even by the three worlds.
This is clear.
"Now, how is it possible for him to stand before such *rākṣasa*s? To this he replied:
"And having encountered him, the night-stalkers are not able to remain, just as deer in the forest upon seeing an enraged lion in battle. (Rām I 18.11ab)
In the word *tena*, the third case ending is used in place of the second case; this is an archaic usage.
And among them, no man other than the descendant of Kakutstha dares to fight,
just as no one dares to face enraged lions except for rutting elephants.
This is clear.
For those wicked ones, intoxicated by their own valor in battle, are like the Kālakūṭa poison;
they are the servants of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, resembling the wrathful God of Death himself.
This is clear.
O tiger among kings, they shall not withstand the arrows of Rāma,
which fall incessantly like showers of dust from a cloud.
This is clear.
And you ought not, O King, to harbor affection for your son;
there is nothing in this world that must not be given away by a high-souled man.
This is clear.
Ah, now I truly understand; know those Rākṣasas to be already slain, for wise men such as ourselves do not engage in action when the outcome is uncertain.
"Hanta" expresses joy; "nūnam" indicates certainty. I know those Rākṣasas to be slain; you too should know this. [The opponent asks:
"But how can I know it merely by your word? To this he replies: "Not so" (*na hi*). "Saṃ" means correctly; "pravṛttiḥ" means activity.
Those for whom [this is true] are such [as I have described].
"I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses—Vasiṣṭha of great splendor and those others who possess far-reaching vision.
This is clear.

"If righteousness, greatness, and fame are established in your mind, then you ought to grant me your own desired son. *Manasi sthitam* means "situated in the mind" or "longed for. *Abhipretam* is stated to mean "desired" for the sake of the task at hand.
And my sacrifice shall last for ten nights, during which the Rākṣasas— my enemies who act as obstructors to my sacrifice— must be slain by Rāma.
This is clear.
O descendant of Kakutstha, let all your ministers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, grant their permission here; therefore, O Rāma, dismiss him.
(This is clear.)

"O knower of time, O Rāghava, act in such a way that this time of mine does not pass away; may you be blessed, and do not set your mind on grief. (The word *atyeti* means "it passes" or "it goes by.")
Even a minute task, if performed at the proper time, becomes a source of benefit; whereas even a great task, due to being mistimed, results in emptiness of benefit.
"Out of season" means at an improper time.
Having spoken these words consistent with dharma and artha, the righteous and highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, lord of sages, fell silent.
This is clear.
He describes Daśaratha’s silence with a verse at the end of the canto:

Having heard the words of the eminent sage, the immensely powerful king remained silent; for it was appropriate for him to speak thus. A wise man does not find satisfaction without a discourse joined with reason, nor does the world when its heart's desire remains unfulfilled. (1.6.28)

Possessed of great power and endowed with great majesty, that Daśaratha, having heard the words of the eminent sage Viśvāmitra, remained silent; the meaning is that he said nothing at all. This silence was appropriate and fitting, because he was wise and possessed of intelligence, [realizing that] without speech consistent with reason—

He does not find satisfaction in speaking or telling; the meaning is that he does not speak. And as for the world—meaning the people—if their heart's desire is not fulfilled, they do not find satisfaction in speaking.
Therefore, the sense is that having heard Viśvāmitra’s argumentation-lacking words, Daśaratha became silent. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the sixth canto in the section on dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings remained motionless for a moment and then spoke thus with dejection:
[This is clear.]
"This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age; I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas.
This is clear.
"O Lord, here is this complete Akṣauhiṇī army of which I am the master; surrounded by it, I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters.
[The term *piśitāśinām* refers to the Rākṣasas.]
For these servants are brave, valiant, and skilled in the use of weapons; and I myself, bow in hand, am their protector at the forefront of battle.
This is clear.
Together with these, I shall give battle to your enemies, even those as great as Mahendra, just as a lion does to rutting elephants.
For since these men are your servants and I shall be their protector at the head of the battle, the connection is this: "Therefore, I give you a battle against your enemies along with them."
But Rāma is a child among armies; he does not know strength from weakness, for no ground of battle other than the inner apartments has ever been seen by him.
This is clear.
He was neither equipped with supreme weapons, nor was he skilled in combat; nor was he one who understood the frowns of warriors on the front lines of battle.
The word "this" (eṣa) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
He always frequented only the flower groves, the city parks, and the bowers within the gardens and forests.
This is clear.
He knows how to sport together with the princes in his own courtyards, which are strewn with the offerings of scattered flowers.
This is clear.
But today, O Brahmin, due to the reversal of my fortune, I am exceedingly like a lotus struck by frost—once flourishing, now green, withered, and emaciated.
Greenish-white.
He is unable to eat his food nor to enjoy himself in the garden of his home; with his soul overwhelmed by inner anguish, he remains merely silent.
To eat, to consume.
O leader of sages, for his sake, I, together with my wife and my servants, have surely become as weak as a cloud in autumn.
Incapacity, emaciation; the state of being unable to endure.
Such is this young son of mine, rendered helpless by affliction; how can I give him to you to fight with the night-stalkers?
This is clear.
O holy one of great intelligence, this affection for a son leads to happiness more than even the company of young women, more than the essence of nectar, and more than sovereignty itself.
This is clear.

Those things which have miserable ends, involve great undertakings, and bring weariness to the three worlds—even the virtuous do not resort to them out of affection for their children; of this there is no doubt.
The meaning is that even though they are peaceful and established [in their nature], they fall into forgetfulness regarding their refuge—that is, their state—due to affection for their sons.
O tiger among sages, human beings may renounce their vital fluids, wealth, wives, and even happiness; however, they do not renounce their sons, for such is the inherent nature of living beings.
This is clear.
"The Rākṣasas are performers of cruel deeds and experts in treacherous warfare;
let Rāma fight them"—such a statement alone is exceedingly difficult to bear.
"Deceitful combat" means fighting through trickery. The meaning is that if it is merely words, what need is there to mention its actual execution?

"Separated indeed from Rāma, I cannot endure to live for even a moment; though desiring life, you ought not to take away Rāma. "I cannot endure" means I am not capable. "To live" means to experience the state of being the agent of the act of living. "Desiring life" means that I, who desire my own life, [am thus speaking].
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed for me; these four sons were brought forth by me with great hardship.
These sons are my cherished children, objects of my compassion."
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the principal one; without him, those other three cannot sustain their lives.
This is clear.
If that very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas, then know me to be as good as dead this very moment, bereft of my son.
This is clear. (MT 1.7.21)
"For among my four sons, my affection for him is supreme; therefore, you ought not to take away Rāma, who is the eldest and consists of dharma.
(The genitive case here is used in the sense of selection.)
O Sage, if it is your desire to destroy the army of the night-stalkers, then lead forth this force, complete with its four divisions, together with me.
This is clear.
"What is the prowess of those Rākṣasas? Whose sons are they, and how did they come to be? What is their size, and who are they? Describe these things clearly to me.
This is clear.
"O Brahmin, how should Rāma strike those Rākṣasas who fight with deceit—either by means of his own forces or by me?
[The word "by him" (*tena*) is used because Rāma was not standing in front of him.]
"O Blessed One, tell me everything regarding how I must stand in battle against those wicked beings, for the Rākṣasas are indeed arrogant in their prowess.
This is clear.
For it is heard that there was a great hero, a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the brother of Vaiśravaṇa himself and the son of the sage Viśravas.
(This is clear.)
"Let it be so. "What follows from that? To this he replied:
"If that evil-minded one indeed causes an obstacle to your sacrifice, then we shall not be able to withstand that wicked-souled one in battle.
At that time...
"But how can he possess such power? To this he replies:
"O Brahmin, at various times, beings of immense power and majesty arise among living creatures and, by the force of time, they dissolve again. (MU 1.7.29)
"Bhūrivīryavibhūtayaḥ" means those endowed with the perfection of great heroism; the locative case in "bhūteṣu" is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa).
Today, at this time, we are not capable of standing before your enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny.
This is clear.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my son; for you are indeed the incomparable deity even to me, who am of little fortune.
Regarding the phrase "of little fortune" (*alpabhāgyasya*): the implication is that otherwise, you would not have entreated Rāma.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, monkeys, and serpents were not able to fight Rāvaṇa; how much less so human beings in battle?
This is clear.
He takes away the vigor of those great heroes who consume ambrosia; because of that, we and his inferiors are not capable in battle against him.

"He takes away" (*ādatte*) means he seizes or, more precisely, obstructs. The sense is that he renders even the great heroic consumers of ambrosia devoid of vigor. "Inferiors" (*avarāḥ*) refers to those who are low compared to him. As for the word "or" (*vā*), one might think: "Surely victory must belong to Rāma simply by virtue of his being a virtuous person. To this, he says:
This was one such time when the virtuous were rendered fragile; even Rāghava, worn out by old age, fell into a state of wretchedness.

The word *api* (even/also) illuminates the great nobility of the descendant of Raghu (*rāghava*). "Worn out by old age" (*vārdhakajarjara*) means one who is decayed by the state of being aged (*vārdhakena*).
Or else, O Brahmin, tell me of that son of Madhu, who is like salt to the sacrifice and a destroyer of it; O one who resembles a god, where indeed shall I release my son?

Alternatively, the connection is with the words supplied from a distance [in the previous verse]: "We are not able to fight that well-known son of Madhu, the salt-demon (Lavaṇa), who is a destroyer of sacrifices. The sense is: "Even if Lavaṇa is one who obstructs your sacrifice, we are still not able to fight him. O you who resemble a god, tell me: "I [shall go against] my little son..."
"Where indeed, in what place indeed? Shall I be liberated? I shall not be liberated"—such is the state of mind.
If you do not desire this, O Brahmin, then I myself am at your command; otherwise, however, I see no eternal victory for myself.

Now, in the alternative case: if you do not desire the liberation of your son, then I am indeed subject to your will; that is to say, I myself shall come. Otherwise, when one reflects upon the natural state of things, I do not perceive—meaning, I do not know—a permanent victory for myself.
He concludes Daśaratha’s speech with a verse at the end of the canto:

Having spoken these gentle words, the great-souled king, overwhelmed by fear and submerged in the surging doubt regarding the sage’s counsel, did not perceive even a moment’s worth of certainty, like one being swept away in an ocean of rising waves. "Submerged" means immersed in the doubt concerning the sage's advice—namely, the uncertainty as to whether to perform the action or not to perform it—and for that very reason, he was "overwhelmed by fear."

"He is that great-souled Daśaratha"— having spoken these gentle and tender words, he did not know, nor did he understand, even for a moment or in the slightest degree, what his resolve was. Like one being swept away in the ocean with its surging waves— just as one being carried away by the sea does not know where he is going— he likewise had no certainty.
He who knows thus is Śiva.
Thus ends the seventh canto in the section on detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having heard those words of his, whose syllables were agitated with affection, Kauśika, filled with indignation, replied to the lord of the earth with these words.
(Rām. I.20.1) [Of that Daśaratha]. (MT_1,8.1)
Viśvāmitra says:
"Having promised 'I shall do it,' do you now wish to abandon your vow?
Having been a courageous lion, you now desire the state of a deer."
This is clear. (MT 1.8.2)
"This reversal of fortune is unworthy of this lineage of the Raghavas;
never indeed do dark rays appear upon the cool-rayed moon."
"Now, how can this reversal of fortune for the lineage of the Raghavas be possible? It is improper. To this, he provides an illustration: "Never... (na kadācana).
"If you are not able to do so, O King, I shall depart as I came; having failed in my vow, O descendant of Kakutstha, may you remain happy along with your kinsmen.
This is clear.
The venerable Vālmīki says to Bharadvāja:
"Then, when that great-souled Viśvāmitra was overcome with anger, the entire earth trembled and the gods were seized by fear.
This is clear.
Perceiving that the great sage, the friend of the world, was overcome by anger, the wise Vasiṣṭha—steadfast, firm in his vows, and intelligent—spoke these words:
"The friend of the world" refers to Viśvāmitra.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says:
"Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, you, the illustrious Daśaratha, are like another Dharma incarnate; adorned with virtues, you pervade the three worlds."
This is clear.
Being possessed of wisdom and firm in your vows, you ought not to abandon dharma;
you ought to carry out the word of the Sage, the Lord of the Three Worlds.
This is clear. This is a pair [of verses].
Renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with righteousness and glory, practice your own duty; you ought not to abandon dharma. "Pratipadyasva" means "accept it as your own."
"O King, since they have promised 'I shall do it' but are not doing so, your merit consisting of *iṣṭāpūrta* will fall away; therefore, dismiss Rāma.
[Rām I 20.8] "Consisting of *iṣṭāpūrta*" means having the nature of *iṣṭāpūrta*. For indeed, by the non-fulfillment of what has been promised, all merit perishes.
Guarded by that lion among men as nectar is by fire, the Rākṣasas shall not behold him, whether he has mastered the divine weapons (*kṛtāstra*) or has not yet mastered them (*akṛtāstra*).
(Note: *Kṛtāstra* means one who has been trained in the use of weapons.)
Even though you are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and are Daśaratha yourself, if you do not uphold his word, who else will?
This is clear.
Living beings do not abandon the boundaries established by the conventional usage formulated by you and others; therefore, you ought not to forsake them in this world.
That boundary.
He is Dharma incarnate; he is the best among the energetic; he is preeminent in wisdom in this world and the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
(The term *parāyaṇa* means a resort or support.)
He knows various weapons within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile; no other man knows these, nor will anyone ever know them.
(This is clear.)
Neither any divine sages, nor immortals, nor rākṣasas, nor nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas, O King, are equal to him.
This is clear.

In former times, when he was ruling his kingdom, Kṛśāśva gave this weapon—which is exceedingly difficult for others to conquer—to Kauśika. "By others" means by other [enemies]; "exceedingly difficult to conquer" means utterly impossible to defeat; "ruling" means he protected it well.

"Now, for what purpose were the weapons given to him by Kṛśāśva? To this he replies: "For those sons of Kṛśāśva were like the sons of Prajāpati; these heroes, radiant and of great prowess, followed after him. (MU 1.8.18) The word *hi* means "because. It is well known that those sons of Kṛśāśva were like the sons of Prajāpati. They followed after him—namely Viśvāmitra. Therefore, out of affection for his sons, he gave them [the weapons].
Such is the meaning.
In response to the inquiry as to who those sons were, he says:
"Jayā and Suprabhā, the two slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa—those two had one hundred offspring who were exceedingly difficult to conquer."

Jayā and Suprabhā were the two daughters of Dakṣa, born in the form of women; they were slender-waisted maidens. Of those two, there were one hundred offspring who were exceedingly difficult to conquer. And here, because the relative pronoun *ya-* occurs within a subsequent clause in relation to the preceding verse, it does not require a correlative *ta-*.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to whose children they were and how many there were, he says: "In former times, Jayā, having obtained a boon, gave birth to fifty sons for the destruction of the Asura armies; they were indestructible and able to assume any form at will. "Indestructible" (akṣaya) means being devoid of destruction.

Suprabhā gave birth to fifty other sons named Saṅgharṣas, who were invincible, difficult to assail, hard to challenge, and exceedingly powerful. [In this context: "Invincible" means incapable of being defeated; "difficult to assail" means impossible for enemies to challenge in battle.
Having concluded this incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand:
"The great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of such heroism and great splendor, has set his mind on going to Rāma; you ought not to entertain a despondent thought regarding his departure.
The first half-verse is to be construed as the reason for the second half-verse.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, Śrī Vasiṣṭha concludes his discourse:
"While this lord of sages, who consists of great being, stands nearby, even a virtuous man attains immortality when death arrives; do not fall into despondency like one who is utterly deluded."
"Just as one who is deluded" means "like a deluded person. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The venerable Vālmīki relates to Bharadvāja:

While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha, intending to send forth his son Rāma, summoned him along with Lakṣmaṇa. (MU 1.9.1) [Rām I 21.1] "Intending to send forth" means "intending to give. (MT 1.9.1)
Daśaratha said to the doorkeeper:
"O doorkeeper, bring quickly and without hindrance the mighty-armed Rāma, whose valor is truth, together with Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of the sage."
This is clear.
Thus concluding Daśaratha’s speech, he, having been dismissed by the king, went to the inner apartments and, returning in just a moment, spoke to the lord of the earth:

*iti rājñā visṛṣṭo 'sau gatvāntaḥpuramandiram / muhūrtamātreṇāgatya samuvāca mahīpatim //* MU_1,9.3 *//* Thus dismissed by the king, he went to the palace of the inner apartments; returning in a mere moment, he addressed the sovereign.
This is clear.
The doorkeeper said:
"O Lord, Rāma, who has crushed all his enemies with the strength of his arms, remains dejected in his own palace at night, like a bee within a lotus."
This is clear.
"I shall return in a moment," he says, yet he meditates all alone; with a weary mind, he does not wish to remain in the presence of anyone.
This is clear.
When he had spoken thus, the protector of the earth consoled all those followers of Rāma and questioned them in due order.
This is clear.
He relates the very question of the king:
"When asked by the lord of the earth, 'In what manner and of what sort does Rāma abide?', the distressed servants of Rāma spoke these words to the monarch."
This is clear.
"O Lord, we who support this slender body of ours are exhausted, O All-pervading One, now that your son Rāma has withered away from fatigue."
"O King, O Lord! For the sake of your son—your son named Rāma—you have offered up this body, this creeper-like frame, just as one kills a leopard for its skin."
Ever since Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, arrived from his pilgrimage along with the brahmins, he has been dejected in spirit.
This is clear.
Through our diligent entreaties, he performs his daily duties in the evening with an unfading countenance, or else he does not perform them at all.
This is clear.
