At the conclusion of his bathing, worship of the gods, and customary rites, the Lord, though entreated, does not eat food because he is weary and lacks satisfaction.
Until satiety, that is, up to the limit of satisfaction.
In the courtyard, he does not sport with playful charms alongside the women of the inner apartments who have set up swings, just as a *cātaka* bird does not play with choice raindrops.
With excellent waters from the lake; the *cātaka* is a particular kind of bird, for it drinks only the drops of rain.
O King, just as the sky does not gladden one who is helpless from being struck by lightning, so too a row of armlets and bracelets set with rubies and pearls does not delight him.
Falling, helpless due to its lack of skill.
In the vine-circled houses, where playful young women move restlessly and where breezes carry the scent of flowers, he becomes filled with extreme despondency.
In the vine-circular houses, that is, in dwellings provided with circular arbors of creepers.
Whatever is delightful, appropriate, sweet, charming, or heart-stealing, one suffers because of that very thing as if with eyes filled with tears.
This is clear.
"Why do these women, who bring only suffering, appear before me and move so restlessly?"—thus he censures the amorous women in their playful dances.
These are those very women who inspire desire.
Food, sleep, drink, pleasure, bathing, and sitting—he does not delight in these when they are censured, as if they were the behavior of a madman.
"Blamed" means made the object of censure.
"What is prosperity? What is adversity? What is home? What is striving? Everything is indeed unreal. Having said this, he remains alone in silence.
This is clear.
He does not engage in jests, he does not sink into enjoyments, nor does he remain occupied with worldly affairs; he maintains only silence.
This is clear.
Women with creeper-like tresses that sway and eyes that roll in playful charm do not bring him joy, just as does a doe to a forest tree.
This is clear.
In solitary places, at the ends of the horizon, on riverbanks, and in forests—in these uninhabited wildernesses—he finds delight like one who has sold himself.
For a creature that has been sold for the purpose of flight finds pleasure only in a place devoid of living beings.
O King, by his turning away from the giving of clothing, drink, and food, he follows the path of those ascetics who possess the nature of wandering mendicants.
The meaning is that it follows—that is, it imitates—the conduct related to ascetics; this is a usage similar to the expression "one should not eat beans."
Dwelling alone in a region devoid of people, O Lord of Men, he neither laughs with a singular intellect, nor sings, nor weeps.
He is characterized by a single intellect, a mind whose nature is the renunciation of everything.
Furthermore, in response to the inquiry "What does he do?", it is said:
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with his mind fixed on the void, he remains seated alone, resting his cheek upon the palm of his left hand.
This is clear.
He does not assume pride, nor does he desire sovereignty; he neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.
This is clear.
We do not know what he has become, what he does, what he strives for; what he meditates upon, what he approaches, or how and why he pursues it.

Regarding the inquiry "we do not know" concerning his activity, he says: "Is he born? For what purpose is he born? The underlying sense is that birth is for the sake of engaging in experiences such as enjoyment (*bhoga*) and so forth.
Day by day he grows emaciated; day by day he becomes pale; day by day he undergoes a loss of passion, like a tree at the end of autumn.
This is clear.
O King, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa followed him alone, appearing exactly like him, as if they were his very reflections.
This is clear.
Although questioned again and again by his servants, kings, and mothers, he said nothing at all and remained silent, devoid of desire.

He is Śrī Rāma; "nirīhitaḥ" means devoid of activity. The word "iti" should be understood as either for the purpose of completing the meter or as intended to indicate the nature of the subsequent statement concerning Śrī Rāma.
"Do not set your mind upon enjoyments that are pleasing only at first sight"—thus does a virtuous friend instruct a worthy person standing by his side.
"Bhavya" means worthy of instruction.
Amidst women delightful with various riches and amidst social conversations, one who lacks affection perceives only their destruction as if it were standing right before him.
This is clear.
He sings again and again with a falsetto voice (*kākalyā*), through gestures alone that are devoid of rhythmic flow, sweetness, effort, and the proper placement of words.

That Rāma sings with a *kākali*—a sweet, subtle sound—characterized solely by his movements and gestures, which are devoid of conventional rhythmic flow, sweetness, effort, or fixed metrical positions.
To the attendant standing at his side who said, "Become an emperor," the sage, with a distracted mind, laughed as if at a madman's prattle.
This is clear.
He does not listen when something is spoken, nor does he look at what is before him; he shows contempt everywhere, even toward matters of great importance.
This is clear.
Even regarding a lotus in the sky or a great forest in the sky, no wonder arises in him as to how this could be so.
It shows the essential nature of wonder as follows: "How can this be so? (itthaṃ etat katham iti).
Even when situated among beloved women, the arrows of Love do not pierce his mind, which is as difficult to break as a great stone by torrents of water.
This is clear.
"Why do you desire wealth, which is the sole refuge in times of calamity? Having thus instructed him, he bestowed his entire property upon the seeker.
Having instructed, that is, having performed the instruction.
"This is adversity, this is prosperity"—this delusion consisting of conceptual construction has arisen in the mind; thus he sings out from grief.
This is clear.
"Alas, I am ruined! I am helpless!"—even while crying out thus, people do not attain dispassion; rather, they simply say, "How strange this is! MU 1.9.39.
The word "even" (*api*) indicates that detachment is indeed appropriate for one who is intent on lamentation.
While Rāma, the destroyer of enemies and a great tree in the forest of the Raghus, remains in this very state, we have come to extreme distress.
This is clear.
We do not know what we should do, O mighty-armed one, regarding him whose mind is such; O lotus-petal-eyed one, you are indeed our refuge in this matter.
This is clear.
O Lord, he disregards the king, or even a learned brahmin who stands before him as his instructor, smiling and remaining unperturbed as if looking at a sacrificial animal.
This is clear.
Having reached the certain conclusion that this vast proliferation known here as the world has arisen, yet it is neither a real entity nor am I myself, he remains established [in that realization].

"This manifold expansion which has arisen, called the world—this entity does not exist as an ultimate reality. The word "eva" (indeed) has the sense of "api" (also): "I too am not an entity. Having thus reached this certainty, that Rāma remained established [in that state].
Neither in woman, nor in self, nor in friend, nor in kingdom, nor in mother; neither in prosperity nor in adversity—there is no resting place for that All-pervading Lord, either within or without.
Attachment is delight.
He is one whose attachment has been cast off, who is free from hope, devoid of desire, and without a refuge; yet he is not liberated from delusion, and because of that, we are tormented.
This is clear.
"What is the use of wealth? What is the use of mothers? What is the use of a kingdom? What is the use of worldly effort?"—thinking thus, he remained inwardly resolved, intent on giving up his life.
This is clear.
He fell into extreme distress regarding enjoyments, life, sovereignty, friends, father, and mother, like a cātaka bird during a drought.
This is clear.
O Lord, for one whose nature is such, the expansive web of saṃsāra, though endowed with all its splendors, acts as a counter-poison.
It acts like an antidote; it becomes an antidote.
Who indeed on this earth could be such a great being, capable of establishing him in this worldly conduct?
This is clear.
Thus, may supreme compassion arise sufficiently to uproot this calamity that has come upon us, spreading like the extension of branches.
The ellipsis is "may it arise for you."
With a verse at the end of the canto, he concludes the speech of Rāma’s servant:

"The high-minded one, having cast away delusion from his mind, indeed brings about the complete well-being of those who are afflicted; just as the sun, dispelling darkness on earth, brings its own fruitfulness to the state of being a light-giver."

The high-minded person, having cast away all delusion—the entire nature of affliction—of an afflicted person, one possessed of suffering, brings his own state of goodness, which resides within him, to fruition.
Like what? Like the sun; just as the sun, dispelling darkness from the earth, brings its status as the maker of light to fulfillment.
It leads; that is the meaning of "tathā. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the ninth canto in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having heard the words of Rāma’s servant, Viśvāmitra said:
"If that is so, then let you all quickly bring that highly wise descendant of Raghu here, as deer bring a lion."
This is clear.
This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arose neither from calamities nor from passion; this awakening, produced by discernment and dispassion, is of great consequence.
Because its great arising is characterized by liberation, it is called "Mahodaya" (of Great Arising).
"Let Rāma come here in an instant; we shall dispel his delusion right here in an instant, just as the winds disperse a thick cloud from a mountain."
Who are we? Like the Maruts. Just as the Maruts, the winds, drive away the cloud—the thunderbolt from the mountain—so too [do we], is the meaning.
O descendant of Raghu, when this delusion has been skillfully cleansed away, you will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have.
In that state called pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is the place of rest.
Having attained truth, joy, wisdom, and tranquility, he will reach fullness and a sublime complexion, as if having drunk nectar.
This is clear.
And with a fully satisfied mind, the venerable one will carry out his own traditional course of conduct, which is the very succession of legal practice, in its entirety and without interruption.
This is clear.
There will be a Great Being who has known the higher and lower states of the world—one who is free from the conditions of pleasure and pain, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal.

"Known" (*jñāte*) means correctly ascertained. "The higher and lower of the worlds" (*lokānām parāvare*) refers to their extremes—the two limits—meaning everything from the highest to the lowest. He is one by whom this has been realized.
Having spoken thus,
when the lord of sages had concluded his words, the king, his heart fulfilled, dispatched yet another succession of messengers to bring Rāma back.
This is clear.
And after this much time, Rāma rose from his seat in his own home to go into the presence of his father, like the sun rising from a mountain.
This is clear.
Surrounded by a few servants and his two brothers, he arrived at that holy assembly hall of his father, which was like the heaven of the Lord of the Gods.
This is clear.
Then Rāma saw Daśaratha from afar, surrounded by a multitude of kings like Vāsava by a host of gods.
This is clear.
It was attended on both sides by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, and protected by a host of ministers who were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.
This is clear.
He was attended by lovely women with beautiful chowries in their hands,
standing in their appropriate places like the cardinal directions personified.
By the quarters, that is, by the directions.
Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others, as well as Daśaratha and his kin, beheld from afar Rāghava approaching like Guha.
Like Guha, resembling Kumāra.
He was supported by his majesty over all beings and possessed a deep voice worthy of universal service, like the Himalaya mountain sustained by its coolness.
The pride that arises from the support or the hand-holding of a sentient being is to be applied as a qualifier for the preceding verse.
Gentle, with an even and auspicious appearance, noble in discipline and vigorous, his body was lovely and serene—a vessel for the highest good.
Of the supreme goal, which is liberation.
With the onset of youth fully dawning, adorned by both exertion and tranquility, free from agitation and effortless, his desires were almost entirely fulfilled.
This is clear.
He had contemplated the course of the world and was the sphere of pure virtues; he was, as it were, attended by his own qualities out of a singular longing for that Great Being.
Of the Great Being of great fortitude: that which is the single greed, namely attachment to that [worldly existence], is what is meant by "greed for association" (saṅgalobha); by that [greed].
He reveals the unsurpassed, noble essence that fills the hollow of the inner organ with an unwavering state of being.

Furthermore, how was Rāma? The connection is that he was displaying such an internal state through such a conduct. "Filled" means completely full on all sides due to a lack of greed regarding enjoyments.
He concludes the epithets of Śrī Rāma:
"Thus, the scion of the Raghus, filled with a multitude of virtues, was visible even from afar, with the sprouts of his white, pure, and bright silken garments and waist-cloth."
He bowed with his head, from which the rays of his shimmering crest-jewel were streaming forth, possessing the beauty of a mountain swaying upon the trembling earth.
"Parimeyāḥ" means measured. "Sitāḥ" means pure and transparent. He is such that his own necklaces and garments are like tender sprouts.
With what kind of head? That which possesses the beauty of a mountain (Acala) swaying due to the tremor of the earth. Such [is the head]. This is a pair of verses.
In response to the expectation of whom he prostrated himself, it is said:
first his father, and afterwards the sages, bowing down with singular reverence; then the Brahmins, then his kinsmen, and then his teachers who possessed superior virtues.
Of what kind was the father? One who is most venerable among those worthy of honor (*mānyaikam*).
And having observed with his own eyes that slight salutation performed by the royal assembly with sweet voices, he accepted it.
This is clear.
Having received the blessings from the two sages, Rāma, his mind composed and as beautiful as a celestial being, approached the holy presence of his father.
"Nearby" means proximate.
Then that lord of the earth, delighted by his prostration at his feet, quickly embraced him on the head and kissed him again and again.
Likewise, that slayer of enemy heroes embraced Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa with deep affection, just as a royal swan embraces a lotus.
This is clear. A pair [of verses].
Then, as the king said, "Child, stay on my lap," he sat down upon a garment spread on the ground by his attendants.
"nyavikṣata" means he sat down. The two occurrences of the word "atha" express two types of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) according to their different relations.
Daśaratha says:
"My son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious; like an ordinary person, you should not subject yourself to weariness through an aged intellect."
The meaning is that "it is not given by you" or "it should not be given. The dative case in *khedāya* is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*).
By one such as you who practices what has been proclaimed by aged Brahmins and gurus, the meritorious state is attained; it is not attained by one who pursues delusion.
This is clear.
O son, calamities remain far away and fragile only so long as no opening is given to the expansion of delusion.
This is clear.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"O prince of mighty arms, you are a hero; by you these enemies that are the objects of the senses—so difficult to sever and so difficult to assail—have been conquered."
This is clear.
Why do you sink, like one ignorant of that [reality], into this ocean of delusion which is fit for the ignorant—a sea deep with waves and characterized by dullness?
This is clear.
Viśvāmitra said:
O mind, whose eyes are like a cluster of swaying blue lotuses, tell me—having abandoned your fickleness, for what reason do you now become deluded?

O you whose eyes are like a cluster of blue lotuses, abandon this mental restlessness and speak! By stating "in dependence upon karma" as the reason, he expresses it as the very nature of karma; the meaning is: "For what purpose do you become deluded?"
Upon what are they based? To what extent? By what means? And for what reason do those anxieties plunder the mind, just as rats ravage a house?

How many are those anxieties? What is their foundation, and what is their object? By how much and by what cause do they indeed ravage the mind? Like what? Like rats; that is to say, just as rats ravage a house, so do these.
The word *nu* indicates a question.
I believe you are not the ultimate object of mental anguish for those who are unaccustomed to it; for the wise man who remains composed in calamities has already conquered his anxieties.
The authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who acts with discernment; for it is not fitting that what is appropriate should take an inappropriate form—this is the intended meaning.
Speak quickly what you desire, and you shall obtain it all without fault; by this, moreover, your mental afflictions will be destroyed.
By which [means] of attaining everything.
He concludes Viśvāmitra’s speech with a verse at the end of the canto:

Having heard these words of the sage—which were filled with the splendor of appropriate meaning—the banner of Raghu’s lineage abandoned his grief, just as a peacock does when a rain-cloud thunders, having inferred through that thundering as a sign the attainment of its desired object.

The phrase *abhyanumitābhimatārthasiddhiḥ* means: he by whom the accomplishment of the desired object (*abhimatārthasiddhiḥ*) was inferred (*abhyanumitā*) through an inference based on the cause of the thundering. May there be auspiciousness! (iti śivam)
Thus ends the tenth canto in the section on Detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages, Rāghava, having been consoled, spoke these words—charming, steady, full of meaning, and measured.
It is steadfast because of its fullness of meaning, slow because it is overflowing; thus it is "steadfast, full, and slow" (dhīrapūrṇārthamanthara).
From this point forward begins the section on dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*).
Having recollected the supreme and most profound reality known as one's own true nature (*svasvarūpa*),
and having diligently touched with the crown of the head the mass of dust from the feet of the Guru;
Having taken constant refuge in the Lord and the King of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), this commentary on the excellent chapter titled "Dispassion" is composed by Bhāskara.
(14) Having heard the words of the venerable Vasiṣṭha and the venerable Viśvāmitra, which were intent on providing consolation, the venerable Rāma reveals the dispassion residing within his heart.
O Blessed One, now that you have questioned me as is fitting, I shall speak even though I am ignorant; for who can transgress the word of the virtuous?
"Become" is an address directed toward the family preceptor Vasiṣṭha. To the question "For what purpose do you speak? he replies here: "Who would transgress [this]? (MT 1.11.2).
He fulfills the promise he himself made:
"I, having been born here in my own father's house, have gradually attained growth and remain established, having acquired knowledge."
The word "tāvat" expresses the absence of contradiction.
Thereafter, O leader of sages, having become devoted to righteous conduct, I wandered over the earth girt by the oceans for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
This is clear.
Then, after such a length of time, my own discernment removed this attachment to saṃsāra from within me, just as a current sweeps away a creeper growing on a riverbank.
Self-discrimination is the inquiry, "Who am I? //MT_1,11.5//
With my mind enveloped by discernment, I myself thereafter reflected upon this with an intellect devoid of interest in enjoyments.
This is clear.
"What have you investigated? To this he replies:
"What indeed is this so-called happiness, alas, that is this wandering in saṃsāra? The world is born for the sake of death, and it dies for the sake of birth. (MU 1.11.7)

Alas, how painful! What indeed can this so-called "happiness" be? It means that it does not exist at all. What is this? It is such a world as this, characterized by wandering and transmigrating within *saṃsāra*. That which is born for the sake of death, and that which dies for the sake of birth.
Having stated that saṃsāra, which consists of birth and death, is suffering, he now describes how the entities that serve as its substratum are themselves joined with suffering:
"All these beings, including those moving and those unmoving, remain established in this state; they are the masters of calamities, evil, and the very ground of worldly existence. (MU 1.11.8)

Possessing the movements of the moving and the unmoving—endowed with the actions of motion and stability—all these experienced entities, things consisting of both the stationary and the mobile, become masters of calamities, that is, they are beset by misfortune. This is because they serve as the locus for the suffering in the form of birth and death mentioned in the preceding verse.
In what state are these entities? They are "established in themselves" (*svasthitāḥ*), meaning established in their own nature, and not [dependent] upon one another.
They are endowed with relations; furthermore, of what nature are they? They are the planes of manifestation, each endowed with its own respective capacity.

[Objection: But how do entities remain established in themselves, given that we observe various kinds of mutual relations among them? To this, he says: "Entities are like iron rods—mutually unattached; they are joined together only by one's own mental construction. (MU 1.11.9)

The meaning is that the mutual relationship between entities exists solely through a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) such as "this is my son" or "this is my father," and not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
"Now, how can the mind possess such power? To this he says:
"This expansive world is seen to be dependent upon the mind; yet the mind itself appears as non-existent here—by what have we been utterly deluded? (MU 1.11.10)
"Expansive" means characterized by extension. The non-existence of the mind is to be understood as its being merely of the nature of a continuous succession of unreal and non-existent objects.
Alas, we of deluded intellect have been sold for nothing, like bewildered deer in the forest lured by the water of a mirage from afar.
By that which is indeed non-existent, and not by that which has become real; "with the mind" is the ellipsis.
Not sold by anyone, yet we remain as if sold; alas, we are all fools, [acting] like a conjurer's trick before people!
Śambara’s illusion.

What indeed are these enjoyments called within these conceptual proliferations? They are truly most wretched; for we have remained here in vain through delusion, with our attachments firmly established.
In the midst of these conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), enjoyments (*bhoga*) are exceedingly unfortunate, being characterized by the quality known as extreme misfortune.
What indeed do they become? Because they are pleasant only for a mere moment, the meaning is that they become nothing at all. The word *hi* has the sense of the word *ataḥ* (therefore);
thus, *hi ataḥ*: we, having fixed our mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) upon these enjoyments, remain here in vain through delusion (*moha*).
Because it would be purposeless.
Unaware for a long time, we have fallen into this dense delusion in vain, like bewildered deer into a pit.
In this delusion called the cultivation of enjoyments, for a long time—indeed, for a very long time.

"What is the use of my kingdom? What is the use of enjoyments? Who am I? What is this that has come? Let that which is false remain false; for whom indeed has anything truly come? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.15). The connection is: "Let that which is false be simply false. (Maitrī Upaniṣad 1.11.15).
O Brahmin, having reflected thus, a distaste for all things then arose within me, just as it does for a traveler in the desert wastes. MU_1,11.16.
This is clear.
He reveals his own intention:
"O Blessed One, tell me this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? And what is it that increases? (MU 1.1.6)
The words *kim* and *iti* are used in the sense of "how" (*katham*).
Old age, death, calamity, birth, and prosperity revolve again and again through their manifestation and disappearance.

The word "in entities" (bhāveṣu) is to be supplied as the object; "by means of entities" (bhāvaiḥ) is an instrumental case used in the sense of "being thus" (itthambhāve); "they evolve" (vivartante) means they go to another form.
Behold, by those very same trivial emotions, we have indeed been reduced to a state of decay, like mountain trees battered by the winds.
This is clear.
Like insentient beings, people stand about making sounds with their breaths called "winds," just as hollow bamboo flutes produce sound in vain.
For hollow bamboos resound in vain.
"How can this suffering be stilled?"—thus am I tormented by anxiety, like an old tree with a fire raging within its hollow.
This is clear.
Although my heart is as solid as a rock due to the suffering of saṃsāra, I do not weep with falling tears merely out of fear for my own world.
The sufferings of saṃsāra are indeed stones; he whose heart is densely packed with them is such [a person].
But my face turned toward emptiness, parched by weeping and devoid of flavor; solitude alone, dwelling within my heart, beholds me in these solitary places.
They are empty and futile; they are those whose functions and operations are directed toward the presence [of others]. The sense is: "In solitary places, I am solely intent upon seclusion."
I am utterly bewildered, recollecting this state composed of existence and non-existence; like a fortunate man [unaware] of poverty, I remain far removed from the anxieties of saṃsāra.

The state called "the world"—that state; who am I like? Like a fortunate man (*subhaga*). Just as a fortunate man is deluded by poverty, so [am I]; this is the meaning. Therefore, [be] far from the thought of *saṃsāra*;
let that [thought] be far away—this is the meaning.
Having thus spoken in general terms of how the objects of cyclic existence bestow suffering, he now describes that which is their primary form, prosperity (śrī):
"Prosperity, intent on deception, deludes the activity of the mind, shatters the fire of virtuous qualities, and delivers a web of suffering. (MU 1.11.25)

They delude, that is, they cause one to be devoid of discernment; for those seized by the intoxication of power become entirely lacking in consideration for what precedes and follows. They are intent on deception, meaning they are intent on cheating.

Having thus described how prosperity brings suffering, he now explains how wealth—which is its primary constituent—also brings suffering: "Wealth, with its crookedness born of a multitude of anxieties, does not lead to my joy, just as houses filled with wives [lead to the misery] of those beset by calamities."

By a mass of anxieties employed for the sake of acquisition and so forth—that is, by a multitude of worries—the crooked and devious houses of those with fierce misfortunes, which possess many wives, lead only to suffering.
In brief,
O Sage, my mind finds no peace as I reflect upon the various states of the afflictions, which are constantly fashioned by fragile causes— just like that of a forest elephant bound in chains.

By means of reflections upon those various states of defect—of what nature? By those causes which are the forms of enjoyments, which are constantly fragile, and which have been fashioned [by the mind] and manifested as its own objects.

He censures the sense-objects, which are the root cause of all defects, with this verse at the end of the chapter: "In this world devoid of light, where the single mist of sharp delusion has descended night after night, there are clever thieves of sense-objects who, at every moment, have set out and exerted themselves in every direction to plunder the very faculty of discrimination in battle; tell me, O wise ones, who are capable of resisting them?"
Today, O brave warriors!

The wicked are like evil persons because they cause extreme suffering; likewise, they are "extremely clever," meaning they are endowed with excessive cunning. They are "robbers who forcibly seize the sense-objects. "At night" refers metaphorically to the night consisting of ignorance. "Sharpened" means sharp—that which is the singular mist of delusion. By that [mist], "light has departed" means the illumination known as discernment has gone far away. In this world, in this saṃsāra, "at every time" means in all [times].

At all times, in every direction—in all quarters—those who possess supreme exertion are thus engaged; they are intent upon that which is the sole, absolute destroyer of worldly detachment and right discernment. O wise ones, tell me now, at this moment: who among you are the true warriors in the battle against those thieves who plunder objects of the senses by force?
They are capable; the sense is that no one else is. May there be auspiciousness! MT_1,11.28.
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 1.11 //
Immediately thereafter, he explains at length the aforementioned censure of prosperity:
"O Sage, this prosperity has been devised for diversion in this cyclic existence; yet even that, it seems, brings about delusion and is surely a source of misfortune."
"Nūnam" means certainly; "anarthadā" is the cause expressed by way of a qualification.
It is precisely her lack of purpose that he describes:
like a river in the rainy season, she pours forth vast, dull, and surging waves within, tumultuous and lacking in order.

This Śrī causes to flow forth—that is, produces—waves known as pride, which are full of exuberance (*ullāsa*), overflowing with joy, devoid of sequential order (*akrama*) due to their intensity in transcending all sequence, and likewise dull (*jaḍa*) because they impart a state of stupor; these are great surges.
Like what? Like a river (*taraṅgiṇī*). Just as a river during the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*) produces great waves possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
It flows forth; that is the meaning of "tathā."
Many daughters of anxiety, uttered with excessive restlessness, arise within her, just as the flickering waves arise from a river.
"Many" refers to those numerous mischievous acts and playful pranks; "set in motion by them" means shaken or, in other words, aroused by them.
For this unfortunate woman does not fix her step in one place; like a bewildered girl, she runs hither and thither with no settled course.
The word *hi* indicates certainty. "Of indeterminate conduct" means acting according to one's own will; this is an adverbial modifier.
Producing an intense burning while her limbs are being touched, she brings about her own destruction within, like a streak of lamp-soot.
This is clear.
Indeed, like the common folk of a king, fools—without any investigation into merits and demerits—cling to one who has mounted [a position] that is difficult to maintain.
Like the nature of a king, that is, like the character of a king; for even a king relies upon those who are at his side without any consideration of their merits or faults.
Through various actions, this [mind] undergoes expansion; it spreads like a flow of milk in response to the venomous force of its faults.
The spreading of milk is its sprinkling; that which acts like this is said to "behave as the spreading of milk" (kṣīravisarāyate).
People remain cool and gentle in touch toward the wealth and persons of others only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity, which is like a whirlwind that scatters the frost.

The summarized meaning is that, upon contact with fortune, a person becomes exceedingly harsh toward both themselves and others; for it is a whirlwind that makes the frost harsh, which is thus taken as the point of comparison.
Those who are wise, heroic, grateful, refined, and gentle—by their very splendor, they are soiled like jewels covered by a handful of dust.
This is clear.
"O Blessed One, prosperity does not lead to happiness; indeed, it conduces only to suffering. Like a poisonous creeper, it conceals its own destruction until it brings about death."
This is clear.
The illustrious man, the one beyond reproach, and the hero who does not boast—these three types of men, who possess equanimity and sovereignty, are difficult to find.
The sense is that one who is touched by prosperity becomes indeed censurable by people due to the presence of arrogance.
For this is a treacherous and deep cave for those who experience suffering, a great forest of the Vindhya mountains for the lordly elephants of dense delusion.
It is clear.
Furthermore, in response to the inquiry as to what it is like, he says:

It is the night-lotus for the theory of pre-existent effects (*satkāryavāda*), the moonlight for the white water-lilies of suffering, the gale for the lamp of right vision, and the river with its surging waves of turbulence. (MU 1.12.13)
The great waves are the surges in the form of pride.

It is the path to the clouds of agitation and other such states, the increaser of the poison of despondency, the small pond for conceptual constructions, and the pit for the snakes of evil enjoyments.
Khadā means a cave; kubhayāni refers to hooded serpents; [the word] "of them" (teṣām) refers to those [serpents].
She is the frost to the creepers of dispassion, the night of the owl for the moon of discernment, the fang of Rāhu to the moon of discrimination, and the moonlight to the lotus of goodness.
This is clear.
Like Indra’s bow, it is captivating with its various flickering colors; like a darting flash of lightning, it arises and perishes, resting upon the dull-witted.
This is clear.
Fickle and devoid of true delight, it is like a female mongoose born of a mongoose; it is a mirage, the cause of intense delusion and the intent to deceive.
"Fickle" (*capalā*) means endowed with the quality of fickleness; for this very reason, she is "devoid of delight" (*ratyā varjitā*), meaning she does not find pleasure anywhere.

Likewise, she is "like a female mongoose" (*nakulī*) due to her extreme fickleness. Furthermore, she is "born of a low family" (*nakulīnajā*) and thus wicked; for one born of a low family is indeed wicked. Moreover, she is the cause of "deception" (*vipralambhane*), that is, of the intent to delude others. This is the underlying meaning.
And this fierce mirage has the essential nature of a harsh mirage.
Like a wave, it does not maintain a fixed position for even a moment; like the flickering flame of a lamp, its movement and sphere of activity are exceedingly difficult to comprehend.
In going and movement, they have no sphere of activity; thus, they have no sphere of activity in what is not a path. Even the flame of a lamp likewise has no sphere of activity in its going.
Like a lioness, she brings down the pride of the elephant-king with her agitated grasp; like the edge of a sword, she is cool yet sharp, resting upon a sharp intention.

"Engaged in combat" means intent on battle. That which falls upon the "race of lordly elephants," that is, the herd of elephants—she is like that because she accomplishes such a task. A lioness is thus: "cool" at the outset because she possesses a greenness of heat [passion]; "sharp-minded" means having hard thoughts. She is one whose "basis" is such. //MT_1,12.19//
I do not perceive, through this ill-fated fortune that is afflicted by its objects and overwhelmed by misfortune, any happiness other than suffering.
"Afflicted" means oppressed by ignorance; "seeks" means desires [them] as objects of perception—thus it is of such a nature.
Fortune, once driven out through the door by the enemy of darkness, returns again—alas! she who has lost her place in the heart, shameless, and the abode of the wicked.
By means of a small door fashioned by the enemy of darkness (the sun) for the purpose of dispelling the darkness situated within the house.
He concludes the censure of Fortune with this verse at the end of the chapter:

"Fortune captivates the mental faculty, yet she is won over by the miserly and is momentary in her destruction; like a flowering creeper that has emerged from a pit but whose body is entwined within a swarm of serpents."
She is to be won over by the miserly and accomplished through evil deeds; in the context of fortune, she is a row of serpents and a succession of sorrows. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twelfth canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus censured prosperity, he now censures life itself: "Life is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of a young leaf; the body departs unexpectedly, like one who has gone mad."

"Life" (āyuḥ) means vitality (jīvitam). The connection is that it "goes" (yāti). "At an improper time" (akāṇḍe) means at an untimely moment; that is to say, by transgressing the convention (samaya) which is recognized as such. [MT_1,13.1]
For those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the poison of sense-objects and who lack mature self-discrimination, life is merely a cause of exhaustion.
This is clear.

But for those who have understood that which is to be known and have come to rest in the expansive state, being fully at ease regarding both existence and non-existence, their life becomes a source of happiness.

They are rested, certain in their selfhood; they are at ease within the vast and immeasurable flux of existence and non-existence, amidst the arising and passing away that comes in a continuous stream, never falling away from their own nature.
O Sage, we have reached a certainty established through limited forms; yet we are not at peace regarding this lifespan, which is like a mass of lightning amidst the clouds of saṃsāra.

"Finite" means being joined with limitation. "Form" refers to the form consisting of the body and so forth. "Established therein" means having reached the culmination in that. "Certainty" is the certainty regarding the self. [The meaning is: those for whom there is such [certainty], for Nirvāṇa is indeed the state of being established in the nature of the immeasurable;
this is the intended sense.
It is as reasonable to attempt to wrap the wind, to shatter space, or to string together waves, as it is to place one's trust in life.
Reliance (*āsthā*) is firmness and trust.
Like a thin autumn cloud, like an oilless lamp, or like a restless wave, it is perceived only as having already passed away.
The word "life" (*āyuḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]; "pelava" means light.
I may exert effort to grasp the moon reflected in a wave, a mass of lightning, or a cloud in the sky; but I do not strive to grasp life, which is as transient as a passing state.
This is clear.
With an undisciplined mind, the deluded person strives for a long, empty life only for the sake of suffering, like a female mule conceiving in her womb.
A *vaḍavā* is a mule born from a mare and a donkey; its fetus does not emerge without the splitting of the belly.
O King, in this ocean of creation, amidst the foam upon the waters of the wandering cycle of existence, the sap within the creeper of the body—life—does not please me.
In what kind of ocean of creation? In such a *saṃsāra*, where *saṃsṛti* means wandering or transmigration. *Ambhaḥphenaḥ* is foam, a transformation of water. This statement is addressed to Daśaratha.
That by which what is to be attained is fully attained, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the locus of supreme bliss—that is called true life.
Of the supreme, that is, the most excellent.
For even trees live, and deer and birds live; but he alone truly lives whose mind does not live by means of mentalizing.
By means of reflection, that is, by means of the pursuit of enjoyments.
Only those beings born in this world have lived a truly virtuous life who are not born here again; as for the rest, O asses, know yourselves!
"You should know. In response to the inquiry "What [is that]?", he says: "The rest. The rest are donkeys.

The scripture is a burden for one lacking discrimination; knowledge is a burden for one possessed by passion; an unpeaceful mind is a burden; and the body is a burden for one who has not realized the Self.

"Of one who lacks discernment" means of one devoid of discrimination (*aviveka*). Furthermore, the "nature of being [merely] a source" (*bhāratva*) of the scriptures and so forth is to be understood as their lack of efficacy in producing the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of right knowledge and the like.
Form, life-span, mind, intellect, ego, and likewise one's endeavors—all these lead to suffering for the person of poor understanding, just as a burden does for the bearer of that burden.

"Durdhiyaḥ" means one who is devoid of wisdom. For one devoid of wisdom falls into a state of helplessness regarding form and the other sense objects due to their perceived equality, and consequently sinks into suffering.
Life is a vessel filled with an unceasing mind, the supreme abode of calamities, a nest for the birds of disease, and a firm source of weariness.
Of what nature is this life? It is unceasing, devoid of rest in the supreme state; it is that by which the mind is filled.
Casting aside weariness every day, one must strive steadily and without ceasing; for in time, the pit of this birth is swiftly filled up.
For it is well known that life is subject to destruction by time.
The body is consumed by fierce diseases that take refuge in its cavities and inflict the burning pain of poison, just as the forest breeze is swallowed by savage serpents.
The word "life-span" (āyus) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Like an old tree being dragged down by cruel woodworms, one is drawn away by base and internal sufferings that arise incessantly.
*Avacchedam* means cutting. *Prasuvānaiḥ* means by those producing [it]. *Ākṛṣyate* means it is drawn away, that is, brought under one's own control.
Surely, death is constantly watching for one who incessantly swallows up dense pride, just as a cat watches for a mouse.
It is observed that one looks on, wondering, "When will this be swallowed? and thus it is seen.
By old age, which is pregnant with qualities such as pride, yet is empty and subject to powerlessness, one's vitality is completely consumed, just as food is digested by a voracious appetite.
By one who is powerless and subject to lack of power, that is, one who is seized by incapacity.
In just a few days, having recognized it with respect, the wicked man is abandoned by youth, just as a good man is abandoned by a wicked person.
This is clear.
Form is constantly coveted by Death—the enemy of destruction and the kinsman of old age and death—just as a beautiful woman is desired by a supreme libertine.
This is clear.
With the final verse of the chapter, he concludes his censure of life:
"In this world, there is nothing so utterly devoid of virtue, so stable yet so prone to robbing one of happiness, and so utterly worthless, as this life acquired through death."
"Uttama" is an address of greeting; "phalgu" means pithless; "maraṇena mārjitam" means wiped away or brought to an end by death. Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto in the section on detachment (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 1.13 //
Now he introduces a censure of egoism:
"Risen up in vain through delusion, it grows in vain; I am terrified by this false enemy, the wicked ego. (MU 1.14.1)
By that which consists of falsehood, having a false nature.
It is solely through the power of egoism that this world, with its manifold forms, inflicts a treasury of defects and torment upon those who are most wretched.
Affliction is suffering.
Through the power of egoism comes calamity; from egoism come afflictions; through the power of egoism comes worldly striving; indeed, egoism is a great delusion.
*Īhā* is the exertion for the sake of enjoyment.
Relying upon that supreme and ancient enemy, egoism, I neither eat nor do I drink water; how much less, O Sage, could I indulge in worldly enjoyments?
This is clear.
The long and delusive rope of saṃsāra has been stretched out in my mind by the fault of egoism, just as a snare is set by a hunter.
By the fault of egoism—that is, by the fault known as *ahaṃkāra*.
Those sufferings which are long-lasting, harsh, and great—all these, born from the sense of "I," have gone forth like *khadira* thorns.
He came from the mountain.
I renounce egoism, which is the mouth of Rahu to the moon of tranquility, a great thunderbolt to the lotus of the possessor of virtues, and the autumn for the clouds of knowledge.
This is clear.
He performs only the renunciation of the ego:
"I am not Rāma; I have no desire for worldly objects, nor do I possess a mind. Like a Jina, I wish to remain peaceful within my own self alone."
The sense is that because the body itself is Rāma, and because I am pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). "Peaceful" means free from egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
Whatever has been enjoyed, done, or taken by me under the influence of egoism—all that is indeed non-substantial; the substance is the emptiness of egoism.
The emptiness of ego is the absence of ego.
O Brahmin, if there is the thought "I am," then I am pained in adversity and happy in prosperity; therefore, freedom from egoism is wealth.

The meaning of the preceding statement is that for one who possesses wealth, there is no contact with suffering and the like, whether in times of adversity or prosperity. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): for that reason, non-egoism (*anahaṅkāritā*) is wealth;

it is wealth because a person who is certain of the body being the self, desiring a web of enjoyments for the sake of the body, [suffers] when in adversity characterized by the absence of such enjoyments.

One becomes miserable; one becomes happy when there is prosperity consisting of the attainment of those [objects]. The sense is: "Once I am certain that my self is pure consciousness alone, I do not become such [a person]."
Having abandoned the ego, O Sage, with a tranquil mind and free from agitation, I remain amidst the flood of enjoyments as one whose abode is indestructible.
I remain; I abide. Of what nature is this ego-sense? It has its unbreakable abode, its imperishable foundation, within the flood of enjoyments—that is, within the multitude of enjoyments.
O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism expands, so long does the cluster of blossoms from the *kuṭaja* tree of craving continue to bloom.
This is clear.
When the dense cloud of egoism has been stilled, the lightning-vine of craving will quickly vanish somewhere, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame that has gone out.
This is clear.
In the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated elephant of the mind roars with thunderous crashes, like a rain-cloud with its peals of thunder.
It crackles and flashes with the slapping of thick ears like the crashing of clouds.
In this great body, which is like a vast forest, there roams the lion of dense egoism; by its expansive manifestation, this entire world is pervaded.
For if there were no sense of "I," the world, even though it exists, would not exist, because it would lack the status of being an object of reference.
The succession of many births, strung upon the threads of craving, has been fashioned by the fierce hunter of egoism into a necklace around his neck.
For a weaver indeed places a string of pearls threaded on a thread around his neck.
Sons, wives, and kinsmen—this entire web, devoid of counsel, has been spread out here by this enemy of false pride.
This is clear.
When this state of "I" has been wiped away by one who is himself free from distress, all mental afflictions are indeed wiped away.
This is clear.
When the "I" has subsided within the cloud-like mind, gradually becoming perfectly tranquil, the mist of the mind's conceptualization and delusion vanishes somewhere beyond reach.
That which is the delusion of the mind's thinking, having the very form of thinking—that alone is the mist, the frost.
O Brahmin, since my mental activity is devoid of egoism and I am sinking in grief due to my folly, you ought to tell me whatever is appropriate in this matter.
The meaning is: "First, I myself shall abandon the ego; afterwards, I will do as you have said."
With this concluding verse of the chapter, he brings his censure of egoism to a close:

"I do not take refuge in that which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, situated within, and abandoned by the highest quality; that state of egoism is exceedingly painful on all sides. O Great-Souled One, instruct me with what remains."

The "station of egoity" (*ahaṅkṛtipada*) is the place known as *ahaṅkṛti*. By the word "the rest," the meaning is: "Setting aside reliance on the ego, whatever you command, that I shall accomplish. Furthermore, egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) should be understood as the production of the state of being an object of the "I-notion" (*ahantā*) within the body, which is otherwise fit to be an object of the "this-notion" (*idantā*). Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the section on Detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus offered this censure of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), he now introduces the censure of the mind (*citta*):
"Like a tuft of cotton blown by the wind, the flickering mind, having become worn out by its own faults, wavers away from the noble deeds practiced by the Aryas. (MU 1.15.1)
"By defects" means by defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. "He deviates from the true goal" means that he does not remain steadfastly established in the true goal.
It runs aimlessly and distractedly here and there, wretchedly from afar to even further away, just like a stray dog in a village.
Kauleyaka means a dog.
One attains nothing anywhere, even with great riches acquired; one does not reach internal fullness, like a small casket with water.
The sense is that one who has already attained something should not desire even the slightest further thing.
The mind is eternally empty, yet it is ensnared by the net of vain hopes; it finds not even the slightest peace, like a deer strayed from its herd.
It is empty and devoid of essence.
Maintaining a state as flickering as a wave, the mind—having fallen into a condition of being cut and shattered—does not attain tranquility even for a moment.
It refers to a state of being torn and shattered, an inability to endure the touch of a hand; that is to say, mental instability.
The mind, agitated by its own thinking, rushes through the ten directions, like the water of the milk-ocean stirred up by the striking of Mount Mandara.
Agitated by reflection and agitated by the pursuit of enjoyments.
I am not able to stem this great ocean of mental delusion, which is filled with the whirlpools of surging waves and garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion.

That mental construction (*kalanā*) which takes the form of waves is *saṅkalpa* (volition); that very thing is the whirlpool (*āvarta*) of which [it is the source]. That is *māyā*, which is erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*).
O Brahmin, like a deer captivated by the mind, one who longs for the sprouts of grass that are enjoyments runs far away, without considering the fall into the abyss.
This is clear.
My mind never abandons that state of being torn and shattered by its agitated activity, just as the ocean never ceases its restlessness.
This refers to being torn and shattered, the inability to withstand the touch of a hand, and, in short, the fickleness of the intellect.
With its flickering mode of activity, the mind—restless with a multitude of anxieties—does not fix its steadiness upon any one thing, just as a lion does not remain within a cage.
By a mass of thought—that is, by a multitude of thoughts—intensely, that is, excessively.
The mind, mounted upon the chariot of delusion, takes away the bliss of tranquility from the body—though that body has exerted effort—just as a swan extracts milk from water.
This is clear.
O Lord of Sages, the fluctuations of the mind, reclining upon the bed of manifold conceptual constructions, do not awaken; therefore, I am tormented and distressed.
The meaning is that the mind, along with its mental states, exists only as something seized by conceptual construction.
O Brahmin, I am bound by my mind, which has woven itself together with the threads of craving through firm knots, like a bird caught in a net.
In this context, the "knots" (granthayaḥ) should be understood as consisting of passion and the other [afflictions].
O Sage, I am consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire—with the constant smoke of resentment and the dense flames of anxiety.
By one who possesses smoke that is constant indignation, which is indeed anger.
O Brahmin, my mind has become dull through cruelty and follows after its wife, craving; it has devoured me like a corpse-devouring jackal.
This is clear.

O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind—which is inert in nature and characterized by a fluctuating movement like the tossing of waves—just as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a torrent.
By one whose mental state (*vṛtti*) is extremely fickle, like the tossing and surging of waves.
Driven far away by my mind—which seeks to fall into intermediate states and to enter into emptiness—I am like a blade of grass tossed by a fierce wind.

To that descent—meaning for the purpose of descending—into those intermediate states which consist of enjoyments and are devoid of supreme rest; [the word] "by the void" (*śūnyena*) is an adjective qualifying the mind (*manas*).
Constantly intent on crossing this ocean of saṃsāra, I have been blocked by that evil-minded one, just as a flood of water is dammed by a bridge.
This is clear.
As I was going from Pātāla and returning from Pātāla, I have been bound by that evil-minded one with a wooden yoke, like a well-rope fastened to a bucket.
This is clear.
I have been seized by my own mind—which is false yet expansive in form and fragile under scrutiny—just as a child is seized by a Vetāla spirit.
"Seized" means brought under one's own control.
O Brahmin, he is hotter than fire, his progress more difficult than that of a mountain, firmer even than a diamond, and his grasp of the mind is hard to restrain.

That whose sequence is more difficult to transcend is one of "more difficult sequence" (*kaṣṭatarakrama*). That mind which is "difficult to restrain" (*durnigraha*)—meaning it can only be restrained with great difficulty—the "seizing" (*graha*) or grasping of that [mind] is the "seizing of the difficult-to-restrain mind. The mind falls upon its objects like a bird upon pieces of meat; in an instant it reaches a state of detachment, just as a child [loses interest] in a toy.
This is clear.
O dear one, this ocean of the mind—with its inert nature, its restless waves, its vast whirlpools, and its lurking serpents in the form of worldly desires—drags me away from afar.
He whose nature is dull, whose very essence is inert, and whose nature is cold; he whose mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) consist of nothing but widespread whirlpools;

he for whom desired objects are themselves venomous serpents; and he in whom there are serpents joined with constant movement—he leads one far away, causing one to wander through various sense-objects.
"If you possess such a mind as this, then practice its restraint. To this, he says:
"O virtuous one, even more difficult than drinking up the great ocean, or leaping over Mount Sumeru, or even consuming fire, is the restraint of the mind. (MU 1.15.24)
This is clear.
[Objection: "Let the restraint of the mind indeed be difficult to accomplish; what will be achieved by it? To this, he says:
"The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist; when it is extinguished, the world is extinguished. Therefore, that [mind] must be treated with effort. (MU 1.15.25)
This is clear.

Surely these hundreds of joys and sorrows have come from the mind, just as forests emerge from the best of mountains; I believe, O Sage, that when that mind has been thinned through the power of solitude, they truly dissolve away.
These are being experienced; from Agavarā, the best of mountains, skillfully and correctly.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes his censure of the mind:

"I have risen here to conquer that enemy, the mind, upon which the great ones have fixed their hope for victory over all virtues. Yet, because it has lost its delight within, I do not welcome its prosperity, which is dull, impure, and vast—just as the moon does not welcome a mass of clouds."
In whatever mind [this] has arisen—that is, become endowed with effort—thus may there be auspiciousness. MT 1.15.27.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 1.15 //
Having thus censured the mind, he now begins the censure of craving:
"By this endless craving, which is like a night of darkness within the heart, rows of owls in the form of faults roam here in the sky of consciousness. (MU 1.16.1)
In the space of volition, that is, the space of the mind, there are defects such as passion and the like; and it is fitting for the owl to roam during the night.
My essence and softness have been consumed by this anxiety, which brings an inner burning; I am being withered by it as a mire is dried up by the heat of the sun.

"Samūḍha" means held; it refers to that [taste] by which there is softness produced by flavor and softness produced by water. Here, "thought" (cintā) should be understood as craving (tṛṣṇā) itself, because craving never ceases to have the nature of thought.
This should be understood similarly in what follows as well.
In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion and empty, the demoness of hope dances wildly and is utterly intoxicated.
Hope is craving.
Dust-like frost has settled upon it, yet it shines with a mass of gold; surely this cluster of Ashoka blossoms is now coming into full bloom within my mind.

"Surely"—this expresses certainty—"my thought, Aśokamañjarī, is coming into full bloom. Of what nature is she? She is one by whom a mist of dullness has been created through passion—that is, greed produced of her own accord. Alternatively, she is one by whom a mist has been produced from *rajas*, meaning pollen. And she is radiant, shining with a collection of gold—that is, a gathering of gold.
And it was as radiant as a heap of gold.
Enough with this craving that devours the inner disposition; it leads only to wandering within, like a wave that has come to the ocean seeking pure splendor.
Within the mind; for delusion, that is, for false knowledge.
Upon the mountain of my body, the river of craving—its form rippled by waves and its roar loud with surging billows—seems to flow.
And as she crosses over, this river of craving—the "Crosser-of-the-Craving-Wave"—is crossed.
Like an old blade of grass driven by a wind, this mind-cataka bird has been led away somewhere by a turbid intellect that has arisen to obstruct its momentum.
One's own momentum; by means of the intellect—that is, by the mind possessed by craving.
Whichever excellence of virtue I have studied and take as my refuge, that very thing craving cuts away for me, like a small mouse gnawing at a string.
"Having studied" means having attained firmness in training; that is to say, "firm."
Like a withered leaf in the water, like a decayed blade of grass in the wind, or like an autumn cloud in the sky, I wander in the whirlpool of anxiety.
In the wheel of thought and in the wheel of craving.
We, whose intellects are powerless, are unable to reach our own true abode; we are bewildered by the snare of anxious thoughts, like birds caught in a net.
One's own abode is the innate station known as the reality of the supreme self.
O dear one, I have been so scorched by the flame called craving that I do not expect its burning to be extinguished even by nectars.
This is clear.
Having gone far, ever further from here, and meeting again and again, the mare of craving, intoxicated, wanders swiftly toward the ends of the quarters.
This is clear.
Craving, which clings to the insentient, causes constant coming and going between the upper and lower realms; agitated and full of knots, it is like the fierce rope of a waterwheel.
"Granthimatī" means possessed of the knots of passion and so forth.
Like a powerful ox led by a rope knotted within its body that is being pulled with frantic haste, so is a person driven by craving.
In the body—that is, in the physical frame—it is carried away, led here and there, by agitation rather than by reason, as it begins to be destroyed, that is, as it starts to perish.
Driven by the constant craving for sons, wives, and kin, Kirātī weaves a net here among the worlds, just as she does among birds.
For it is indeed through sons and the like that people in this world incur bondage within saṃsāra.
Like a dark night, craving terrifies even the wise, blinds even the eye of insight, and exhausts even the joyful.
This is clear.
Crooked, soft to the touch, and signaling the imbalance of poison, craving burns like a black female serpent even when only slightly touched.
This is clear.
Treachery, which creates illusory appearances, is wretched and bestows misfortune; it pierces the hearts of men like the demoness Kṛṣṇā.
Illusion itself is the ailment, the disease; she who produces that is such [a one]. She bestows misfortune and causes discoloration.

O Brahmin, the lute of craving—its strings worn out by thirst—is not radiant in the bliss of Brahman, for it remains coiled within the storehouse of the body, enveloped by a multitude of lethargic strings.

Lassitude consists of despondency regarding sense objects; these are themselves the "strings. Their collection is that which is completely encircled and firmly bound. [This occurs] in bliss—which is the state of resting—and in the drama.
The creeper of the abyss of craving is eternally exceedingly filthy, characterized by bitter madness; it is long, slender, and thick with affection.
Craving itself is the creeper of the abyss, the vine of the chasm.
Bringing no joy, empty, utterly fruitless, and exceedingly haughty; inauspicious and cruel, craving is like a withered flower-cluster.
The cluster of blossoms is withered; the cluster of blossoms is devoid of essence.
Even when the mind has not been won over, craving pursues everything; yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman in love.
Their minds were not won over because of the lack of a pleasant environment, and the hearts of the people remained unsubdued.
In the great dance of saṃsāra, crowded with various sentiments, on the stages of the vast expanse of worlds, craving is the aged dancer.
The various flavors (rasas) consist of forms such as pleasure and so forth, as well as forms such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and so forth.
In the long wilderness of saṃsāra, the poisonous creeper of craving has spread far and wide; it is in full bloom with old age and bears a succession of fruits consisting of falls and rises.
Rūḍhā means having grown or attained sprout-like development.
When she can no longer do so, even then she adopts a dancing gait; devoid of joy, craving dances like an aged actress.
This is clear.
When the mist thickens, light fades upon its arrival; so does the peahen of craving, restless with thirst, set foot amidst the surging floods of suffering.
In the mist of delusion; in the light of knowledge.
The river of craving, thick with dull surges and for long empty within, occasionally attains a momentary swell during the monsoon season.
By "dull waves" (*jaḍakallolaiḥ*), [he means] waves consisting of dullness (*jāḍya*) and also waves of water (*jalakallola*).
Leaving behind that which has perished, it moves from one tree to another; craving goes from person to person like a restless bird.

Craving, having abandoned the man who has perished, approaches another man of a different form, one who stands firm and is endowed with stability. Like what? Like a bird; just as a bird, having left behind a tree that has perished, goes from that perished tree to another tree of a different form that stands firm—so it is.
The meaning.

Though she has already attained her fruit, she seeks further reward; though she is satisfied, she sets foot even upon that which cannot be transgressed; the restless female monkey of craving does not remain in one place for long.
This is clear.
"Having done this, that follows"—all of this is utterly inconsistent; yet craving strives incessantly, like some divine impulse.
*Daivikī* means pertaining to the divine (*daiva*).
In one moment it descends to the netherworld, in another it ascends to the vault of heaven; in a moment it wanders through the bowers of the quarters—such is the bee of craving upon the lotus-heart.
This is clear.
Craving alone is the giver of long-lasting suffering among all the defects of saṃsāra; it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme distress.

The genitive case in "doṣāṇām" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). He explains the state of long-lasting suffering (*dīrghaduḥkhatva*) with the latter half of the verse, beginning with "antahpurastham."
The garland of clouds of craving, dense with the mist of delusion, bestows supreme dullness and obstructs the supreme light.
This is clear.
For all the multitudes of living beings wandering in the cycle of existence, craving is the binding rope that weaves together the garlands of their minds.
This is clear.
Diverse in color, devoid of qualities, long, and existing in a state of impurity; having both empty and non-empty bases, craving possesses the nature of Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
In the case of Indra’s bow [the rainbow], its state of being a locus for impurity should be understood as its having the clouds as its support.
The thunderbolt is to the crops of virtue; autumn, laden with fruit, is a calamity; frost is to the lotus of prosperity; and the long night belongs to the darkness.
What is thirst? It is for calamity; it is for the sake of misfortune. "The fruitful autumn" means the autumn endowed with fruit; the meaning is that it brings about calamity.
She is the actress in the drama of saṃsāra, the female bird dwelling in the body-abode, the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the song of passion.
This is clear.
It is a wave in the ocean of worldly affairs, a chain for the elephant of delusion, as beautiful as the nyagrodha tree at the crossroads, and a moonlight for the night-lotus of suffering.
The meaning is that, like the shade of a banyan tree on a path, it brings about the suffering of transformation (*pariṇāmaduḥkha*).
She is a single jewel-casket for the sufferings of old age and death; she is a woman eternally intoxicated by the charms of mental anguish and physical disease.
A small box or casket.
For a moment craving is pure light, for a moment it is a fragment of darkness; for a moment it is like the path of the sky, and for a moment it is dense with mist.
This is clear.
Let craving go to its pacification for the sake of calming the exertion of activity, just as the thick, black darkness of night subsides for the sake of warding off demons.
That night was for the sake of calming the exertion performed for the sake of duty.
This world remains deluded, mute, and with its inner disposition agitated, for as long as it continues to pursue the cholera-like poison of craving.
*Viṣaviṣūcikā* is a specific type of disease caused by the ingestion of poison.
This entire world abandons all suffering when it is freed from anxiety; indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of anxiety.
Suffering is the nature of anxiety; it is suffering.
Grasping at everything—grass, stones, wood, and so forth—with the suspicion that it is a source of enjoyment, craving throbs within like a female fish in a pond.
This is clear.
The affliction of disease residing in the limbs and the thirst for existence quickly bring even a man of profound depth to the surface, just as the rays of the sun cause a lotus to rise.
"Uttānatām" means having open palms; that is to say, the state of being a beggar.
Oh, how truly wonderful! Even those of great intelligence cut through craving—which is so difficult to sever—with the stainless sword of discernment.
This is clear.
Neither the edge of a sword, nor a vajra-fire, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron are so sharp as this craving, O Brahmin, which dwells within the heart.
This is clear.
Dark as collyrium with sharp tips, dependent on wicks long with oil, luminous yet painful to touch—cravings are like the flames of a lamp.
And they are black as collyrium and sharp-pointed; "sneha" means passion and oil; "daśā" means state and the wick of a lamp.
Even the wisest man, even the hero, even the steadfast one—even the best of men—craving alone can reduce to a mere blade of grass in the blink of an eye.
"Tṛṇīkaroti" means he treats as lightly as a blade of grass; it signifies making something insignificant.
The great Vindhya forest of craving is vast and dense, terrifying, composed of masses of clouds and dust, and filled with blinding darkness and fierce mist.

And it is vast and dense; on the side of the great Vindhya forest, it is that whose expanses are thickets. "It" (sā) refers to this: it is thick because of its binding nature and is like a net. Such as it is, it is composed of dust and consists of the quality of *rajas*;
on the side of the forest, it is pervaded by a mass of clouds and by dust. It is shrouded in darkness, joined with the blindness of ignorance, and filled with fierce mist.
It is characterized by intense delusion.
He concludes the censure of craving with this final verse of the chapter:

Craving alone, having found its mark within all the worlds, yet remaining difficult to perceive, stands as if right before one; it abides in the world which is like a mass of shimmering waves, just as the power of sweetness resides in the waters of the milk-ocean.
The sense is that it has become impossible to perceive because of its absolute non-existence. *Madhurā śaktiḥ* refers to the quality (*guṇa*) known as sweetness (*mādhurya*). Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus censured craving, he begins the censure of the body:
"The body—dense with the strings of moist intestines, subject to transformation, and full of torment—throbs within saṃsāra; even that [body] leads only to suffering. (MU 1.17.1)
The *ārdrā* [constellation] is moist with blood; that which consists of the cords of the intestines is dense and difficult to traverse; it is subject to transformation and possessed of disease.
He further qualifies the body in detail:
"Though ignorant, it is like one who knows; though its self-experience is folded [inward], it is capable through reasoning; yet it is not fit for me, being neither insentient nor conscious."

Though ignorant and insentient like a stone, he appears as a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and is thus similar to one who knows that [Reality]. "Obstructed" means that the wonder of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is veiled by the very notion of "I-ness" regarding the body. "By means of reasoning" refers to reasoning in the form of yoga and so forth. Though "fortunate" (*bhavya*), meaning excellent because he is a means to liberation, he is "unfortunate" (*abhavya*) from my perspective—that is, unfortunate according to my view.
Hesitating between the views of the insentient and the sentient, one whose mind is wavering with false expectations is neither a man of discernment nor a fool; he merely yields to delusion.

The meaning is that if it were insentient (*jaḍatva*), it would not be the locus of activity like a stone; if it were non-insentient (*ajaḍatva*), it could not become an object of perception (*grāhyatā*).
With the slightest thing one attains joy, and with the slightest thing one falls into distress; there is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue.
For the base person attains joy with very little, and likewise falls into distress.
He is perpetually adorned by a smile that comes and goes, possessing beautiful filaments of teeth, and blossoming like a flower at every moment.
This is clear.

With the multitude of his arms as its branches, well-supported by the pillars of his teeth, overspread by the forest of the bees of his eyes, and possessing the great fruit of his head as its pedestal;
This is clear.
With streams of flowing tears for its sap-courses, hands and feet for its beautiful sprouts, possessing ankles, it is the dwelling place for the birds that are the collection of bodily functions.
It is a vast and extensive abode for the birds that are the aggregates of effects.

This tree of the body, possessing its own shadow, is a resting place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings; to whom does it belong as one's own, and to whom is it another? For what reliance or non-reliance can there possibly be here?
The meaning is that, regarding what is possible and what is impossible, equanimity alone is appropriate here.
When the boat and the body-creeper are both grasped again and again for the purpose of crossing over the burden, for whom could there be the notion of a self?
In the case of the body, it is for the purpose of crossing over the burden; that is, for the sake of bringing an end to the burden of saṃsāra, for indeed, without the body, saṃsāra perishes.
In this empty forest called the body, crowded with many pits and filled with countless trees that are its hairs—who can find confidence therein?
The sense objects here are like pits.
In this firm body-drum, covered with skin, sinews, and bones, I do not remain within it—uninterrupted by its sound—any more than a cat does.
The sinews are the subtle channels within the drum; for a cat does not remain there.
Grown within the forest of saṃsāra, the monkey of the flickering mind takes the form of a *cintāmaṇi* blossom, yet it is gnawed by the woodworm of long-standing suffering.
This glorious tree has craving for its body, anger for its abode of crows, smiles for its flowers, and the great fruits of good and evil.
With his trunk as a sturdy stem, his web of arms as a cluster of creepers, and his hands as beautiful blossoms, all the sprouts of his limbs were set in motion by the wind.

He is the support for all the birds of the senses, with well-formed knees, beautiful skin, and a prominent stature; he is endowed with a luster full of vitality and is frequented by travelers in the form of desire.
Upon its head was a long row of hair like blades of grass, and its hollow interior served as a nest for the aged vultures of egoism.
With the root of the web of latent tendencies severed, this tree of my body has become weak and has ceased its exertion; it brings me no pleasure.
The very ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is the vulture. That which is its nest-like hollow or cavity is what it has in its belly;

such is it. Its form is weak and flaccid. For the body, once seized by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the sense of "I," indeed becomes firm in form. It is that which perishes through exertion and impact. This is a *kulaka* (a group of verses).
O Sage, this body is the great house for one who dwells within the home of the ego; whether it rolls about or attains stability, what does that matter to me?
For it is not fitting that pleasure or pain should arise from the plundering or the stability of another's house; such is the meaning.
This house of the body is not desired by me, for its senses are like tethered cattle, its courtyard is the leaping field of craving, and all its limbs are stained with the dust of passion.
By this, it is stated that the body is like a rustic house.
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is a hollow cavity constricted by the friction of wood against bone and wood, and bound together by strings of entrails.
"Wood" refers to the form of wood, namely bone-wood; its "clashing" is its state of being joined together without any gaps.
That which is "narrowed" by this, being constricted on all sides, is such that it has a "cavity. It is [further] characterized by "strings of entrails," meaning cords of intestines.
This house of the body is not pleasing to me: its strings of sinews are stretched out, it is made muddy by the water of blood, and it is whitened by the moss of old age.
This is clear.
I do not desire this house of the body, which maintains its stability by supporting infinite activities through the application of various paints, and which has false delusion as its great pillar.

In various artistic works and manifold activities, those infinite efforts by which it is held fast and filled—such is its structural stability. In the case of the "house," these are the paintings; that [body] has false delusion, which is merely false knowledge, as its great pillar. Indeed, it is by false knowledge alone that the body is sustained.
This house of the body is not desired by me; it resounds with the cries of suffering infants, is charming only with its comfortable beds, and has a maidservant burnt by wicked desires.
The beds themselves are pleasures; by them it is enchanting. He whose wretched servants—the base desires resulting from evil efforts—are destroyed.
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is congested with the vessels and utensils of the multitude of sense-objects rich in impurity, and it is encircled by the brine of ignorance.
The sense organs have objects as their domain; alkali is ashes.
This house of my body is undesirable: it has ankles for its threshold, knees resting upon it, and high pillars for its head; it is very firm with the wood of its long arms.
Gulgulu is the stone that serves as the foundation for the pillar.
O Brahmin, this house of the body is not pleasing to me; its windows are the manifest eyes, its inner courtyard is the dwelling of the playing wisdom, and it has anxiety as its daughter.
This is clear.
