This house of the body is not pleasing to me, for its roof-terrace is the beauty of the ears covered by the thatch of hair, and its portico consists of the very long fingers.
*Channā* means covered or enclosed; *candraśālikā* is a room at the top [of a building]; *niryūha* is a wooden structure projecting outward.
With sprouts of thick body hair growing from every limb like grass upon a wall, and with its seats and vessels utterly empty, this house of my body is not desired by me.
The region of Madhyadeśa is Pīṭhapiṭhira.
This house of my body is undesirable, for its interior resounds with the noise of the wind moving through the hollows of the navel and the throat, producing a whistling sound.
*Nilayāḥ* means abodes; *śāram* means variegated.
This body-house of mine is not desired, for it is filled with the incessant force of winds agitated by inhalation and exhalation, and it is riddled with wide-open windows in the form of the eyes.
Vāta is the vital breath (prāṇavāta).
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is terrifying with the gateway of the mouth overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and its fragments of teeth and bones are visible.
This is clear.
This house of the body, smooth with the plaster of skin, flickering with the movement of its mechanical parts, and excavated by the rat of the mind—this is not desired by me.
That which moves like a machine; by that, it is flickering.
For a moment my body-house shines with the light of the lamp of a smile, beautiful with bliss; for a moment it is pervaded by floods of radiance, yet it is not desired [by me].
This is clear.
This body of mine is an abode for all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, and a forest of the deer of all mental afflictions; it is not desired by me.
All mental anxieties are indeed deer; their forest is this [world].

This forest of the body is undesirable to me; it is treacherous with the agitation of the senses and the constellations, empty, hollow and pithless within, and its heart-thicket is a dense thicket of darkness.
The senses themselves are the bears; their agitation makes [the path] uneven. "Tamas" refers to ignorance as well as darkness.
O Lord of Sages, I am unable to sustain this body-abode, just as one of little strength cannot rescue an elephant sunk in the mud.
The "abode of the body" refers to the house known as the body.
What is the use of prosperity, what of the body, what of honor, and what of worldly effort? In just a few days, Time cuts away everything.
This is clear.
O Sage, tell me: what beauty can there be in this body, composed of blood and flesh, including its interior and exterior, whose sole nature is destruction?
That which has destruction as its sole property is "destruction-only-property-possessor"; [the word] "of that" refers to this.
O dear one, what reliance can a wise person have on those ungrateful bodies which do not follow the life-force at the time of death? Alas! MU_1,17.39.
This is clear.
As long as this body—trembling like the tip of an intoxicated elephant’s ear and fragile as a dangling drop of water—does not abandon me, so long shall I abandon it.
The meaning is that it is because [the object] is not apprehended as being the referent of the notion of "I" (ahantā).
This body-sprout is flickering, stirred by the wind, fragile, withered, thin, and round; it is undesirable, being both harsh and sapless.
It is both slender and round; thus, it is "slender and round" (*tanuvṛtta*).
Having eaten and drunk for a long time—food as delicate as young shoots—it effortlessly falls into emaciation and pursues its own destruction.
At first it attains thinness; thereafter, it pursues destruction without effort.
Indeed, that ordinary body feels no shame as it repeatedly experiences those very same pleasures and pains, consisting of both existence and non-existence.
This is clear.
Having exercised dominion for a very long time and having enjoyed the glory of wealth and power, why is this body maintained, which attains neither height nor stability?
"Kim" means for what purpose; "pālyate" means it is protected or guarded.
O knower of distinctions, at the time of old age the body undergoes decay, and likewise at the time of death it meets its end; this is exactly the same for both the wealthy and the poor.

O you who know the distinction: the body of both the wealthy man and the poor man is exactly the same and without difference; at the time of old age it undergoes old age, and likewise at the time of death it undergoes death. Therefore, the sense is that effort for the sake of providing enjoyment and means for the body is entirely in vain.
Within the belly of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the midst of the cavern of craving, this mute tortoise of a body remains asleep, though it is called "liberated."
*Kacchapa* means a tortoise; *kuharaka* means a cavity or hole.
The many logs of bodies, fit for the single purpose of burning, are carried away like those in the ocean of saṃsāra; do you know even one man among them?

The single object or purpose called "burning" (dahanākhya) is that toward which they are fit; the meaning is that [they are fit] for some [state] based on a living being who has known what is to be known. The locative case in "among them" (*teṣu*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The implication is that others are like cattle.
For the discerning person, there is no purpose whatsoever in this physical body, which is long subject to corruption, unstable, and destined for the fruit of downfall.
By the fruit of falling and the fruit of destruction; for the discerning one who is engaged in self-investigation.
Having thus suddenly reached old age within the mire-filled pits of the bathhouse, it is not known where or how this frog-like body will soon depart.
The body itself is the frog, the *bheka*.
All undertakings are devoid of essence; bodies are like fleeting winds. As they travel along the path of dust, they are not seen here by anyone.
By the path of passion, by the path of greed, and by the path of dust.
O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind as they go is perceived, as is their returning; but such is not known for our body or for the arrow.
The meaning is "belonging to us," that is, related to us.
Fie, fie again and again upon those who place their hopes in the body and those who place their hopes in the maintenance of the world—those who are intoxicated by the wine of delusion!
This is clear.
"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; this [body] is not I, nor am I it"—those whose minds rest thus in peace, O Sage, are the supreme among men.
I am thus, in that same way; this body is not I.
Abounding in honor and dishonor, and delightful through abundant gain, those who perceive only faults destroy a man whose attachment is bound solely to the body.
The perceptions of faults consist of passion and so forth; their state of being delightful due to abundant gain is to be understood as occurring only at first sight.
We have been deceived by the guile of the demoness of egoism, who dwells in close contact with the body and possesses a delicate form.
Alternatively, the reading is "śarīrotsaṅge" (on the lap of the body).
Alas, this wretched wisdom alone has been deceived by this cruel eye of false knowledge, which is bound to the body with a firm attachment! MU 1.17.56
For a rākṣasī deceives only one person at a time.
That self-destructive person possesses not even a trace of truth; it is a marvel that he deceives the people with his burnt body.
"Any means of deception" refers to any object whatsoever by which one is deceived or cheated.
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away without effort, just like a drop of water from a mountain stream.
This is clear.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble upon the ocean; it flickers fruitlessly and without result amidst the turning of worldly affairs.
In this cycle of existence where actions revolve.
O twice-born one, I have no reliance for even a moment upon this body—a city arisen from dreams and delusion, a transformation of false knowledge, and one whose destruction is most evident.
"In a city produced by a dream-delusion" means in a city equal to one seen in a dream-delusion.
He who has determined stability in lightning, in autumnal clouds, and in cities of the Gandharvas—that man places his trust in physical combat.
He trusts; he places his confidence.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes the censure of the body:

"Having cast aside like a blade of grass this wretched body—which is full of every defect, which triumphs over the succession of ever-perishing activities, and which has achieved victory through deceitful ways—I now abide in happiness."

That which possesses victory over those successions of actions that are constantly fragile—meaning, that which accomplishes such fragile successions of actions—is [the subject]. Therefore, it has achieved victory over deceitful conducts, that is, over contemptible activities. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 1.17 //
Having thus offered this censure of the body, he now introduces the censure of childhood, which constitutes its first stage:
"Even after obtaining birth in the ocean of saṃsāra, whose waves are the burdens of worldly activity and whose form is flickering, childhood leads only to suffering. (MU 1.18.1)
This is clear.
He explains that very suffering caused by it in detail:
"Incapacity, calamity, thirst, muteness, dull-wittedness, greed, restlessness, and wretchedness—all these prevail in childhood. (MU 1.18.2)
This is clear.
In states that are fierce with anger and weeping, and shattered by wretchedness,
childhood is a bondage, like a tethering post for female elephants.
In the phrase "in the ten states" (*daśāsu*), the locative case denotes a locus of experience (*vaiṣayika-ādhāra*). That in which one is bound is called "bondage" (*bandhana*).
Those anxieties which do not tear at the heart during childhood—neither in death, nor in old age and disease, nor in misfortune, nor even in youth—do not exist.
Old age itself is the disease; thus, "the disease of old age. In that [disease].
The undertaking of animal births is despised by all; the fickle conduct of the foolish brings suffering even beyond death.
He whose undertaking is like that of the animal species; the meaning is that his undertaking is equal to that of the class of beasts.
To whom can youth—merely a fragile reflection of dense ignorance consisting of various volitions, with the mind cut down and shattered—bring happiness?

Of what nature is childhood? It is that in which the mind is torn asunder, shattered, and utterly fickle; such is its state. It is a reflection—that is, an illustration—of those possessed of dense ignorance and extreme dullness.
In childhood, when one is constantly terrified at every step by the dull darkness of ignorance, what calamity could there be that would cause such fear through the intellect?
Fear is created by the intellect; fear does not exist in anything whatsoever—such is existence.
O you of evil intent, through playful diversions, wicked amusements, and base desires, the fool incurs supreme delusion and powerful calamity.
In a base mind characterized by evil intent; what kind of delusion? That which arises because of a powerful calamity—such is it.
Childhood, with its onset muddled by conceptual constructions, its difficult playfulness, and its precarious foundation, serves only to discipline a person, not to bring peace.
For the sake of instruction and for the sake of killing; for the sake of peace and for the sake of happiness.
Whatever faults, whatever misconducts, whatever evil courses, and whatever wicked anxieties there may be—all these reside in childhood, like owls in a ruined dwelling.
The *kauśikas* are owls.
O Brahmin, may those foolish men of ruined intellect—who, with their minds clouded by vain thoughts, declare that childhood is delightful—be cursed!
This is clear.
Where the restless mind flickers among its fluctuations, how could even the sovereignty over the three worlds bring satisfaction there?
It bears—that is, it exercises power over—both the sovereignty of the three worlds and that which consists of the sovereignty of the three worlds.
O Sage, for all sentient beings indeed, in all conditions whatsoever, the mind attains a state of flickering instability that is tenfold greater in childhood.
The word "tu" (but) is to be supplied [in the verse]. O Sage, in childhood, however, the mind attains a tenfold degree of fickleness.
The mind is restless by its very nature, and youth is the worst form of restlessness; O dear one, when these two are joined together, by what means can there be an end to this wicked fickleness?

"Moving" means the best or most excellent; that is to say, "moving excessively. O dear one! When those two—the mind and childhood—are joined together, by what means whatsoever could there be an end, an internal conclusion, to the fickleness of the breasts? The meaning is: by no means at all.
O Brahmin, women’s eyes have learned fickleness from masses of lightning, garlands of flames, and waves—or perhaps from the mind during childhood.
The sense is that childhood is more fleeting even than the glances of women and the like.
Indeed, both childhood and the mind, in all their various states, are seen to be constantly unstable in their condition, like two brothers.
Of fragile existence and unstable existence.
All malevolent spirits, all defects, and all evil intentions subsist upon childhood alone, just as men depend upon one who possesses wealth.
Those of evil intent are harsh; they live off others and depend upon them.
If a child does not obtain something new and delightful every day, he falls into a swoon from the onset of poison.
A thing that is ever-new, ever-new, fresh, and ever-fresh.
With a little he comes under control, and with a little he undergoes change; like a dog, the fool delights only in what is impure.
This is clear.
With a face constantly streaming with tears, his inner being numbed within the mire, the child resembles a parched plot of land drenched by rain.
"Within the mud" means in the midst of the mud. "One whose disposition is dull" refers to such a person. Even a parched spot drenched by rain becomes exactly like this.
Devoted to fear and food, wretched, and longing for whatever is seen, the child possesses a fickle intellect and a body that serves only for suffering.
This is clear.
Failing to obtain the things desired by his own imagination, the weak-minded fool suffers in misery, as if his heart were being cut away.
This is clear.
O Sage, those sufferings of a fool—whose aims are difficult to attain and whose many factions are fierce—belong to no one else.

By those [arrows] which have found their mark—that is, their target or foothold—through wicked intentions (*durīhā*) consisting of evil deeds performed by them; which are formidable and harsh due to the numerous factions or their own groups;
here, the comparison to arrows is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The fool is constantly tormented by his mind—which, like a powerful horse, sports according to its whims—just as a forest glade is scorched by the summer heat.
Regarding "aśvena": here the reading is "aśva eva".
A youth who has entered the house of learning undergoes supreme torment, like a lordly elephant in its tethering post, terrified by the harshness of poison.
This is clear.
Consisting of various desires, this false conceptualization born of imagination—the childish state with its fragile disposition—leads to suffering that is exceedingly long-lasting.
That [night] was such that its inner disposition was soft and dull.
How could that foolishness which desires to eat frost and seize the moon from the sky lead to happiness? (MU 1.18.27)
"Sambhṛṣṭam" means roasted or fried.
O one of great intelligence, what difference is there between an insentient stone, which is incapable of warding off cold and heat, and a young tree?
This refers to the consciousness within the body, but not to the expanded consciousness; "consciousness" here means the cognition of cold and heat.
Devoted to hunger, they desire to fly up with their two wings; children, whose nature is like that of birds, are constantly intent on fear and food.
Those who are intent on fear and food are "fear-and-food-obsessed."
In childhood there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father; fear of people and of elder children—childhood is a temple of fear.
For it has been stated that "the elder fool indeed overcomes the younger fool," and thus [it is said] "and from the elder fool."
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes the censure of childhood:

"O Great Sage, in this world, there is no one for whom childhood—which has its intentions thwarted by every state of defect and which even those who revel in lack of discernment take as their refuge—can provide sufficient satisfaction. (MU 1.18.31)

Lack of discernment alone is the playful one; its refuge is its home—meaning it is the abode of non-discernment. The word "api" (also/even) is for the purpose of completing the meter. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the eighteenth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus censured childhood, he now introduces the censure of youth as it follows in sequence:
"Then, having abandoned the misfortunes of childhood, a man with a corrupted disposition ascends to youth, which leads to a fall like the precipice of a chasm. (MU 1.19.1)
That which possesses agitation like that of a precipice; and here, "fall" should be understood as the onset of old age.
He explains the relevant scriptural passage in detail:
"There, following the fluctuations of his own restless mind which possesses infinite playfulness, the dull-witted one goes from suffering to further suffering. (MU 1.19.2)
He is dull-witted, not a man of knowledge.
Helpless, one is overwhelmed by the demoness of desire, which dwells within the cavity of one's own mind and causes manifold agitation, acting with sheer force.
The word "therein" (tatra), which appears in the preceding verse, should also be understood as carrying over here.
Like a son [to his mother], he helplessly delivers his mind to thoughts that are as fickle in their movements as women on all sides, just as one hands over a flame.

The summary meaning is this: just as a man in his youth devotes his mind to young women, so too does he devote his mind to anxieties concerning the maintenance of his family and other such matters. "Who is like? means "like a young child"; the sense is that just as a child devotes its mind to flames, so [does the adult] devote his mind to anxieties.
Those various faults, difficult to undertake, utterly ravage that youth who possesses such an intention; O Sage, they are not even visible to him.
They plunder—that is, they deprive of rest—a man who is young and possessed by youth. Who are "they"?
O Sage, they are those faults of yours which are not seen at all; the meaning is that you have emerged from them.
Alternatively, it should be construed as: those faults are not seen by anyone else either.
Those people who have not been destroyed by youth—which acts as the seed of the great hells and causes one to wander incessantly—have indeed been destroyed; they cannot be destroyed by anything else.
This is clear.
He who has crossed the terrifying realm of youth—which consists of various passions and is filled with a multitude of mental fluctuations—is called steadfast.
This is clear.
Youth, with its form flashing for but a moment, with the thundering of restless clouds, and with the constant glare of lightning—this does not please me.
This is clear.
Abounding in various whirlpools, mired in mud, with a dull depth, and terrifyingly treacherous with its breaking waves—I find no pleasure in this youth of mine.
The whirlpools are the impulses of desire; "mired in the mud" means seized by evil; "dull" refers to the disposition within which [these exist]—such is it.
Youth, which leads all men and is charming for but a moment, does not please me; it resembles a city of the Gandharvas.
The singular number in "of every person" (*sarvasya puṃsaḥ*) is used in the sense of a genus; the meaning is that it is the foremost and non-deviating [cognition].
Indeed, youth—which lasts no longer than the flight of an arrow, which offers pleasure while shining with suffering, and which constantly brings the defect of burning—does not please me.
"Only the distance of an arrow's flight" means for only a moment.
Sweet, delicious, and bitter, yet corrupting and a mere ornament to the vices, this youth of mine—resembling the surging waves of wine—is not pleasing to me.
Sweet at first, bitter in its after-effect.
Unreality appearing as reality, which soon brings about deception—youth, which is like union with a woman in a dream, does not please me.
This is clear.
Flickering like a flash of lightning in an instant, falsely constructed as a cycle, and resembling a whirling firebrand—this youth of mine does not please me.
This is clear.
Tender at first, then expanding and vast, yet empty within and destroyed in an instant—this youth of mine, resembling an autumn cloud, does not please me.
This is clear.
Youth does not please me; it is delightful only at first sight, its inner nature is devoid of true reality, and it resembles union with a courtesan.
Existence, beingness, and affection.
Whatever evil undertakings there may be, they all bring about every kind of suffering; they manifest in youth just as great portents appear at the end of an eon.
This is clear.
Even the Blessed One fears the night of youth, which creates a darkness within the heart and possesses a terrifying form.

"Hārda" means pertaining to the heart; "she who creates darkness" refers to such [a woman]. The Blessed One is Śrī Mahādeva. The intention of the word "api" (even/also) is to imply: "What need is there to mention others? // MT_1,19.18 //
This delusion of youth causes one to utterly forget virtuous conduct, brings about a failure of the intellect, and bestows excessive confusion.
That in which virtuous conduct has been utterly forgotten.
In youth, a living being is consumed by the unassailable fire born of separation from a beloved within the heart, just as a tree is consumed by a forest fire.
By the unassailable fire of desire, which is difficult to restrain.
For even a mind that is expansive, serene, and pure may become turbid in youth, just as a river becomes so during the rainy season.
This is clear.
A river, fearsome with its dense, surging waves, can be dammed; but not so the thirst that agitates the inner self, flickering with the restlessness of youth.
By this [verse], "tāruṇyataralety," it should be understood that this is a censure of youth.
"She was my beloved; those were her full breasts; those were her charms; that was her face; that was youth"—through such reflections, a person falls into a state of decay.
In youth, in the prime of life.
In this world, the virtuous honor a young man who is afflicted by ever-surging thirst; they do not honor one whose desire is trivial, like a mere fragment of withered grass.
"Tarantī" means moving restlessly; "yā taralā" refers to craving (tṛṣṇā); by that [craving], one is "ārta," meaning distressed or wretched.
Indeed, youth is the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of pride—that which is blinded by intoxication and wears the pearls of its own faults—leading only to its destruction.
The "faults" (doṣāḥ) are passion and the like. "Pride itself" (abhimāna eva) is the "great elephant" (mahebha); [the genitive] refers to that [elephant].
Youth is a fresh forest for trees whose roots are the vastness of the mind, which harbor the venomous serpents of faults, and whose trunks are anger and weeping.
Those very tears shed out of anger became trees; [he stands] among them.
Know youth to be a lotus flower: crowded with the filaments of passion, filled with the petals of evil conceptualizations, and frequented by the bees of wicked thoughts.

Youth is the lotus; the objects of enjoyment are but evil thoughts, indeed bad reflections. Know—that is, understand—that the bees are the [bees] themselves, and their support is the lotus. Of what nature is it? Its filaments are the stamens, which are the flavors—the tastes of sensory objects—and it is crowded, that is, congested, by them. Likewise, wrong conceptualizations are merely base, corrupt thoughts.
The petals; by them it was crowded and filled to overflowing.
Fresh youth is the abode of the birds of mental and physical afflictions, which frequent the shores of the lake of the heart and possess both formed and unformed wings.

"Done and not done" refers precisely to what is prescribed and what is not prescribed. For those who possess such "bad sides," even that which is prescribed is called "done and not done" because it causes one to deviate from the purity and impurity known as Dharma.
The ocean, whose playful waves are insentient and beyond counting, has reached its full youth, disregarding all boundaries.
"Having disregarded the boundary" means being devoid of restraint.
Then, the uneven wind of youth stands ready to remove the dust from all the leaves of virtue in order to strip them away.

He stands ready to remove everything, having the nature of removing all things. He is pervaded by *rajas*, meaning by the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*) as well as by dust. From that, the uneven wind of youth becomes skillful in removing—that is, in casting far away—all the leaves of the qualities.
The fierce winds of the hands of women in agitation turn the face pale; the harsh dust of youth ascends to the highest peak.
"Ākula" means restless or agitated. "Avakara" refers to rubbish; that is to say, dust gathered by a broom. Like that, they are "utkaṭāḥ," meaning prominent or formidable.
The exuberance of youth in men awakens a multitude of faults, cuts short the series of virtues, and is the very playfulness of the fortune of evil deeds.
This is clear.
Having bound the flickering bee of the mind to the pollen of the lotus-body, this moon of youth deludes man.
The meaning is that, solely by the power of youth, a person becomes attached to the body.
The lovely creeper of youth, sprouting from the thicket of the body, intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has attached itself and reached its full growth.
This is clear.
The deer of the mind, rushing toward youth—which arises from the heat of the body's vital winds and is but a mirage—fall into the treacherous forest.
The body itself is a desert; therein, the uneven forest consisting of objects such as women—which arises from the heat of the body—is a wilderness of suffering born of that bodily heat.
Youth does not please me—it is the moonlight for the night of the body, the mane of the lion of the mind, and the wave of the ocean of life.
This is clear.
This autumn of youth has borne fruit within the wilderness of this body for only a few days; indeed, you ought not to place your trust in it.
*Phalitā* means endowed with fruits such as the fullness of beauty and so forth.
In an instant, this bird of youthfulness flies away from the body of one with little fortune, just as a wish-fulfilling gem slips from the hand in a moment.
This is clear.
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, the passionate desires leap up, leading only to destruction.
"Sarasāḥ" means full of the flavor of sense objects; "kāmāḥ" means desires.
The female demons of passion and hatred continue to dance about for just as long as the night of youth has not yet come to an end.
This is clear.
Exercise compassion toward youth, which is full of various duties, wretched, and perishing in an instant, as if it were a dying son.
This is clear.
That greatly deluded man who, out of delusion, experiences joy because of youth—which is subject to momentary destruction—is indeed known as a "human deer."
This is clear.
The person of very poor intellect who desires youth, which is intoxicated by pride, delusion, and passion, will before long be joined with remorse.
The meaning is: by means of remorse, which brings about the destruction of that [fault].
They alone are righteous, they alone are great-souled, and they alone are true men on this earth, O virtuous one, who have happily crossed over the perilous strait of youth.
This is clear.
The ocean, though filled with formidable sea-monsters, can be crossed with ease; but one’s flawed youth, shimmering like a forest of surging waves, cannot.
This is clear.
He concludes the censure of youth with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O dear one, such excellent youth—adorned with discipline, the abode of noble people, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues—is indeed rare in this world, like a forest situated in the sky. (MU 1.19.46)
The sense is that such youth is indeed praiseworthy. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the nineteenth canto in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrī Mokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus completed the censure of youth, he introduces the censure of women by way of that same context:
"In this puppet of flesh, within a cage of limbs set in motion by machinery, adorned with sinews, bones, and joints—what in a woman can truly be beautiful? (MU 1.20.1)
In that cage of limbs which is as fickle as a mechanical doll—wherein even the doll itself is situated by means of a mechanism—nothing at all of a woman is beautiful.
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears, look closely with your eyes; if it is still pleasing, then why do you delude yourself in vain?
This is an illustration of all the limbs.
"Here are the hairs, here is the blood"—such is this body of a woman; what can a person of vast resolve do with it once it has been thus reviled?
The meaning is that it is not fitting for one of vast intention to find delight in this.
Those very limbs of all embodied beings, which were repeatedly cherished with garments and ointments, are now being torn apart by flesh-eating scavengers.
Therefore, the sense is that even for women, the flesh-eaters will tear them apart.
Upon her breast, pearls were seen that bore a resemblance to the surging current of the Gaṅgā as it flashes upon the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks.
In cremation grounds or at the ends of the horizon, that very same breast of a woman is at another time devoured by dogs like a small morsel of food.
This is clear. [This concludes] the pair.
Just as the limbs of a camel in the forest are smeared with blood, flesh, and other filth, so too are the limbs of a passionate woman; for what attachment can there be even toward her?
This is clear.
The mere quality of being pleasant at first sight is attributed to a woman; O Sage, I believe that even this does not exist here, for she is the sole cause of delusion.
In this female body.
What distinction is there here between intoxicating liquor, which bestows expansive joy after first agitating one's senses, and a woman who brings about transformation?
The word "madirāyāḥ" is in the ablative case.
O Sage, the elephants of human beings, tethered to the hitching post of the tongue, do not attain awakening even with the long goads of tranquility.
This is clear.
Women, who bear hair like soot and are by nature always sharp, burn a man like straw, being as it were the flames of the fire of his own misdeeds.
This is clear.
They are to be revered, they are great-souled ones, and they alone are true men on this earth, O virtuous one, who have easily crossed over the perilous strait of youth.
From the peril of youth, which is termed a multitude of women.
For women, though they burn even from afar and though they are full of moisture, are dry; they are both beautiful wood and terrible fuel for the fires of hell.
"Even women, though full of sap, become wood devoid of sap"—this is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
Her dark tresses were scattered like thick darkness, her eyes were like shimmering stars, her face was like the orb of the full moon, and she smiled like a cluster of night-lotuses.
With men agitated by her playful charms, she effects the destruction of their undertakings; she is a supreme deluder of the intellect, a passionate woman who makes the night seem long.
This is clear.
Delightful and sweet with flowers, graceful with her hands like tender shoots, rich in the playful movements of her creeper-like brows, and bearing clusters of blossoms as her breasts; MU_1,20.16.
The beloved and great poisonous creeper, her limbs as fair as the filaments of a flower and intent on slaying men, bestows supreme helplessness.
This is clear.
By the mere sound of her sighs and panting, the lover is drawn out by his beloved who longs to crush the serpent, just as a female elephant draws a snake from its hole.
"Bhujaṅgas" refers to both libertines and serpents; "uddhriyate" means it is drawn out or pulled up.
Women are the snares for binding the limbs of those bird-like men whose minds are deluded; they are scattered by the hunter named Desire.
This is clear.
O Brahmin, the elephant of the mind, intoxicated with passion, remains bound like a mute by the chain of *rati* within the vast tethering post of the *lalanā*.
This is clear.

For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, with the waters of their karma dwelling in the hollows of their actions, woman is the baited hook on the line of their difficult-to-eradicate latent tendencies.
For indeed, a lump of food and the like is placed on a hook for the purpose of catching fish.
Beautiful-eyed women are the tethering post for men, just as a manger is for horses and a hitching post is for elephants; they are the binding, like a lotus-stalk for bees.
This is clear.
O Sage, this variegated realm of enjoyment, consisting of manifold flavors, has attained its supreme state here by depending upon women.
This is clear.
May I always have enough of this woman, who is a casket for all the jewels of faults and a chain of suffering.
Let it be enough; let it be far away.
What use have I for the breast, or for the eyes, or for the hips, or for the brows—this mere substance of flesh, which is in itself no real thing?
This is clear.
O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin—here her flesh, there her blood, and here her bones.
The word "iti" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
O Sage, those women who were cherished by their husbands with soft cotton pillows now sleep upon the ground of their ancestors, their limbs exposed.
With soft, non-harsh cotton products—that is, with beds made of cotton—[they lie] in their ancestral lands, that is, in the cremation grounds.
O Brahmin, that face upon which a lover has fashioned thick, fresh affection and the beauty of leaf-like sprouts withers away in the wilderness.
That in which there is fresh, thick affection; this is an adverbial modifier.
The hair becomes like the bristles of a fly-whisk upon the trees of the cremation ground, and within days, the bones shine like stars upon the circle of the earth.
"In days" means in a very short time.
The dust particles drink the blood, and many carnivorous creatures devour it; the flames of the fire consume the skin, and the vital breaths depart into the sky.
Thus, I have described to you this imminent state of the limbs of women; why do you pursue such delusion?
This is clear.

How indeed could one endowed with intelligence [not understand] that this [channel], called lalanā, which has the configuration resulting from the conjunction of the five elements, conveys [the essence] from the rasa? MU 1.20.32.

The "conjunction" (saṅghaṭṭa) is the coming together of the five elements; its "configuration" (saṃsthāna) is a specific arrangement. "From desire" (rasāt) means from longing. "May it carry forth" (abhivahatu) means may it follow after.
The anxiety that follows after a beloved woman becomes a dense thicket with spreading branches, abounding in bitter and sour fruits, and reaches a towering height through its extensive growth.

*Vitānam* means a multitude. By *pratānaiḥ*, meaning by the secondary branches (*upaśākhābhiḥ*). *Uttālatām* refers to that state of being prominent or intense. *Kāntānusāriṇī* means directed toward the beloved. The sense is that the thought following after the beloved becomes exceedingly dense.
A young man devoted to a young woman reaches a state of supreme pitiability, like an elephant bound in a pit in the Vindhya mountains out of greed for a female elephant.
This is clear.

He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, there is no ground for enjoyment. Having abandoned the woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy.
Regarding enjoyments in the form of women and so forth; "the ground of enjoyment" refers to the desire for enjoyment.
He concludes the censure of women with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O Brahmin, I do not take delight in enjoyments that are sweet only for a moment yet difficult to transcend, fragile as the wings of a bee; out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I seek peace and shall clearly enter the forest with diligence. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the twentieth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Having thus delivered this incidental censure of women, he introduces the censure of old age as it pertains to the present context: "Indeed, childhood is insufficient; youth drinks up childhood, and old age follows after youth. Behold their mutual harshness! (MU 1.21.1)
He drinks; he swallows.
Just as a thunderbolt destroys a lotus, as a whirlwind disperses an autumnal cloud, and as a river erodes a tree on its bank, so does old age wither the body.
It causes decay; it leads to a state of decrepitude.
Women regard with equanimity a man whose limbs are all slack and long, and whose body is decayed by old age, just as they would a young camel.
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction.
When people are seized by old age, which torments them with labored breathing and exhaustion, their wisdom flees away like a woman who has fled from a rival wife who has struck her down.
By her who thus torments [him] with labored breathing and exhaustion.
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends alike laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman.
This is clear.
For greed approaches old age—old age that is witless, decrepit, wretched, and deficient in virtues and prowess—just as a vulture approaches a tree that is not yet full-grown.
In old age, a long-standing longing—consisting of the defect of wretchedness, burning within the heart, and the sole companion of all calamities—increases.
"Long from the beginning" means long throughout. "Gardha" means greed. "Abhyeti" means it resorts to. "Vṛddhatām" means old age. This is a pair [of verses].
"What painful and most terrible deed must I perform for the sake of the next world? Indeed, in old age, grows a fear that is impossible to remedy."
This is clear.
"What am I, this wretch? What indeed can I do, or how shall I remain? I shall simply maintain silence"—such is the dejection that arises in old age.
This is clear.
Longing arises with eager delight, yet it is impossible to enjoy; indeed, the heart is consumed by the wretchedness of one's lack of power in old age.
*Gardhaḥ* means greed for enjoyment; *sollāsam* is an adverbial modifier of the action.

As long as the old female crane, worn out by age and emitting the croaking sounds of coughing, cries out while perched upon the top of the tree of the body, which is infested with the serpents of disease; so long [does one remain].
Just then, O Sage, the owl of Death, desiring the thick darkness of night, was seen arriving swiftly from somewhere or other.
Cough is a specific type of disease.
Just as darkness pursues the twilight as soon as it has arisen, so does old age, upon seeing the body, pursue death.
This is clear.
O Brahmin, as soon as she sees from afar the tree of the body in full bloom with old age, the bee of death approaches the man swiftly and with great eagerness.
She was exceedingly eager, truly eager.
An empty city appears; a tree with its branches lopped off appears; a region suffering from drought appears; but a body worn out by old age does not appear [as such].
The meaning is that even compared to things such as empty cities, old age is indeed the ultimate impurity.
Like a vulture seizing its prey, old age swiftly devours a man, causing him to cough as if to swallow him whole in a single moment.
This is clear.
Upon seeing it, as if eager, old age seizes the body instantly by the head and shatters it in a moment, just as a maiden plucks a white water-lily.
This is clear.
Making a whistling sound, this wind, harsh with dust, wears away this body—already worn out—as a gale wears down the tender leaf of a tree.
This is old age. A person seized by old age and seized by wind makes a whistling sound.
The body, struck by old age and having reached a state of decay, bears the beauty of a withered lotus strewn over with a mass of frost.
This is clear.
Like the rising moonlight of old age upon the peaks of the mountain of my head, this [breath] causes the night-lily of coughing—already agitated by wind—to blossom.
"Saṃrabdha" means "commenced"; it refers to that [fever] by which wind (vāta) or a wind-disease is initiated. That [is what is meant]. //MT_1,21.20//
Having observed that the gourd-like head of a man has ripened and is withered by the caustic of old age, Time, it is said, devours it as its master.
The head is indeed the *kuṣmāṇḍaka*, a particular kind of fruit.
The daughter of Jahnu, exerted by old age, swiftly cuts away the roots of this body, which is like a tree on a riverbank, while its life-span is still unstable.
"Exerted" means engaged. "Roots of lifespan" refers to the roots designated as lifespan.
The old cat, inflamed by the mouse of youth that has been devoured, attains supreme exhilaration, greedy for the flesh of the body.
This is clear.
There is nothing in this world so inauspicious as this female jackal born of the body that howls with the cry of old age.
This is clear.

This flame of old age blazes forth, consisting of the smoke and darkness of suffering, accompanied by coughing, labored breathing, and whistling sounds; indeed, by it, this [body] is utterly consumed.
He is old.
O dear one, through old age the slender body of men becomes crooked, like a flowering creeper bent low with its white-limbed shoots.
This is clear.
O Sage, the elephant of death surely uproots in an instant the camphor-tree of the body, which is as white as aged camphor.
This is clear.
O Sage, as King Death approaches, with old age as his white fly-whisk, his army of personal afflictions and diseases marches ahead.
This is clear.
O Sage, behold those who were not conquered by enemies in battle—those who crushed the peaks of mountains—have now been swiftly defeated by this old, decrepit Rākṣasī!
This is clear.
Within the interior of the body-dwelling, white with the frost of old age, the infant senses are not able to stir even slightly.
The "akṣa-children" are the young children of the sense faculties.
Upon this body-staff, which has reached the pinnacle of this fragrant chamber of the wandering through saṃsāra, the beauty of the fly-whisk named "Old Age" shines resplendently.
A fly-whisk is placed upon the top of the *gandhakuṭī*; or rather, there is a reading as *ghaṭakuṭī*.
O Sage, while the city of the body remains white with the rising moon of old age, the night-lotus of death blooms in an instant.
This is clear.
Within the inner apartments of the body, which are white with the plaster of old age, women dwell happily in a state of incapacity, mental anguish, and suffering.
This is clear.
O Sage, where there is abundance at first yet old age eventually overcomes living beings, what consolation can there be here for me, of dull intellect?
Before death, which is non-existence, there is attachment.
He concludes the censure of old age with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Of what use is that miserable life held in such a poor grasp, since one lives even after reaching old age? For old age, O dear one, when it has conquered men in this world, strips away all their desires."

By that well-known, evil-grasping [condition] called a contemptible life—a wicked seizure—even when one has reached old age, what is lived for? For what purpose is one lived? That is to say, one lives in vain. Indeed (*hi*) is used for certainty.
O father (*tāta*), because (*yad yasmāt*) in this world (*jagatyām jagati*), unconquered old age [destroys] all the desires of men.
It overcomes the activities; it leads [one] away. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-first canto in the section on Detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus offered this censure of old age, he now introduces a censure of time:
"By those of small intellect, through various distinctions imagined by the fire of conceptual construction, the delusive wandering of saṃsāra has been led to its present state. (MU 1.22.1)

By what kind of divisions? By manifold (analpam) conceptual constructions (vikalpa-kalpanābhiḥ), that is, by those which are imagined (kalpitaiḥ), meaning they are unreal (asatya-bhūtaiḥ). How can this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is but a deceptive delusion (kuhakabhramaḥ)—a false illusion—arouse any reliance (āsthā) here in the cage of the net for the wise? Only fools desire to grasp the fruit reflected in a mirror.
The meaning is: "here in this cage of a net," that is, in *saṃsāra* which has the form of a magical net (*indrajāla*). The usage is like [the word] *bhāma*. "To eat" means to devour.
Even here, there exists this fragile cultivation of happiness; yet time cuts it away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread.
"Entirely" (*aśeṣam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action; [it refers to] that cultivation of happiness (*sukhabhāvanām*).
There is nothing here that this all-devouring time does not swallow up; it devours every being born in the world, just as the submarine fire consumes the great ocean.
This is clear.
As the Great Lord (Maheśvara), Time is terrible in its universal uniformity; it is intent upon swallowing this entire existence of the perceptible world.
This is clear.
Even for the great, O Lord, Time waits not even for a moment; having become the soul of the universe, it swallows the infinite world.
He does not wait for, nor does he expect, the state of being the self of all, which is omnipresence.
Manifesting slightly through forms known as the ages (yuga), years, and kalpas, he who is himself of an imperceptible nature remains pervading all things.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "known by virtue of the day of the sun and so forth. //MT_1,22.7//
Those things which are delightful, those auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—all have been swallowed up by Time, like tender shoots by a young camel.
This is clear.
Cruel, hard, fierce, harsh, miserly, and base—there is nothing that this Time has not yet swallowed even today.
The employment of tautology indicates an abundance of the onset of anger.
Time, whose mind is solely intent on devouring, eats even mountains; this great consumer is not satiated even by an infinite flood of enjoyments.
A great eater; one who eats much.
Time takes away, destroys, creates, devours, and slays; indeed, in the dance of saṃsāra, it acts through various forms like an actor.
This is clear.

Established in its state of differentiation, it incessantly shatters the seeds of the elements within the world, like a parrot with its beak [pecking at] pomegranate seeds while they lack true existence.
"He abides in differentiation" means he is one who effects differentiation.
With the tips of his tusks of virtue and non-virtue lopping off the sprouts of worldly people, this elephant of the Buddha roams, sustaining the rows of living beings among the flourishing populace.
"Sphītā" means having attained expansion; "jīvarājīvinī" means a lotus-pond endowed with living beings.
The vast Brahma-forest stands encompassing the expansive bilva-tree of the cosmic egg, whose marrow is Viriñca. MU 1.22.14.

For since Viriñca alone is the essential core within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), it is called the "marrow of Viriñca. By the word "āvṛtya" (having enveloped), meaning having covered, the contact with time is stated to exist even in Brahmā.
Creating clusters of days filled with nights like female bees, and creeper-like arts of seasons and kalpas, he is never weary.
The word "time" (kāla) is to be understood as the subject. What is time doing? It should be construed as "creating the creeper-like divisions of years, kalpas, and kalās."
O Sage, though he is split asunder, he is not shattered; though he is burned, he is not consumed; though he is gazed upon, he is not fully seen—he who is the crest-jewel of rogues.

The extreme perceptibility of Time is to be understood through the observation of the qualities of the seasons and so forth; yet it is not seen [as a substance] because it lacks a formal shape (*ākāra*). It is called the "crest-jewel of rogues" because even a rogue can be of such a nature.
In a single moment, it can sufficiently raise up something and utterly destroy something else, spreading out like an expansive kingdom of the mind.
This is clear.
With his fully developed behavior like that of a woman of loose conduct, he remained there, stirring the people about like a cook stirring a soup with a ladle.
Turning it around, causing it to revolve.
Through the expansion of his own self, he is intent on assimilating everything—straw, dust, Mahendra, Mount Sumeru, a leaf, and the ocean—into himself.
By means of that expansiveness, which is the pervasiveness of the self; [it is used] to make [something] one's own, that is, to bring it under one's own control.
Cruelty is fully present right here; greed is firmly established right here; all misfortune is right here, and all fickleness is right here.
Right here, at this very time; sufficient, that is, complete.
Playfully impelling the sun and moon, he sports here in the vault of the sky like a child with two balls placed in his own hands.
A ball is a vīṭā.
With a form encircled by garlands of the bones of all beings down to his feet, he sports like Time at the end of an aeon, fashioning his own fictions.
He is the one by whom conceptual constructions—those conceptualizations which take the form of the world—are imagined.
In this wild dance, at the end of the eon, Mount Meru trembles in the sky with the winds issuing from its limbs, like the bark of a birch tree tossed by the gales.
It throbs and wanders in the sky.
Having become Rudra, he becomes Mahendra, then the Grandfather (Brahmā), Śukra, and Vaiśravaṇa as well; yet again, he becomes nothing at all.
This is clear.

He sustains within himself successions of creations that arise spontaneously and are then destroyed—emanations of immeasurable splendor, both diverse and yet non-different from him, just as the ocean contains its own various waves.

"Those who are constantly rising"—that is, those creations (sargas) and emanations (sṛṣṭis)—the repetition "one after another" (*anyān anyān*) expresses frequency. The word "api" (even/also) is connected with the phrase "not different" (*ananyān*).
Standing there, he was plucking from the trees called Mahākalpa the ripe clusters of fruit that were the hosts of gods and asuras.
Shaving off and cutting away.
He has attained the state of a great tree for the masses of cosmic egg-figs, which fall down with the humming of restless gnats that have become like bees.
"Ghuṅghumeti" is an onomatopoeic imitation of a sound. "Uḍumbara" is a particular kind of fruit; for indeed, mosquitoes dwell there in great numbers.
Accompanied by his beloved Action, he delights his body with the night-lily of pure existence, which is made to blossom by the moonlight of consciousness.

That time is accompanied by action as its beloved; consciousness itself is the moonlight because it is of the nature of luminosity. By that [moonlight], which is fully blossomed—that is, manifest—as the night-lily of pure existence (*sattāmātra*), it amuses its own body; that is to say, it remains endowed with the activity of constant being.
He remained standing, leaning upon his own body as a firm seat—towering like a great mountain and extending to the very limits of the infinite realms of misery.
"Having infinite destruction as its limit" means being devoid of a limit characterized by destruction; that is to say, it is free from perishing.

In some places he meditates on that pervasive reality as dark as deepest gloom, in some places as endowed with splendor, and in both cases, remaining steadfast, he contemplates its nature as being sequentially devoid of both.
That which is dark is "śyāma"; by that, [cultivating the nature] means bringing about one's own form—this refers to the triad of night, day, and twilight.
With his own essential being—whose essence consists of countless dissolved transmigrations—he has come to a state of fixed station, as if weighed down by a heavy burden.
It is that in which the essence of countless transmigrations is dissolved; by means of that [essence]. For it is said to be "heavy" because it attains a state of firmly established footing.
It does not weary, it does not die, it does not remain, and it does not go; it neither sets nor rises, even throughout hundreds of great eons.
This is clear.
Merely through the effortless play of initiating the world, with profound ease, he passes his time by means of the self for the sake of the self—one who is free from egoism and bowed in humility.

In that [state] where sport is intense, she causes [time] to pass—that is, to be brought to an end. For when there is an absence of egoism, time perishes; the sense is that she herself even performs the play of her own destruction.
He remained there, gently causing the lotus-beds in the lakes to appear as if turbid with the mud of night, while the rows of day-lotuses seemed like a dizziness of activity.
"In the lakes"—that is, in the forms of the worlds—"superimposing" means imagining [himself] in the form of the sun; this is the ellipsis.
Taking up the night as a terrifying broom and the stars as golden dust, he sweeps the earth on all sides.
The meaning is that he brings it forth, cleanses it, and having established the night, provides illumination.
Moving the sun-lamp from corner to corner with his finger, he gazes out of compassion upon the house of the world, wondering, "What is there, and where?"
"In the corners" means in the intermediate directions; for even another person, having lit a lamp in his house, looks about to see what is where.
Beholding with the eye of the sun the days that have reached their full maturity in a mere blink, he devours this world like a decayed forest, taking as his fruit the guardians of the quarters.
"With the sun-eye," that is, with the eye called "sun"; the meaning is: "having gazed upon the days," that is, having waited for some time.
Death gradually deposits the world’s jewel-like people, who are scattered within the dilapidated hut of the universe, into its fierce cavern—the casket of mortality.
[He gathers] those scattered and strewn about in the dilapidated hut of the world; for even another person places jewels scattered in a hut into a casket.
That very series of world-jewels which is abundantly filled with virtues, he takes upon his body as if for the sake of ornament and then cuts it away once more.
Even another king or such might, having placed a string of jewels upon his body, cut it off with ease.
The fickle moon constantly and excessively encircles the night-lotus garland that follows him day by day, with the stars as its filaments.
It encircles, that is, it causes to revolve; "the world" is the word understood to complete the sense.
The mountain, the woolly cloud, the mountain peak, the world, and the spider—these are the butcher who, day after day, drinks by gazing even upon the red specks of the stars.
That whose wool is the mountains; such is it. And that whose two horns are heaven and earth;
such is it. That world which is like this is itself the wool-bearing ram. The butcher of that [ram] is its destroyer.
He is the moon to the lotus of youth and the lion to the elephant of life; there is nothing, whether trivial or significant, that he does not plunder.
This is clear.

Through the playful sport of the cosmic cycle, by which living beings are ground down and cast away, He rejoices in His own Self by means of His own Self through the laughter of the emergence of subordination.

"Pounded" means reduced to powder; therefore, it refers to that by which living beings have been struck down. "By such [a person]"—the word *kāla* (Time) is to be supplied as the subject. The three words ending in the instrumental case are to be construed as adjectives qualifying *svātmanā* (by himself).
He is the agent, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the rememberer who has attained every state. He performs all this, yet he does nothing at all.
Because it has the nature of nothingness, no instrument of cognition is to be known [as its object].
He concludes the censure of Time with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"Indeed, the power of Time manifests here among men by suddenly revealing and then concealing the body—which, though entirely devoid of parts, possesses both beautiful and ugly forms."

The states of being "with parts" (*sakala*) and "without parts" (*akala*), and so forth, are to be understood according to the classification of their respective objects. In the phrase "revealing" (*prakaṭayan*) and "concealing" (*gopayan*), the addition of the *num* augment is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*), occurring even though there is no following *sarvanāmasthāna* case ending. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-second canto in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus offered a censure of time, he now describes the play of time:
"In this world, of this prince Time, whose sport is formidable, from whom all calamities have been cast far away, and whose power is immeasurable..."
In this shattered web of the world’s wilderness, the hunt is practiced by the wretched and the deluded against the herds of living beings.
The great ocean at the time of the kalpa’s end is a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire blazes like a lotus in one corner.
This is clear.
The daily sustenance [of the world] is provided by those very worlds, which consist of oceans of curd and milk enriched with pungent, bitter, and sour elements, yet have become stale.

"Pungent, bitter, and sour" refers to those beings, both moving and non-moving, who are characterized by extreme tamas, tamas, or rajas, and who possess specific qualities such as pungent flavors and so forth; this also includes perfected substances (*siddhadravya*). "Endowed with these" means possessed of them. "Having stayed overnight" (*paryuṣita*) means having been kept for a night, and not fresh; this is the meaning. "Morning meal" (*kālyavartana*) refers to the breakfast; the word "his" (*asya*) refers to the one mentioned in the first verse of the creation.
This is to be applied everywhere.
Caṇḍī, who moves with fourfold gait and is accompanied by the entire host of Mothers, is a she-wolf that drags away the human deer placed within the forest of saṃsāra.

The connection is that the power (śakti) named Caṇḍī, belonging to this time, becomes a she-wolf (vṛkī). The group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇa) is well known. Even a prince protects a she-wolf for the sake of hunting.
The earth is the palm of her hand; the earth is her wine-cup filled with nectar, garlanded by swarms of restless bees hovering over lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies.
The earth is vast.
Roaring, with his broad chest heaving, Nṛsiṃha is held within the cage of his arms; with his mane and broad, muscular shoulders, he is a lovely pet bird at play.
*Nṛsiṃha* means *narasiṃha*. Even for the sake of the prince's amusement, a lion is kept in a cage.
Sweet with the lute of the bottle-gourd, possessing the stainless splendor of the autumnal sky, the Lord Mahākāla is indeed a playful young cuckoo.
Mahākāla is a specific deity who holds authority over the process of withdrawal.
With a form of incessant radiance, having cast forth the thunderbolt of the arrows of suffering, the bow named Non-Contemplation vibrates everywhere.

"Vāntāḥ" means vomited forth; "duḥkhāny eva śarāśanayaḥ" means the very sufferings are the arrows and the bowstring; "yena" means by which; "saḥ" refers to that; "abhāvanāmā cāsau kodaṇḍaḥ" means this is the bow named Non-Contemplation (abhāvanā); thus it is "abhāvanāmakodaṇḍaḥ."
He concludes the description of Time’s play with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Augmented by his unsurpassed, throbbing play, wandering, seizing, shining forth, and tearing asunder, Time—like an old, decrepit, and restless monkey—strives here with a shimmering body. (MU 1.23.10)
He strives; he performs various kinds of activities. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the twenty-third canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Having thus described the play of time (*kālavilāsa*), he introduces the play of fate (*daivavilāsa*): "In this very context, something else that is like a crest-jewel among mischievous things is called 'fate' (*daiva*) and 'time' (*kāla*) by the world, saying 'it exists' and 'it acts'. (MU 1.24.1)

"Does" (*karoti*) is a statement of action; "is" (*asti*) is a statement of existence. Here, "time" (*kāla*) is intended to mean destiny (*kṛtānta*), because that [destiny] is a synonym for fate (*daiva*).
Apart from mere activity, no other form of action is perceived for that which consists of its own internal vibration, nor is any intended result [observed].
Therefore, this entire succession of beings, eternally fragile, has been brought to a state of extreme distress by suffering, like a garland of snow by heat.

Of that deity, whose form is not perceived apart from mere activity, nor is the intended object of action—the desired objective of the act—perceived. For what purpose? [It is thought: "He does something"; by that [thought], this continuum of elements is brought into a state of disorder.
Whatever expanse of the world-circle is seen here, that is his dancing hall; herein he performs his dance.
Of that divine one.
With the intention of stating another name for this, he says:
"And bearing the third name, 'Kṛtānta' (the End-maker), which is most terrible, Destiny dances in the world, intoxicated and wearing the form of a Kāpālika."
Having the form of a Kāpālika, he was equal to a Kāpālika.
He describes this very [Brahman] as the support of all:
"O Sage, for Kṛtānta (Death), who is intensely impassioned and eternally desirous of his beloved Niyati (Destiny), is constantly dancing. (MU 1.24.6)

The remainder is Śeṣa, white as a digit of the moon; and the stream of the Gaṅgā—these two, appearing as the sacred thread (upavīta) and the upper garment (avīta), rest upon the chest of transmigratory existence.
Those two are the arms; the remainder is the flow of the Gaṅgā. Possessing splendor that dispels [darkness], the very cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is the chest; therein [they rest].
The discs of the moon and sun are his golden bracelets on his wrists; in his hand is the lotus of play, with the cosmic egg as its pericarp—this is the Brahma-form.
The "Brahmic" [lotus] is the lotus that serves as the seat of Brahmā; it is the pericarp of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), because it constitutes its central core.
The single sky is the supreme garment, strewn with stars like pearls, its fluttering fringes the Puṣkara and Āvarta clouds, and washed by the waters of the universal ocean.
*Ambara* means the sky; *ambara* also means clothing.
Before such a person as this, Nityakāminī, whose passion never subsides, dances with her various undertakings.
By means of undertakings consisting of restraints and observances; for indeed, in the presence of a male dancer, even a female dancer dances.
Within the hollow of the pavilion of the world, she is intent on dancing; her nature is unimpeded movement, and she is ever-active in coming and going.
With beautiful ornaments upon her limbs, she was like a row of celestial realms; her broad mass of hair hung down as far as the netherworld, reaching into the sky.
The series of those intermediate worlds belonging to the gods serves as a beautiful ornament upon her limbs. Of what nature is the sky?
It reaches down to the Pātāla; that is, it is as extensive as the Pātāla. And the braid of the dancing woman is likewise long and pervasive.
And Narakālī, a garland of anklets filled with a tumultuous clamor, is strung upon the thread of evil deeds and moves upon the feet that tread the underworld.
A garland of anklets, a garland of small bells.
In that very night, Citragupta painted upon her forehead-slip the musk-tilaka prepared by his friend Kriyā.

On the *yāma*, that which pertains to Yama; on the *vadanapaṭṭaka*, the facial tablet—that is, on the face in the form of the tablet of Yama’s decree—there is a musk tilaka painted by Citragupta, meaning a script written by Citragupta. Of what nature is it? It is by means of *kriyāsakhī*, who is the embodiment of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
It was prepared by her friend; having entered into Citragupta, it was composed [by him], for a female friend indeed applies a decorative mark upon her friend.
Assuming the form of Kālī at the end of the kalpas, this goddess dances once more amidst the multitude of ritual activities, with the solid mountains resounding with her clear roar.
Kālī is the power of time (kāla-śakti). Having assumed—that is, having resorted to—her form, the word "again" (punar) is employed with reference to what occurred previously.

Subsequently, [he was pursued] by those with dangling and wandering locks of hair like those of a youth, with chariots adorned with peacock feathers, and terrifying with the great, deep resonance of their three eyes.
With the hair on Śiva’s head bestowed by the long, dangling autumn moon, and with the whisks of Gaurī’s beautiful, rising, and pale tresses of mandāra flowers;
With Tumburu, who was terrifying due to his form resembling a mountain in a wild dance, and with the begging-bowl skulls of Indra’s body, which resounded through their thousands of apertures;
With its dry skeletons filling the sky by the breaking of its frame, it terrifies even itself, though it is already darkened by black clouds.

A *kulaka* (a group of verses): "Dry," meaning characterized by the quality of desiccation; because it is the subject under discussion, this refers to *niyati* (destiny/fate). "By itself dense-black" means extremely black. It "terrifies even itself," that is, it causes even itself to be seized by fear; the sense is: "what need is there to mention others? In what state is it? [It is] those fractures of the bed-posts (*khaṭvāṅga*) of the body—that is to say, having the form of the broken pieces of the bed-posts.
The members [of the chariot]; by them the sky is filled. With what kind of body-skulls (khaṭvāṅga)? "Behind," and so forth.
Hanging behind, and for that very reason wandering, i.e., moving about; "kaumāra" means belonging to Kumāra. Those whose chariot-peacocks [are such]; by them.
The whirring sounds (*bhāṅkāra*) are to be known as produced by the wind. That which is both hanging and swaying is the autumn moon.

By those [gods] who have been "conveyed" (vitīrṇāḥ), meaning given; that is to say, by those whose hair is like that of Hara (Śiva). Just as the hair of Hara is illuminated by a digit of the moon, so too is hers by the full autumnal moon—this is the sense.
By those for whom the rising, beautiful mandāra flowers constitute a shimmering, beautiful chowrie, which is the very braid of Gaurī herself.

He is one who is wildly dancing yet possesses a mountain-like form; he is Bhairava, the Great Terrible One. He is [accompanied] by those for whom the *ādaratumbaka*—a specific musical instrument that is the object of their devotion—is present. He is such that his thousand-fold apertures, which take the form of eyes, resound.
He is the body of Indra himself, and he is [accompanied] by those for whom he is the alms-bowl (*bhikṣākapālaka*). Likewise, he is accompanied by those who are dark.

And this external meditation has been taught for the sake of those with coarse vision; however, for those with subtle vision, the touch of necessity (niyati) has been described even in relation to youths and others by way of a different approach.
With the beautiful lotus-garland of the wheel that is the head of Viśvarūpa, she shines as she dances through the great kalpas.
The wheel that was the head of Virāj, who possesses all forms—that indeed is the beautiful garland of lotuses; with that [he is adorned].
It is said that at the end of the eon, even Tumburu and the other celestial musicians flee from her due to the terrifying sounds of the drums of the intoxicated Puṣkarāvarta clouds.
*Ḍamaravas* are specific types of musical instruments; *uḍḍāmaras* means formidable or fierce; *tumburu* is a name for a *gandharva*.
At the end of the dance of Kṛtānta, who laughs with the orb of the moon, he wears as a crest the sky, beautiful with stars for moonstones and lovely peacock feathers.
In one ear there is a long Himalaya mountain as a ring; in the other, there is the great Mount Meru as a lovely golden earring.

"At the end of the eon" (ante kalpānte); "the smile" is the lunar disc itself; "of him who is endowed with that"; "moon-like things" [...]; "that which is beautiful by means of them"; "the sky itself is the peacock feather"; "he whose crest-ornament is such a tail-feather"; "a ring" (mudrikā) is a specific white ear-ornament.
Right here, her two dangling earrings are the sun and moon; her two cheeks are the Lokāloka mountain range; and her girdle encircling her waist is the entire series of world-systems.
On the surface of the cheeks—that is, on the cheeks themselves—the girdle situated at the waist is the "waist-girdle."
Moving here and there, the lightning, colored like a golden bracelet, shines like a strip of cloud-silk tossed by the wind.
She whose distinctive ornament (*varṇikā*)—a specific kind of decoration—is a circle of lightning; such is she, "possessing a circle of lightning as her ornament" (*vidyudvalayavarṇikā*).
With spears, sharp-edged missiles, pikes, darts, lances, and mallets—sharp weapons gathered like the Destroyer himself, intent on annihilating the multitude of living beings.
Upon the long noose of the bonds of saṃsāra, cast by the hand of Time, this garland shines, strung upon the great thread of remaining enjoyments.
For the purpose of binding one to *saṃsāra*; completely; for a long time; of this *kṛtānta* (the end-maker), which has just been mentioned and is synonymous with *daiva* (fate).
The row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans, radiant with the brilliance of the jewels in the makara-shaped mounts shimmering with life, is the ornament of his two arms.
Those [rivers] in which there are sea-monsters (*makara*) that are "gladdened by life"—that is to say, living beings; for even in bracelets there are figures of sea-monsters, but they are lifeless.
The great whirlpool of worldly affairs, a succession of pleasure and pain, filled with passion (rajas) and darkened by ignorance (tamas)—this row of hair upon him shines forth.

The line of body hair (*romālī*) upon her shines like a succession of pleasure and pain (*sukhaduḥkhaparamparā*) characterized by great whirlpools of worldly affairs (*vyavahāra*) that recur again and again. Of what nature is it? It is filled with *rajas* (passion), being saturated with the quality of *rajas*; likewise, it is dark with *tamas* (ignorance), being defiled by the quality of *tamas*.
For a line of body hair is also possessed of whirlpools, filled with dust (*rajas*), and dark with darkness (*tamas*).
Having thus brought to an end this dance, so fierce with its cataclysmic Tandava, at the conclusion of the aeon, the Great Lord Maheśvara withdraws it along with all creation.
Furthermore, she displays this playful dance of laughter, which embodies all forms and is adorned with the dramatic gestures of old age, suffering, and sorrow.
Together with *sṛṣṭi* (emanation) and together with *niyati* (destiny); again, at the commencement of creation, [she perceives] this world-form.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the canto:

"Again he creates worlds, forests, other realms, and the arrangement of the multitude of living beings; he fashions the beautiful practice of conduct and all things moving and unmoving, just as a child tirelessly constructs various unstable figures out of mud. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto in the section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the play of destiny, he speaks of its result:
"O great sage, when this very world-process called saṃsāra has occurred through these factors such as time and the rest, what reliance can there be here for those like me?"
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be understood as the ellipsis [at the beginning]. "Vṛtte" means in conduct; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), factors such as destiny and others are included.
We stand as if sold by these cheats, such as fate and the like—cheats clever in their deceptions—like deluded forest deer.
This is clear.
This ignoble conduct is Time itself, intent upon devouring; it ceaselessly casts the world into the ocean of calamity.
This is clear.
In the end, fate, through its cruel workings, burns one with evil desires, just as fire consumes the world with flames that resemble flowers.
This is clear.
Fate, which is naturally fickle due to its feminine nature and is intent on restriction, disturbs my steadfastness by means of this single beloved wife, who possesses a form that inspires longing.
Causing illness, she is the giver of disease; not beloved for her form, she is one whose lover is formless.
Like a serpent seizing the wind, Death, whose conduct is cruel, having brought the world-body to old age, devours the multitude of living beings without ceasing.
He whose very body is the world; such is he.
The king of Yama, who is merciless, does not show compassion even for one who is suffering; a person whose conduct is characterized by mercy toward all beings has become rare to find.
Afflicted and miserable.
O Sage, all classes of beings whose nature is fragile and insignificant are for nothing but suffering and endless misery; they are dreadful grounds for greed.
Those with meager resources are possessed of worthless wealth.
Life is exceedingly fickle, yet death alone is relentless; youth is extremely transient, while childhood is stolen away by dullness.
This is clear.
The world is stained by the impurity of time; kinsmen are the bonds of existence; enjoyments are the great diseases of worldly life; and craving is but a mirage.
He is stained by the arts known as deceiving others.
The senses themselves have become enemies; truth has turned into untruth. The mind itself is the enemy of the mind, and the self strikes down the self by its own hand.

The self, by means of the self, strikes itself down; the remainder [of the sense] is "by means of evil conceptualizations. It is the mind alone—specifically the impure mind—and not anything else—that becomes the enemy of the mind, the adversary of the pure mind.
Egoism leads to blemish; intellects have become feeble; actions yield only evil fruits; and pastimes have come to depend entirely upon women.
They are very soft and not sharp.

Women have been made possessed of charms that are objects of longing and endowed with aesthetic wonder; yet they have become banners of faults, and the aesthetic flavors (rasas) have fallen into a state of flavorlessness.

And those women, who are the objects of desire, modest, and charming at first sight—such women have been made (or fashioned) with aesthetic charm (*sacamatkṛti*), that is to say, endowed with wonder. What kind of women? Those bearing the banners of faults (*doṣapatākinī*);

because they consist of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, they bear the banners of passion and other defects. "Flavors" (*rasāḥ*) refer to desires for the subjects of the sciences and so on; [the state of being devoid of these] is "flavorlessness" (*nīrasatā*).
They have become withered.
When a real object is grasped as unreal, and the mind is surrendered to the ego-sense, beings are obstructed by non-existence, and the end of existence is not attained.

By us, the real entity—the true reality—has been grasped as a non-entity (*avastu*) in the form of "I am the body," having been seized through such a state of unreality. Likewise, the mind has been placed within egoism; that is to say, it has been swallowed by the ego. Phenomenal existents (*bhāvāḥ*) have been obstructed by non-existence, meaning they have been seized by destruction. The ellipsis is "they were not known. Therefore, the end of existence (*bhavānta*) is not attained, nor is it reached.
It is attained.
O virtuous one, the mind, its interior agitated, suffers in vain; the serpent of passion plays there, and it does not attain detachment.
Dispassion is the absence of passion; one does not approach it, nor does one go toward it.
When the vision is struck by the quality of passion (rajas), darkness increases; and the essence of being, the ultimate reality, is not attained, remaining exceedingly remote.
Reality is the ultimate truth.
Stability has become instability; death is on the verge of arrival; fortitude falls into despondency; and delight is fixed upon that which is unreal.
In that which is non-substantial, such as the body and so forth, which have become non-substantial.
The intellect is clouded by dullness, the body is intent solely on falling, old age seems to blaze within the frame, and past misdeeds erupt with force.
By sluggishness, that is, by dullness.
Youth arrives with effort, while association with the virtuous remains far away; there is no recourse whatsoever, and truthfulness does not arise anywhere.
Youthfulness, by way of its characteristic mark, is attachment to women.
The mind is as if utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away. Compassion does not arise with its former brilliance; baseness approaches from afar.
This is clear.
A person intent on falling and rising moves between steadiness and instability; association with the wicked is easily found, but union with the virtuous is difficult to attain.
Steadfastness turns into lack of steadfastness; the meaning is that it perishes.
All entities are subject to coming and going; the cultivation of existence is the bond of becoming. This constant succession of beings is merely led here and there.
"It is led"—the word "by time" is to be supplied as the remainder.
For even the directions are no longer seen, and even place is beyond description; even mountains crumble—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
