"A place" (*deśa*) would not even possess the designation "place," meaning that even the name "place" would no longer exist for a location due to time. The sense is: when such conditions will come to pass for such things, what reliance or what trust could there be in a person like me?
Even the oceans run dry and even the stars perish; even the perfected ones do not remain perfected—what hope, then, for a person such as I?
This is clear.
Even the sky is devoured by non-existence, and even the world is shattered; even the earth falls into distress—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
By its non-existence, that is, by its destruction, even the sky is devoured—that is, swallowed.
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder; even Dhruva’s life is uncertain; even the immortals are slain—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
"They are killed"—the word "by time" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Even Śakra is assailed by other Śakras, and even Yama is indeed subject to restraint; even for Vāyu there is a state of non-Vāyu—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
By new Śakras, by Śakras.
Even the moon reaches the state of being like the sky; even the sun suffers fragmentation; even fire falls into a state of being extinguished—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
"Vyomatām" means destruction. //MT_1,25.28//

Even Parameṣṭhin, though he has reached the ultimate state, undergoes change; even the Unborn takes on the form of Hari; and even Bhava enters into non-existence—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Bhava, even Śrī Mahādeva, attained the state of non-existence, the state of no longer being Mahādeva.
Time reaches a state of fragmentation, and even destiny is brought to an end; even space dissolves into the infinite—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
When some object has disappeared into infinity.
By some inscrutable being, whose form is unknown through a tantra that is difficult to hear, difficult to speak, and difficult to see, the worlds are mocked, causing delusion.

The *tantra* is unspeakable, likewise inexpressible, and likewise difficult to perceive; it is a means of deception. "Of whom" means "by some such [person]," which signifies "by one who is indefinable."
Having attained even a fraction of egoism, there is no one in the three worlds who is not bound by that which dwells within them all.
The notion of selfhood regarding the body and so forth is egoism (*ahaṅkāra*). By that [egoism], it means "by anyone at all."
Upon the slopes of rocky mountains, the sun, together with its horses and charioteer, is perpetually whirled about, as helpless as a stone in a forest.
"Stone-mountains" (śilāśailāḥ) are mountains joined with stones; "masses" (kaṭaprāḥ) are their collections. Upon them, she is made to swing—that is, the act of swinging is performed.
The terrestrial globe, the abode of the hosts of gods and demons dwelling within it, is encircled by the wheel of celestial spheres, like a ripe walnut by its husk.

The terrestrial globe (dharāgolakam) is surrounded—that is, it is made to be encircled—by the wheel of the celestial spheres (dhiṣṇyacakreṇa); here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument.
In heaven the gods, on earth the men, and in the netherworld the asuras and serpents—all are reduced to a state of decay by the mere passing of a kalpa.
The *asurabhogins* are the Daityas and serpents; "by the measure of a kalpa" means by a duration equal to a single kalpa.
And Desire, having acquired prowess through the battle for sovereignty over the world, leaps about after having assailed the world with its very first assault.
The valor which was obtained by him through the battle with Īśāna—by means of that, he became such as he was.
Spring, like an intoxicated elephant, with its rutting ichor raining down flowers and perfuming the entire circle of the quarters, leads the heart toward crookedness.
"With intoxicants" means with the waters of passion; "crookedness" refers to skill in the arts of love. Here, the mention of spring is made in connection with the pursuit of love.
Even great discernment is unable to clarify the mind when its form has been gazed upon by the eyes of women full of passion.

Even great solitude is not capable of making the mind clear or pure. Of what nature is the mind? It is such that its form is like the glance—the casting of a look—of the world of women who are full of passion; the meaning is that it is extremely fickle.
I consider only the Buddha truly happy, for his mind is cooled by its own self-interest, whereas others are consumed by the distress of seeking to benefit others.
The Buddha is the Knower; for his own sake—that is, for his own purpose—he acts with coolness, meaning not with a mind distressed by the pursuit of his own self-interest.
Who is able to count the waves of the ocean of life—those that arise and perish, falling into the submarine fire of Time?
The meaning is that "living beings" are the waves of the ocean of life.
All men, through delusion, fall into the snares of evil desires; like deer caught in a thicket of faults, they are swallowed up in the wilderness of birth.

"Deer of the humors" (doṣagulmakasāraṅgāḥ) means those who are fond of the humors (doṣapriyāḥ). A deer is fond of thickets (gulma). "Swallowed" (nigīrṇāḥ) means seized; "by delusion" (mohena) is the ellipsis. Even the deer (sāraṅgāḥ), when falling into snares in the forest, are seized by the hunter (kirāta).

By those evil deeds here in this world, the lifespan of people in the succession of births in the universe is exhausted; for we do not know of any fruit of such acts, even for those who possess discernment, that is comparable to a noose made from the branches and creepers of a tree in the sky.
The meaning is that [the self] is non-existent, like a noose fashioned from the sky, trees, and creepers; the intention is that [if it were real], they would perform actions here.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Today is a festival; this is the season; likewise, there is a procession here; these are my kinsmen; this is happiness; this is a special enjoyment"—thus, vainly weaving the web of his own conceptual constructions, the world falls away here, its mind fickle and fragile. (MU 1.25.43)

"Unsteady and soft-minded" means one whose intellect is extremely fickle and very limited. By the phrase "the web of one's own conceptual constructions," the absolute non-existence of festivals and the like is expressed. Thus, all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Furthermore, he speaks again of the very wickedness of saṃsāra, and something else as well:
"O Father, in this nature of the world, whether it be exceedingly desolate or delightful, there is not even the slightest collection of objects by which the mind attains supreme rest."

The ellipsis is "I say. O dear one, I say this and something else as well. In response to the expectation of what it is that you say, he says: "exceedingly" (*atitarām*). Or rather, "in a delightful manner," as if it were delightful. "A collection of objects" (*arthajātam*) means a multitude of things. The sense is that when there is ultimate repose, the desire for other objects will no longer arise again.

When childhood has passed and the deer of life, restless with imagined play, has scattered into the caves of old age, and the little body has reached a state of decay, the world suffers only in its utter desolation.
In the deer of youth, known as the "deer of life," one is tormented—that is, afflicted—by decrepitude, which is old age.
Having cast far away the lotus-plant of the body struck by the frost of old age, and as soon as the bee of life has departed, the lake of worldly existence for all people has dried up.
Having abandoned, having cast aside; in the bee called life, [which is] flickering with regard to life.
Whenever it surely reaches maturity, then and there this creeper-like body of men puts forth a new blossom; yet, burdened by old age, it is utterly withered, bearing only a few scanty new flowers.

*Nūnam* signifies certainty; *navam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no tautology. Furthermore, it is a marvel that for a creeper that has reached maturity, there is the fresh unfolding of new blossoms.

In this world, the river of craving flows with its most powerful current, sweeping away the entire multitude of infinite objects; it is uniquely capable of eroding the roots of the sturdy tree of contentment that stands upon its bank.
This is clear.

The boat of the body, bound with the fastenings of skin, tossed about and wandering in the ocean of existence, is carried downward by the five crocodiles known as the sense-faculties, over which it has no control.

The connection is as follows: the ship of the body is caused to sink—that is, it is made to submerge—by the five crocodiles known as the sense-faculties (*indriya*). "Agitated" means trembling on all sides.

These deer of the mind, wandering through the forest of the creepers of craving and roaming among the hundreds of branches of the trees of desire, exhaust themselves at will, yet they do not obtain the fruit.

*Kāmaṃ* means "certainly. That which is a forest (*kānana*) for the creepers of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—those who roam there are such [beings]. Likewise, "wandering about" means having the habit of roaming. These are the deer of the mind (*manomṛga*). Upon the trees of desire (*kāmahīruha*) found in that forest—that is, upon the trees called "supreme desire"—there are hundreds of branches; by implication, these are hundreds of branches in the form of intermediate desires. They exhaust and shake their own domain.
Even so, they do not attain the fruit.

In times of hardship, those who have cast far away despondency and delusion; who are pleasing to the mind yet not arrogant toward their masters; and whose inner hearts remain unassailed by beautiful women—such great souls are exceedingly difficult to find nowadays.
In hardships and calamities, and in lordships and prosperities—remaining unsullied, that is, free from pride—the mind [is thus]; therefore, they are delightful.

Those who cross the ocean of battle, with its waves consisting of throngs of elephants, are not heroes in my view; those alone are heroes here who cross this ocean of their own senses, which has the mind as its wave.
This is clear.

No action whatsoever is seen belonging to anyone that, delightful with its final fruit free from affliction, brings the world—whose mental states are struck down by false hopes—to rest upon reaching it.
This is clear.

Those great ones who fill the world with their fame, the quarters of space with their majesty, their home with their splendor, and prosperity with the strength of their virtue—being bound by unshakable fortitude, such as these are not easily found in this world.
This is clear.
Whether situated within the walls of mountain crags or dwelling inside a fortress of diamond, all fortunes and all calamities, with their full force kindled, constantly come upon everyone.

This is of stones, thus it is "stone" (śailā). That which is both that [stone] and a wall is a "stone wall" (śailabhitti). A stone wall belonging to a mountain is a "mountain-stone-wall" (giriśailabhitti); [it refers to] that [wall].
Sons, wives, wealth, and even elixirs—these are all mentally constructed, my dear; yet in the end, they all result in what is called a most delightful swoon of poison.
It is conceptualized through imagination and cultivated as an elixir, like nectar; the word "ca" has the sense of "like"; and "ante" means at the end, that is, in the final transformation.

Overcome by despair and having reached a precarious state at the end of his physical life and youth, the person who has grown old burns within, remembering his own former states that were empty of the true nature of phenomena (abhidharma).
At the end of the body's lifespan, in old age; *bhāvān* means desires; *abhitaḥ* means entirely empty of the Dharma, that is, empty of the Abhidharma; *antaḥ* means within the mind.

Having spent the initial days with activities that are thin and internalized for the sake of attaining desire, wealth, and dharma, by what means can the minds of men—tossing like the quivering tail-feathers of a peacock—attain rest?

The sense is that no one performs an action for the sake of liberation by means of those [actions] which result in the acquisition of desire, wealth, and dharma—[actions] which are characterized by narrow intervals and lack of essence.

Even by those results of action that have already appeared before one, yet whose true form has not been attained—resembling the lofty waves of a river—and which arrive by the power of destiny, the world is mocked; for people have diverse tastes.

The word *hi* indicates certainty. One is "mocked" or "deceived. Furthermore, the fact that the fruits of actions do not attain their [intended] form should be understood as being due to their momentary perishability.

These and those activities, which appear to be infinitely delightful when analyzed as "this" or "that," wear out the minds of people through the pursuit of pleasing one's wife until they are worn by old age and matted locks.
The instrumental case in "jāyājanarañjanena" expresses cause; it means that which ends with the decay of the matted locks.

Just as the withered leaves of trees, having come together, quickly go to their destruction at birth, even so do worlds devoid of self-discrimination, having come together, depart from somewhere by means of the days.
Devoid of self-discernment means lacking inquiry into the self.

Having wandered here and there to a great distance and entered his home at the close of day, when the sun has set and the day—devoid of virtuous deeds performed by those who seek solitude—has passed away, who can find sleep?
This is clear.
While all enemy forces have been routed and prosperity has arrived from every side, one enjoys these pleasures—yet at that very moment, death arrives from somewhere unknown.
This is clear.

Deceived by these entities whose forms are increased from somewhere yet are trivial, which are seen for a moment and then perish, the people in this world do not perceive what has come nor what has gone—alas! MU_1,26.21.
From some indefinable source, from some entity, there has come about the arising of objects—that is, of entities—and there has gone forth the movement toward the realm of entities.

Those who, having forcibly attained corpulence, indeed become bound to the body—those people and sheep, with their bonds of karma destroyed, are made into "black-faced" ones by those desiring to depart.

By "janaiḍakaiḥ" (human-sheep), [it means] by those called humans who are like sheep; they are made to have their bonds of action destroyed—that is, their expansion of despicable actions is eliminated. Who are they? Those who remain established in their own [nature], having attained fullness—indeed, not emaciation—by force, that is, by compulsion. They [serve] for your sake, for the purpose of binding your body; indeed, they certainly come into being.
The meaning is this: for it is solely by the power of karma that a person undergoes bondage to a body.
This restless multitude on earth comes incessantly with haste and departs without ceasing with haste; it is like a garland of waves, fragile for a mere moment.
The populace is a multitude of people.

Women—whose lips are red, whose eyes are as flickering as bees, and who are like poisonous trees with trembling creepers—steal away the minds of men by their charm, intent solely on taking away their lives.

They carry away, bring under their control, and delude [men]. They have red coverings, red petals, and red lips; they are like restless creepers with trembling branches—and by metaphorical extension—with trembling arms.
Coming from here and from there, bound by the convention of commonality, the illusory practice of men regarding wife and friend is equal to their attachment to the journey itself.

The destination (*saṅketa*) is the place to be reached. Just as people on a journey meet one another at night along the way and depart together for their common destination in the morning, so too in *saṃsāra*, having met with sons and others, they die and go to the place called the next world (*paraloka*). Therefore, the sense is that it is not appropriate to have emotional attachment (*bhāvabandhana*) toward them.

Just as when lamps have gone out after consuming many wicks that were bound by excessive oil, so too, within the flickering illusions of saṃsāra, which are devoid of reality, the true nature is not known.

*Atisneha* means an excess of passion and an abundance of oil. Those [women] for whom that is the *nibandhana*, the cause; they are such—unsteady and wavering, exceedingly fickle, and unreal, lacking true essence.

This wheel of the breast of the frantic activity of saṃsāra, though as fragile as a bubble in the rain-clouds of the monsoon, produces in the mind of the heedless person the conviction that it is long-lasting and stable.

Even a wheel, though revolving incessantly, produces in the mind of an inattentive person the conviction of stability; the use of the word "ku" (bad/evil) is due to its being permeated by an extreme state of detachment (*vairāgya*).
Splendor has been extinguished by the power of wretchedness; virtues that once endured now remain in a state of decay; and all consolation has retreated far away, like the winter from a lotus.
"In a state of decrepitude" means being on the verge of destruction; "consolation for people" refers to the consolation provided by a person.
When a tree, having repeatedly approached by the power of fate, inflicts harm through the weight of its own body, and is then cut down with axes—what occasion indeed is there for consolation in that?

In this world, when by the power of fate a tree has repeatedly approached—that is, come near—and has caused harm with the weight of its own body and the weight of its branches and twigs, that tree is cut down by people with axes; indeed, this is certain. In that case, what possibility is there for comfort, and what logic could there be for it? [The word] *upetya* is connected with the word *kṛta*.
The intention is that acting together with a single agent leads only to great fear.

Even from the company of a person who is charming yet whose conduct is exceedingly corrupt, and who has arisen for one's own internal destruction—just as from a poisonous tree—one now encounters only a state of fainting.
He whose activity is characterized by an excess of faults; of him [it is said].

Which are those directions in which there are no defects? Which are those quarters in which there is no burning pain of suffering? Which are those beings in whom there is no fragility? Which are those actions in which there is indeed no illusion?
*Māyā* is deceit.

Even the Viriñcas, who live for a single kalpa, perish when the calculation of the multitude of kalpas is completed; therefore, within the web of time which possesses all its parts, even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.

Regarding the phrase "in the reckoning" (*kalane*), the word "when being performed" (*kriyamāṇe*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. When that is being performed, even the *viriñcas*—even the Brahmās—become those whose lives last for only a moment called a *kalpa*. He states the result [of this]: "therefore," meaning: [O Goddess] who art adorned (*śālini*) with those *kalās* which consist of the *kalpas* and so forth.

Everywhere the mountains consist of stone, the earth of clay, and the trees of wood; likewise, people consist of flesh, their existence bound by human effort. There is nothing here that is unprecedented or devoid of transformation.
Those entities which are bound within human effort—that is, within *puruṣakāra*—are they.

Pervaded by consciousness and bound together like water, this collection of atoms situated in space is perceived through the distinct divisions of the categories of objects; this is the world, and there is nothing else whatsoever.

"Pervaded" means permeated by volition (*cetanā*). "Situated in space" means bound by water, that is, held together by water. "An aggregate of atoms" means a collection of ultimate particles (*paramāṇu*). "By the distinct division of the characteristics of objects" means by a separate differentiation belonging to the characteristics of objects. It is observed that it is precisely these atoms, possessing the aforementioned qualifications, that appear in the form of various entities.

To the extent that this world exists, it is one thing; otherwise, there is no other world at all, because the world is nothing but the manifold nature of entities. Therefore, the sense is: what here is loveliness, or what is unloveliness?
In this world of the wise, a marvel that causes wonder in the minds of men—such a thing of variegated form, O virtuous one, never even in a dream becomes an object for anyone at all.

"In this saṃsāra," [the phrase] "in the world of the wise" (*manasviloke*) functions as a locative of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). The summary meaning is that even among those very wise ones, there is no wonder for anyone that brings joy to the mind within this saṃsāra.

Now, even though the magnitude of conceptualization has departed like the fruit of a creeper in the sky, there does not arise for those struck by even a fragment of greed a single word concerning noble conduct.

Now, at this time of dispassion, regarding the conceptualization of cyclic existence—there is a discourse consisting of noble accounts, namely the discourse of the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra). The meaning is: "for us who are free from greed, having struck down even a trace of avarice.
The intention of the word *eva* is: "what need is there for any other discourse when one has this experience?"
Desiring to attain the station of the supreme ones, the world today is ruined by its own mind; it falls fearlessly from the mountain peak like a beast longing for the leaves of a dark blue creeper.
This is clear.

With their branches, leaves, fruits, and flowers—the shadows, limbs, foliage, fruit, and blossoms—cast down and rendered useless within, the trees of the chasms and men of the present day alike have their prosperity destroyed while still standing in their bodies.
Of what nature were those trees in the ravines? They were placed—not in a place of rest—but set down;

they were useless, being devoid of purpose due to the absence of utility for others. [They were such that] their branches, shade, creepers, leaves, fruits, and flowers [were for no one]. Of what nature are men of today? [They are such that] it is only in the body—that is, solely for the sake of their own bodies—and not...

For the sake of benefiting others; their prosperity has been destroyed. Here, the word *aṃsa* (shoulder) is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote the trunk of a tree. The rest is to be inferred by oneself.

In some places people move about in conditions beautiful with gentleness, and in others in terrible ones; they pass through these continuous intervals of states like black antelopes through thickets at the edge of a forest.
"In the ten intervals" means within the periods (*daśā*).

Whose minds are not amazed by the Creator—the Daiva—by those daily works which are terrifying yet beautiful, which agitate all mankind, and which, with their rising hopes destroyed by the ripening of bitter fruits? "Daily" means every day. "Agitated" means led into restlessness. "All mankind" refers to those by whom [all men] are so affected. By the word "of the rogue," there is indicated an excess of anger toward the Creator.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"In this world, a person devoted to desire and intent on practicing various base arts is common even in dreams; but a virtuous man is not easily found today. All actions, rendered utterly distressed by attachment to suffering, are surely thwarted; I know not how they are to be carried out."
The period of life consists of ten [years]. //MU_1,26.41//
Attached to sensual desires, intent merely on the pursuit of dreams; "āvedana" means making manifest. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the impermanence of the world, he now speaks of its contrary nature:
"O Brahmin, whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all that is unstable, resembling a dream or a meeting with a lover."
This is clear.
He explains this very instability in detail:
"O Sage, that which is seen today as a dug-in pit resembling a dried-up ocean becomes a mountain shrouded in clouds by morning."
A pit has been dug.
That mountain which is vast with its array of forests, which has licked the sky and is immovable, in just a few days reaches the level of the earth or sinks into a well.
Having licked the sky, he pervaded the space.
That very limb which today is clothed in silk, garlands, and ointments, tomorrow shall be naked and cast far away into a pit.
On the morrow, it will fall apart; it will become shattered.
In that very place where today a city was seen, bustling with diverse activities, in days to come there arises the state of a desolate wilderness and desert.
The desert is a bowman.
O King, that man who today stands as a radiant sovereign over the realms will, in a few days, become a mere heap of ashes.
He taught the mandalas; [he reduced them] to the state of a heap of ashes, to the condition of a mass of ash.
That very great and terrifying forest, which resembled the vault of the sky and whose space was covered by banners, became a city.
This is clear.
O Sage, that formidable forest range which today shines, entwined with creepers, will in just a few days become a desert land.
The state of being a desert-land, the condition of a desert-land.
Water becomes dry land, and dry land becomes a watery place; indeed, the entire world—including its wood, water, and grass—is turned upside down.
It becomes inverted; it undergoes perversion.
Youth, childhood, the body, and accumulations of wealth are impermanent; they pass incessantly from one state to another, like waves.
From one entity, which is its own nature, another entity would be a different nature.
In this world, life is as flickering as the flame of a lamp in the wind; the splendor of all things in the three realms is like the flash of lightning.
Afflicted by wind, seized by wind.
This vast succession of beings falls into error, like a heap of seeds that sprouts again and again without ceasing.
Expanding while being poured.
With the heavy cloth of the dust of living beings tossed about by the wind of the mind, it is adorned with the graceful gestures of falling, rising, and turning back.
This worldly state is perceived as a delusion produced, like an actress on the stage of saṃsāra who has entered into a dance.

Those many beings who are tossed about and impelled by the wind of the mind constitute the dust-cloth—the cloth covered in dust—of which [the world] consists. *Parāvarta* is a whirling motion consisting of repeated return. *Jāgatī sthitiḥ* is the state of existence in the form of the world.
The *āveśa* (possession) that occurs in dance—[the world] is set in motion therein. The *ārabhaṭī* (energetic performance) is that which takes place upon the stage called *saṃsāra*.
Its *naṭī* is *ārabhaṭī*, which is a specific mode of action (*vṛtti*) characterized by the *raudra-rasa* (the Furious sentiment).
It produces the delusions of a city of Gandharvas, yet it is enchanting through its noble conduct, which is as graceful as the play of a sidelong glance.
O Brahmin, repeatedly casting forth a light as flickering as lightning, the passion for worldly existence shines like a woman intoxicated by dancing.

The passion (*rāga*) that colors cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) shines like one intoxicated by dancing. Of what nature is it? It is such as that which produces the inversion (*viparyāsa*) whose form is like a city of Gandharvas. Likewise, it is as fragile as a sidelong glance (*apāṅga*); it is fragile even in its very corners. It is delightful through its noble conduct (*udāravyavahāra*). Furthermore, it is as flickering as lightning, exceedingly unstable, [casting] light upon its own object.
She repeatedly extends her knowledge and the illumination of her own body.
Those were great days; those were riches and those were deeds; everything has become a mere memory, and we too shall depart in an instant.
The connection is with the words "those days. By the word "those" (tat), there is a recollection of the days previously experienced.
Day by day it undergoes decay, and day by day it is born again; even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of existence, though its form has been destroyed.
This is clear.
Men go to the state of animals, and animals even to the state of men; gods likewise become non-gods. O Lord, what indeed is stable here in this world?
The transition of animals and others to the state of being human and so forth should be understood either by way of their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) or by way of rebirth (*janman*).
Creating a web of rays again and again, the sun passes through nights and days; having traversed its course, it beholds the body's limit of destruction.
Having passed over [the night] and having set [the wheel] in motion.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all classes of beings alike hasten toward destruction, just as bodies of water rush toward the submarine fire.
This is clear.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters—this entire world is the fuel that will be completely consumed by the submarine fire of destruction.
The term "completely dried up" (*saṃśuṣka*) indicates the state of being thoroughly burnt.
Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and all possessions—all these have become tasteless for one who is terrified by the fear of destruction.
The word "mine" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
These entities in the world continue to taste sweet for the wise man only so long as the wicked demon of destruction has not entered the path of his memory.
This is clear.
In one moment sovereignty arrives, and in a moment poverty comes; in one moment there is freedom from disease, and in a moment the onset of illness.
This is clear.
Who indeed, even among the wise, has not been deluded by this great worldly confusion that brings about error at every moment?
This is clear.
For a moment the circle of the sky was smeared with the mire of darkness; for a moment it was beautiful with a soft radiance like a flow of molten gold.
At one moment its hollows were encircled by garlands of dark-blue lotuses like clouds; at another moment it resounded with a fierce roar, and at another it remained silent.
For a moment it is the play of stars, for a moment adorned by the sun; for a moment it brings delight through the moon, and for a moment it is utterly cast aside.
Who, even if wise, would not fear this world of saṃsāra, which is characterized by coming and going, by persistence and destruction? MU_1,27.30
The meaning is: "By means of stability" refers to the stability of the world; what, then, can be said of one who lacks fortitude?
Calamities come for a moment, prosperity comes for a moment; birth and death likewise come for a moment, O Sage—what indeed is not momentary?
The meaning is that everything occurs in an instant alone.
"O Father, he who was here before was indeed one, yet by the days he has become quite another. O Blessed One, is there anything whatsoever that remains stable, even for a single moment?"
Father is Daśaratha; other than another is "anyetara" (the one other than another).
The nature of a cloth is seen in a jar, and the state of a jar is seen in a cloth; there is nothing that has been perceived which does not undergo reversal within cyclic existence.
"Seen" means that at another time, by way of its becoming clay and so forth, it undergoes reversal—that is, it goes to a state of perversion.
A hero slain by one who is not a hero—even a single man may slay a hundred; commoners have attained lordship, and the entire world revolves.
It revolves; it undergoes revolution.
This multitude of people constantly pursues error, like a succession of waves arising from the perception of dull movement.

"Janatā" means a multitude of people. "Jaḍa" refers to that which is inert; from its "parāmarśa," meaning from contact—that is to say, from its insentience. It also refers to the "parāmarśa" found in the movement of water; it is from that [insentience] as well. (MT 1.27.35)
Infancy lasts but a few days today, then comes the beauty of youth, and after that, old age; since even the body possesses no single, constant form, what stability can there be in external objects?
This is clear.
In one moment the mind attains joy, in another it falls into despondency; in another moment it reaches a state of serenity—in every respect, the mind is like an actor.
In all things, toward all living beings.
In one direction this rule creates one thing, in another direction another, and in yet another direction still another; in fashioning these objects, it never grows weary, like a child at play.
This is clear.
The Creator gathers this world that has arisen here, intoxicates it, devours it, slays it, strikes it down, and makes it his own through hundreds of calamities and upheavals.

He gathers and increases; he maddens, making one possessed by madness; he devours, that is, he consumes; he strikes down, that is, he destroys; he makes [things] his own, bringing them under his control; he smites, destroying everything—sometimes in an instant, sometimes in another day, sometimes in the morning, here and there. Thus Fate, skilled in deception, is seen by no one as he fashions [the world].
It is not seen, because it is not an object of the senses.
What exists today does not exist tomorrow morning; what exists tomorrow morning does not exist today; and what exists at another time does not exist today—all this revolves incessantly.
This is clear.
In this world, sufferings are continuous while pleasures are rare; they revolve around a person constantly, like nights and days.
Continuous and uninterrupted, with respect to each man—that is, for every individual person.
For people subject to worldly existence, who are partakers of appearance and disappearance, neither calamities nor prosperities attain permanence.
Of such a one who undergoes manifestation and disappearance; in *bhava*, meaning in *saṃsāra*; of such a one who possesses *bhāva*, that is, manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
This wicked one stands as a mere fragment of time—a villain who, with every step, causes everything to fall into calamity, casting aside all else with effortless ease.

The word "going" (*gacchan*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "With ease" (*helayā*), and not with effort. "Turned away" (*vivalitam*) means brought to another state. "Entirely" (*aśeṣam*). He by whom [this was done]—he. (MT 1.27.44)
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"The floods of fruits—the successions of beings in the three worlds, divided by the ripening of their even and uneven conditions—fall day after day from the vast trees of saṃsāra, blown down by the winds of time."
They are distinguished by the ripening and transformation of their even and uneven states; that is to say, they are endowed with those [results]. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto in the section on detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the world’s perversion, he demonstrates the detachment produced by it:
"When the great mind has been consumed by the forest fire of wisdom, desires for enjoyments do not flicker, like mirages in lakes. (MU 1.28.1)
Thus, it was Medhā herself who, having approached the forest fire, was consumed by it.
And day by day, the state of cyclic existence becomes exceedingly bitter, like a neem vine whose flavor intensifies as it ripens in time.
She is she whose rasa (sentiment) is exuberant by virtue of that ripening which occurs in due time.
O King, wickedness increases and goodness diminishes day by day within the hearts of people, which have become as harsh as the karañja thorn.

"O King"—this is addressed to Daśaratha. "Like the *karañja* tree," meaning like a thorn; it is harsh. Therefore, the sense is: "From this association with people, detachment has arisen in me. In the same way, the application of the underlying intention (*bhāva*) should be understood in the subsequent verses as well.
The boundaries on earth are instantly shattered in every direction, like parched bean stalks, with a sharp and harsh *ṭāṅka* sound.
This is clear.
For lords of the earth who dwell on kingships and heaps of enjoyments, a life of solitary conduct—free from the thorn of anxious thought—is better than being burdened by such concerns.
"For the sake of kingdoms" means from the kingdoms. He states the result with the words "nirasta" (cast out). The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied [as the subject].
My garden is not for my delight, nor are my riches for my pleasure; the hope for wealth brings me no joy; I am at peace along with my mind.
I am pacified; I go to a peace that consists of the cultivation of nothingness.
The world is impermanent and unhappy, O father, and craving is difficult to overcome; my mind is struck by restlessness—how shall I attain peace?
This is clear.
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life; I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
And by this, the attainment of the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is indicated; for indeed, abiding as one truly is is not possible without liberation while living.
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for my endeavors? By virtue of egoism, all of this has dissolved away from me.
For in the absence of ego-consciousness, the Puruṣa is of the nature of nothingness; what, then, could he do with kingdoms and the like?
On the rope of the succession of births, the knots of the senses are firm; those who strive for their release from that which they are bound to are the supreme ones.
For the sake of liberation from that—that is, for the sake of liberating the knots of the sense faculties.
The mind of the proud women was crushed by the god of love, just as a delicate lotus is trampled by the hoof-strikes of an elephant.
In the phrase "māninīlokaiḥ," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument; in "makaraketunā," it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*).
O Lord of Munis, if today it is not treated with a healthy mind, what opportunity indeed remains for the treatment of the mind, and from where could it come?
Today, at this time endowed with all necessary conditions, may you remain composed, free from concern for those conditions.

Now, one might ask: "Having abandoned the indulgence in sense objects, for what purpose does one become intent on medical treatment? To this he says: "Poison is the imbalance of sense objects; poison is not called [merely] 'poison. Sense objects destroy future births, whereas [ordinary] poison destroys only a single body. (MU 1.28.13)

The inequality caused by objects is "inequality of objects" (*viṣayavaiṣamya*). They are called "destroyers of other births" (*janmāntaraghna*) because they persist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and thus destroy [the fruits of] other births.
"But how can they abandon you? To this he replies:
"Neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen, neither life nor death serve to bind the mind of the wise man. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.8)
"For the sake of bondage" means for the purpose of bondage in the form of passion and aversion; "of the wise one" refers to one endowed with discernment.
Now, in response to the inquiry "From where does your state of being a knower arise?", he requests the very means for attaining that knowledge:
"O Brahmin, best among those who know what precedes and follows, teach me quickly so that I may become a knower, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion."
This is clear.
Enveloped by the net of latent impressions, crowded with the thorns of suffering, and abounding in falls and upheavals, the forest of ignorance is of terrifying form.
This is clear.
O Sage, I am able to endure the fierce crushing of the saw—the calamity as deadly as poison that arises from the worldly affairs of saṃsāra.
That which is done with malicious intent (*āśaya*) is uneven, harsh, destructive, and violent; it is indeed the "poisonous destruction" (*āśā-viṣa-vaiśasa*).
"This does not exist, this exists"—such is the delusion of worldly people; this [wisdom] shakes the flickering mind as the wind disperses a mass of dust.
It shakes and causes to tremble.
The collection of living beings, strung upon the threads of craving like pearls, is the eternally manifest leader of the mind, appearing as the pure limb of consciousness.
I shall tear asunder this necklace of saṃsāra, adorned with the serpent of Time, which causes aversion, just as a lion tears through a cruel snare.

That whose very limb, its own nature, is consciousness alone—of that [consciousness], the state is "that-ness" (tattā); by that, meaning by way of being composed of consciousness (cinmayatvena). It has become manifest, having attained the state of being an object of knowledge (vedyatā). For otherwise, how could it be an object of knowledge if it were not composed of consciousness? This is because only that which is not opposed to consciousness and has become the object of consciousness can possess the quality of being knowable. Even a necklace becomes manifest and clear; it is indeed the mind itself.
That which has him as its leader, its producer, and its central gem; that [necklace], which is gentle and soft.
O best among the knowers of reality, quickly dispel for me the mist of the forest of the heart and the darkness of the mind with some lamp of knowledge.
The "heart" is the lotus of the heart itself; it is the "forest. Therein is the "mist. The meaning is: by someone such as myself, who is incapable of speaking.
O Great-souled One, those mental afflictions do not even exist here for you; they do not reach destruction, for they are like dark nights by the moon when it has met with those of most exalted minds.

O Great-souled One! In this world, those evil anxieties do not exist which do not reach destruction through association with the excellent; for by association with the minds of the excellent, evil anxieties perish—thus the Lord concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"Life is as fragile as water hanging from a cluster of lotus petals shaken by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds."
Reflecting that youth is a torrential rush of fondling and that it is fleeting, I have indeed swiftly placed a seal as firm as a mountain upon my mind for the sake of long-lasting peace.

*Vitāna* means a collection; *lālanā* means playfulness; *mudrā* means silence—that is to say, the non-perception of sense objects. Of what nature is she? Firm like a mountain, like a peak. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus established the state of detachment, he introduces the description of the stages produced by that detachment:
"Thus, having observed the world—its hollows filled with the perilous multitude of rising misfortunes—to be submerged in the mire of mental constructions and discursive thought... (MU 1.29.1)
My mind seems to whirl, and a great confusion arises within me; my limbs tremble like the leaves of an aged tree.
"Abhyutthitaḥ" means having risen or attained prosperity. That which is a "non-benefit" (anartha)—a collection of misfortunes—constitutes a "distress" (saṅkaṭa) or confinement.

That which has a "hollow" (koṭara), meaning a center or interior, is that [which is being described]. The "mentalizing" (manana) of the mind is the dharma called "thinking" (manana), which is synonymous with "volition" (saṅkalpa). That itself is the "mud" (kardama). Within that, there is "agitation" (sambhrama), meaning a state of intense flurry. "Limbs" (gātrāṇi) refers to the bodily members.
The mind, its lap agitated by conduct that lacks supreme contentment and is unattained, fears here as it has an empty foundation, like a young girl under a weak ruler.

"Anāpta" means one who has not attained the practice and activity of supreme contentment. "Utsaṅga" means a lap or embrace. She by whom [that is attained]—she is such; and for that very reason, she is agitated. Even a young girl, when deprived of the embrace of a dear friend, becomes agitated. One whose lord or husband is of little strength—she is such; one whose lord is weak. Indeed, a young girl whose dwelling place is empty is clearly [distressed].
Thus he fears.
These fluctuations of the internal organ roll about amidst conceptual constructions, like female deer lured by hollow objects into pits.

They roll about among conceptual constructions; the meaning is that they move from one conceptual construction to another. Alternatively, it means they go toward delusion. Of what nature are these functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? They are "insubstantial" (*tuccha*), being devoid of essence because they are sweet only for a moment.

They are "mocked" (*viḍambita*)—that is, deceived—by those "supports" (*ālamba*), which are the sense objects, such that they are turned toward themselves [instead of their true object]. //MT_1,29.4//

Having fallen from the ground of discernment, these wretched ones—the eye and the other senses—have taken root in misery rather than in the state of the virtuous; they have entered as if into a blind well.
"In a difficult place" means in a harsh state known as the sense-objects.
Thought, dependent upon the Lord of Life, neither remains stationary nor proceeds as one desires, like a wife in the house of one who is unkind.
"Abiding" means stability. "As desired" means her own intended object. The Jīva alone is the Lord (īśvara) or master (pati); she is dependent upon him and subject to his will, but not independent.
Having worn out all things, my fortitude has fallen into a state of distress—neither relinquishing nor yet sustaining them—like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
"Having worn out [them] and become disenchanted,"—the word "bearing" implies "bearing new ones. "Fortitude" (dhṛti) refers, by metaphorical extension, to an intellect endowed with steadfastness.
Having cast aside all objects, non-abiding is established; and having grasped and then released the self, abiding is established.
"Cast aside" (*apahastitāḥ*) means passed from the hand; [the compound] refers to that in which all objects [are thus]. The meaning is "devoid of purpose.

"Instability" (*anavasthitiḥ*) is lack of delight (*arati*). "Established" (*āsthitā*) means become firm. "Stability" (*avasthitiḥ*) is delight (*rati*). "Established by grasping and then releasing the self" means a loose or unstable state.
By my internal support, which is both moving and unmoving, my mind is mocked, as it were, by the root of a tree that has been cut down by a poor man.

The base of this tree has been cut by the poor; indeed, it has been severed at its root. By that root—the agent—characterized by a support, namely fortitude, which for a moment remained unshaken even while trembling, my mind is the object of the action and is mocked, that is, imitated. The sense is: "My mind is like the root of a felled tree, incapable of producing new sprouts."
And this mind, flickering, expansive, and wandering through the various worlds, does not abandon its agitation, just as an immortal [god] does not leave his own celestial chariot.
It is expansive, endowed with the expansion known as conceptualization.
Therefore, what is that excellent state of stability—non-empty, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and beyond delusion—in which no doubt exists?
The word *sthitipada* means a state suitable for stability; *nāśaśaṅkā* means the apprehension of destruction.
All undertakings and enterprises—Sujana, Janaka, and the others—are solely devoted to worldly activity; how then have they attained the state of excellence?
Those for whom there is an undertaking in all undertakings—meaning, those who perform everything—are "good people" (*sujanāḥ*), that is, virtuous persons (*sajjanāḥ*).
O bestower of great honor, how could a person here not be smeared by the mire of saṃsāra, even though it clings to his limbs in abundance?
One is not defiled by the pleasures and pains produced through self-absorption, nor is one grasped by merit or sin.
Relying upon what view do you great-souled ones, free from defilement, live liberated while yet alive, and wander here as noble beings?
The intended meaning is: "Tell that to me as well."
How can those who enjoy the indulgence of sense-objects, luring others toward fear itself, ever attain a state of auspiciousness, given that their wealth takes a fragile form?

They lead only to fear and not to happiness. "Objects" (viṣaya) refers to enjoyments; "enjoyers" (bhogin) are those possessed of enjoyments, meaning they have the nature of snakes with well-nourished bodies. "Bhaṅgurākāra" means having a perishable nature. "Vibhava" refers to the source of their arising; such are they. "Bhavyatām" means loveliness, in the sense that passion is not produced [by them].
How can the lake of the intellect, trampled by the elephant of delusion and defiled within by stains, attain supreme clarity?

In this context, "stain" (kalaṅka) should be understood as the pursuit of worldly enjoyments; "intellect" (śemuṣī) means the faculty of understanding (buddhi); that very intellect is the lake (sarasī).
How is it that a person, though dwelling within saṃsāra itself and engaged in worldly affairs, does not incur bondage, just as water on a lotus leaf?
This is clear.
Creating this entire world as if it were himself or as if it were a blade of grass, how can one who does not touch the mind’s passion attain the state of supremacy?

"Producing" means generating; by implication, it means knowing. For the mind produces everything only through the gateway of cognition. The intended meaning is that in both cases, there is liberation alone.
Which Great Being, having reached the further shore of the ocean of existence, does this person follow by emulating his conduct so that they do not fall into evil deeds?
This is clear.
What is that which is appropriate and beneficial? What would be that appropriate fruit? And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this discordant cycle of existence?
In that which is improper and uneven.
Therefore, O Lord of this world, tell me something by which I may understand the beginningless and endless, unstable course of the Creator’s activity.

By that which was spoken, [he explained] the world—which is characterized by the two extremes of prior and posterior—as being "entire" (meaning complete) and as having an "unstable state" (meaning a discordant condition). Of what kind of world? Of the world whose "element" is its activity—that is, whose form consists of the activity of Brahmā.
O Brahmin, act so that the cleansing of the impurity of my mind—the moon within the sky of the heart—may come to pass without obstacle.
The cleansing of impurity is the cleansing of the impurity known as doubt.
What here should be accepted, what should be rejected, or what is otherwise? How may the flickering mind find rest, like a mountain?
Now, what else remains that should be disregarded?
By what purifying mantra is this cholera of miserable saṃsāra—which causes hundreds of hardships—pacified without effort?
This is clear.
How may I attain that internal coolness, a cluster of blossoms on the tree of bliss, which is as inexhaustible as the full moon on the night of the full moon?
Rākā is the full moon day.
Just as I no longer grieve within myself after attaining fullness, so may you, who are holy and knowers of reality, instruct me accordingly.
This is clear.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O Great-souled One, for what purpose do conceptual constructions so intensely torment the mind here—which is devoid of rest in the preeminent state of unsurpassed bliss—any more than dogs [torment] the body of a small creature in the forest? (MU 1.29.27).
They disregard and churn [it]. Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth canto in the section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the state produced by dispassion, he introduces the inquiry regarding the means [to attain it]:
"In a life-span as fragile as a drop of water hanging from a leaf trembling on a high tree, and in a body as delicate as a digit of the cool-rayed moon of the Lord... (MU 1.30.1)
In the circle of snares that is the gathering of friends and kinsmen, which is as fragile as the throat-skin of a frog croaking in a field of grain—*kedāra*.
When the cloud of the mist of delusion flashes with the lightning of base desires, stirred by the wind of latent impressions, it thunders and roars intensely.
When greed—the peacock of desire—is fierce, restless, and fully expanded, it dances the wild *uttāṇḍava* dance, bursting forth amidst the *kuṭaja* tree of calamities.
In this cruel cat of Death, who carries off all living beings like mice, whose movement is neither heard nor seen, and who pounces from somewhere above— ||| MU_1,30.5 |||
What is the means? What is the way? What is the reflection? What is the refuge? By what might this forest of life, which has such an inauspicious outcome, not come to be?
The digit of the cool-rayed moon belonging to Īśāna is the digit of the moon residing upon the head of Śrī Mahādeva. The throat-skin of a croaking frog becomes exceedingly fragile;
thus, it is taken as a point of comparison for her. In *mihikā*—that is, in a cloud accompanied by mist—of what nature?
One in which the lightning is the very hope that is coiled by the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). In such a cloud, which is manifest and clearly visible, there is a wild dance (*uttāṇḍava*).
"Udbhaṭam" means accompanied by a *sphoṭa*, that is to say, with a sound; this is the meaning. In what kind of "Kṛtānta-cat" (the cat that is Death)?
It is one whose movement (*sañcāra*) has not been heard. In such [a cat], the result is "of inauspicious future," meaning having an undesirable subsequent fruit. Life itself is the forest (*aṭavī*).
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all, which—even if it be trivial—does not become pleasing to a man of refined intellect.

The word *naramyatām* is not a compound; its meaning is *aramyatām* (let there be delight). The sense is that in every respect, the wise reach only toward that which is delightful. The particle *api* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
For how can this world, which is burnt by the cycle of existence and agitated by incessant mental constructions, become sweet-tasting unless it is devoid of sapidity through folly?
The intended meaning is that in the absence of foolishness, it does not attain sweetness.
By what means can the poison of hope be sweetened with a bath of milk? It becomes beautiful like a fine creeper when it reaches spring, which is as bright as a flower.
Hope itself is the "counter-poison," a specific kind of bitter substance. By what means, and in what form?
By what means can the moon of the mind—which is stained by desire—be made to rise with its nectar-like luster cleansed, through that very process of washing?

"Apamṛṣṭa" means wiped away; she is one whose impurity (*mala*) has been destroyed. By the phrase "by what [was it wiped away]? there is a question. Of what kind of moon-mind? It is of such a mind as possesses desire (*kāma*) as its stain (*kalaṅka*).
By whom should one navigate the pathways of the forest of saṃsāra, having seen its course and having destroyed both the seen and the unseen?

By whom the course of saṃsāra has been seen—by such a person; that is, by one who possesses the destruction of both the seen and the unseen, meaning by one who has transcended the categories of objects, merit, demerit, and so forth, in other words, by a *jīvanmukta*.
In what manner, and by what means, should he conduct himself—that is, perform his worldly dealings—within the pathways of the forest of saṃsāra?
How is it that the great diseases of passion and hatred, preceded by the pursuit of enjoyments and extreme impurities, do not afflict a living being wandering in the forest of saṃsāra?

Attachment and aversion are indeed great diseases. How could they not afflict a living being wandering in the wilderness of *saṃsāra*? Of what nature are they? They are those for which sensual enjoyments (*bhoga*) are the prior cause. Furthermore, they are "extremely putrid" (*atipūti*), meaning they possess an exceedingly foul odor;

the "putridity" here refers to attachment and so forth. By implication, exhilaration and resentment are to be understood [as the causes]; however, in the context of disease, the meaning is well-known.
Thus it is.
And how is it that even when falling into the fire of heroic passion, one is not consumed, just as mercury is not burnt by fire because of its mercurial nature?
This statement is made because of his being of the kṣatriya caste; "with pārata rasa" means with the mercury known as pārata.
"In that case, do not engage in worldly activity at all. To this he replies:
"Because, indeed, in this world, stability is not possible without the performance of worldly activity, just as for one fallen into the ocean there can be no water [to stay afloat]. (MU 1.30.14)
Stability is remaining in a state.
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of pleasure and pain, there is no virtuous action here, just as a flame of fire is without heat.
This is clear.
O most excellent ones, tell me: for the proud woman who broods upon her lover, there exists no means to end her suffering in the three worlds except through his destruction; say that clearly enough!

The three worlds are entirely filled with suffering. Within them, there is no means to end that suffering for one who prides herself on the mental constructions of the mind—this is the ellipsis, meaning "no means to ward off suffering. Therefore, O noble ones, speak—that is, tell us—of that method for ending [suffering]. In the phrase *ābhuvanatrayam*, the prefix *āṅ* is compounded in the sense of pervasiveness. [Likewise in] *ānagaram*.
...as in the case of [the word] *itivat*.
O noble ones, tell me that supreme path by which suffering does not come to me through reasoning while engaged in worldly activity, or rather, for one who is free from such activity.
The course, that is, the logical reasoning, of that which is beyond conventional discourse and devoid of worldly transaction.
How, by what means, or by whom was it performed by one of supreme mind, such that the mind attains this most purifying state of rest?

By what supreme being was that performed in the past, and how was it done? "What was that? is the remainder [of the question], referring to that by which my mind, becoming purified, attains the highest rest.
O Blessed One, as you know, please tell me for the sake of dispelling delusion that by which the virtuous have attained freedom from suffering.
To the objection, "How indeed can I speak?", he says here: "The virtuous."
Or else, O Brahmin, if such a logical justification does not exist, or if no clear justification exists for me, even though it may be present; MU_1,30.20.
And yet, I myself do not attain that unsurpassed state of rest; therefore, having abandoned all worldly effort, I have attained a state free from egoism.
I shall not eat, nor shall I drink water; I do not put on clothing; I perform no activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating.

O Brahmin, or rather, if such a reasoning does not exist; or even if such reasoning exists, someone might say to me, "This is not [correct]"—this is the ellipsis. And as for myself, through whatever reasoning I have somehow obtained that state of rest, I do not attain that repose because of extreme dullness. Therefore, having become free from egoism, I am one who has abandoned all worldly concerns.
I am present. I shall not eat. [This is] the sesame-mark.
I do not remain attached to my duties, whether in times of prosperity or in times of adversity; O Sage, I desire nothing at all except for the abandonment of this body.
This is clear.
Free from doubt, devoid of the sense of "mine," and rid of envy, I remain here in silence alone, as if fixed in the act of painting a picture.
This is clear.
Then, gradually abandoning even the consciousness of inhalation and exhalation, I shall cast off this useless structure known as the body.

Inhalation (*śvāsa*) and exhalation (*ucchvāsa*); these two are "inhalation and exhalation. That which exists together with them is "accompanied by inhalation and exhalation" (*saśvāsocchvāsā*). Such is consciousness (*saṃvit*); [the word] "that" refers to it. "Configuration" (*sanniveśa*) means structural arrangement (*saṃsthāna*).

[Objection: But how can the abandonment of the body—which exists as related to oneself by virtue of being the object of equanimity—be accomplished? To this he says: "I am not this [body], nor does the body belong to me; I shall be extinguished like a lamp without oil. Having renounced everything, I abandon this physical frame. (MU 1.30.26)
This is clear.
He concludes Śrī Rāma’s speech with a verse at the end of the canto:

"Having spoken thus—Rāma, who is as delightful as the stainless cool-rayed moon, his mind blossoming with supreme discernment—he became silent before the great ones, like a peacock (*nīlakaṇṭha*) ceasing its cries out of exhaustion from its *kekā* calls. May there be auspiciousness. *iti śivam.* (Thus all is well. *Mayūra:* peacock. *Iti śivam:* may there be auspiciousness. *MT_1,30.27* refers to the manuscript or edition number and verse.
Thus ends the thirtieth canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The venerable Vālmīki speaks thus to the venerable Bharadvāja,
uttering words that bring about the cessation of the delusion of the mind regarding that prince Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals.
All those present there stood with eyes wide with wonder, as if the hairs on their bodies had risen up to catch the words like garments held aloft.
Having cast off all worldly tendencies through the latent impression of cessation, they remain for a moment as if tossed by the waves of the ocean of nectar.
"With body-hairs" means with their hair; "wearing garments" means wearing clothes—the sense is that they were endowed with a bodice of hair.
Of what kind were the body-hairs? As if they had risen up to hear the words of Śrī Rāma.

By the latent impression of renunciation (*nivṛtti-vāsanā*), all latent impressions of worldly existence (*bhava-vāsanā*) were cast off and abandoned by them; those [body-hairs] were thus agitated and set in motion.
Those songs of Rāmabhadra, as if depicted in a painting, were heard within by listeners whose hearts were overflowing with joy.
By the listeners, who are eager to hear.
He speaks specifically to Śṛṇuka alone,
while sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra are seated in the assembly, along with ministers headed by Jayanta and Ghṛṣṭi, who are experts in counsel.
This is clear.
By kings such as Daśaratha, by citizens including those of Pāraśava descent, by vassal lords and princes, and by Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda;
This is clear.
Likewise, with servants and ministers, with birds confined in cages, with pet animals devoid of movement, and with horses that have ceased chewing;
By those who have finished chewing and abandoned their food.
And by the throngs of women, headed by Kausalyā, who stood at their own windows with the sound of their ornaments silenced and themselves motionless; MU_1,31.8.
This is clear.
With birds dwelling in garden creepers and even in the eaves of the roof-ridges, their flocks remained undisturbed and their cries had ceased.
By the Siddhas and the sky-dwellers, as well as by the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, and by the preeminent sages headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha;
This is clear.
And those words of Rāma, full of diverse meanings and most noble, were heard by others as well—the lords of the gods, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents.
This is clear.
Then, while that lotus-eyed Rāma—beautiful as the moon in the sky of the Raghu dynasty—remained silent;
Accompanied by voices of acclaim uttered by the assembly of perfected beings (siddhas), a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy.
This is clear.

He distinguishes the rain of flowers as sounding with the humming of pairs of bees resting within the buds of *mandāraka* trees, and as gladdening intoxicated women who were already delighted by the beauty of the fragrance of wine.
This is clear.
Like a succession of stars scattered by the wind in the sky, it was like the flash of a celestial woman’s laughter fallen upon the surface of the earth.
This is clear.
It was like a falling line of drops from a single autumn cloud during the rains, or like a succession of lumps of fresh butter being cast forth.
In the case of rains, [the interval] is within the rain.
Noble as a rain from the Himavat mountains, resembling a mass of pearl necklaces, like a garland of moonbeams, and akin to a succession of waves of milk.
It is clear.
Enveloped by the fragrance of filaments, with swarms of bees hovering about, it was stirred by a breeze sweet with the humming song of sighing bees.
"Sītkāra" is an onomatopoeic imitation of sound.
With clusters of *ketaka* flowers drifting about, with masses of *kairava* lilies spreading forth, with circles of *kunda* blossoms falling down, and with abodes of blue water-lilies turning;
This is clear.
Filling the courtyards, houses, gardens, and rooftops of the women’s quarters, he was gazed upon by the finest city-dwelling ladies with their necks upturned.
She by whom the courtyards, gardens, roof-terraces, and crossroads were filled; for one who is eager to see someone indeed holds up their neck.
A rain from the cloudless sky, resembling blue lotuses, fell without agitation; it was something never seen before by any person, and it inspired wonder in all.
This is clear.
Impelled by the hands of a multitude of Siddhas who had never been seen before, that rain of flowers fell during the fourth part of a Muhūrta.
The particle *ha* is for the purpose of completing the metrical foot.

When the assembly had been filled and the rain of flowers had subsided, those present in the hall heard these words from the hosts of Siddhas: āpūritasabhāloke śānte kusumavarṣaṇe / imān siddhagaṇālāpāñ śuśruvus te sabhāgatāḥ // MU_1,31.23 //
This is clear.
The very words of the Siddhas declare:
"Wandering all around the heavens for kalpas among the hosts of Siddhas, we have today heard something unprecedented—a true elixir for the ears."
In the ear; the elixir is nectar.
Indeed, that noble speech which was uttered by this moon of the Raghu dynasty, through his state of freedom from passion, lies beyond the reach even of the Lord of Speech himself.
This is clear.
"Oh, what great merit has been gained by us today, having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma, which bring the refreshment of nectar to the intellect!"
This is clear.
He recites the concluding verse of the canto:

"Because the Joy of the Raghus has spoken that which is appropriate—beautiful with the nectar of tranquility and having attained the state of supreme excellence—with such reverence, we have been instantly awakened by it."
They have been awakened, endowed with knowledge, and perfected. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the thirty-first canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

The Siddhas themselves spoke among one another regarding this purifying speech uttered by the banner of the Raghus, saying that it was fitting for the great seers to hear the decision that was about to be declared.
"O foremost of sages, headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha, may all you great ṛṣis come here without any obstacle."
Let us wander all around this holy assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha, just as bees hover about a lotus pond filled with dense golden lotuses.
This is clear.
The venerable Vālmīki said to the venerable Bharadvāja:
"Having spoken thus, that entire divine succession of sages, dwelling in the abode of the sky, descended there into that assembly."
She is one who dwells there, in that which is the abode in the sky.
He further qualifies the lineage of sages:
"The lordly sages were seated upon the backs of winds standing at their head, playing lutes; the sky was made dark with the sight of Vyāsa, who was as black as a cloud swollen with water."
That [city] in which the Maruts stand in front, and that [city] in which the lords of sages have lutes resounding on their backs.
It was adorned by the leaders of sages such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Pulastya, and protected by Cyavana, Uddālaka, Uśīra, Śaraloman, and others.
This is clear.
Due to their mutual touch, her deer-skin was ill-positioned; she held a rosary, a bracelet, and a beautiful water-pot, yet her eyes were restless.
From grasping, from the friction.
Like a row of stars mutually enhancing each other's beauty, it was like another shower of flowers, or like a second solar disc.
This is clear.
Vyāsa shone there like a cloud amidst a host of stars; Nārada shone there like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
This is clear.
Pulastya shone there like Svarādhīśa among the gods, and Aṅgiras shone like Āditya among the gods.
This is clear.
Then, as this army of Siddhas descended from the sky to the earth, the assembly hall of Daśaratha’s son rose up, filled with sages.
This is clear.
Intermingled, those beings who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth shone forth, their bodily splendors blending with one another as they illuminated the ten directions.
Those by which the luster of the limbs was mutually enveloped.
They distinguish themselves as both sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers;
their hands are covered with flutes and bells, they hold play-lotuses, their hair-tips are entwined with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and their locks of hair are adorned with crest-jewels.
This is clear.
Their matted hair was tawny like a forest fire, their heads were adorned with crowns and garlands, their forearms bore rosaries, and they were equipped with bracelets of rubies.
By means of a mass of matted hair—that is, by a collection of matted locks—they are tawny.
Clad in garments of bark and rags, yet draped with garlands and fine silken cloths; their waist-bands dangling and their strings of pearls swaying.
This is clear.
In an instant, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored those great hosts of sky-travelers with offerings of water for their hands and feet, as well as with words.
This is clear.
The king honored the assembly of Siddhas with every form of respectful conduct, and the assembly of Siddhas likewise greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare.
This is clear.
Having received due hospitality from one another through various expressions of affectionate zeal, those who move through the sky and those who dwell upon the earth sat down upon their seats.
With the impetuousness of affection and the impetuousness of love.
With words, a rain of flowers, and shouts of "Well done!", they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
This is clear.
And there, resplendent with royal fortune, he took his seat along with Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Vāmadeva as his ministers.
He is that Śrī Rāma.
Nārada, the son of a god, and Vyāsa, the bull among sages; then Marīci, Durvāsas, and likewise the sage Āṅgirasa.
This is clear.
Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Śaraloman, the lord of sages, Vātsyāyana, Bharadvāja, and Vālmīki, the bull among sages; MU_1,32.22//
This is clear.
Uddālaka, Ṛcīka, Śaryāti, and Cyavana; likewise Ūṣmapa, Ghṛtārcis, Śāluḍi, and Vāluḍi.
This is clear.
These and many others, masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, great-souled leaders who had realized that which is to be known, were present there.
The leaders are the most excellent.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, those learned sages, Nārada and the others, spoke these words to Rāma, whose face was cast down in humility.
Anūcānas are those who know the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (aṅgas).
Oh, how wonderful! The prince has uttered words endowed with auspicious qualities, filled with the most noble essence of dispassion.
This is clear.
The meaning of the sentences is perfectly established, easy to understand, appropriate, clear, noble, worthy of being practiced with affection, undisturbed, and unerring.
Whom does this speech uttered by Rāghava—not only clearly articulated, but also definitive, distinct, and satisfying—not fill with wonder?

"Pariniṣṭhita" means free from desire; that in which the meaning of the sentence is complete is "pariniṣṭhitavākyārtha. Such being the case, it is "subodha," meaning easy to understand, and "sphuṭa," meaning its meaning is manifest. It is "priyacaryārhata," meaning it is worthy of being treated with affection or pleasant discourse. "Avihvala" means free from agitation or confusion. "Avipluta" means incapable of being contradicted by anything. And it is "tuṣṭimat," meaning it brings satisfaction.
It possesses satisfaction because it causes satisfaction in the listener.
From among a hundred [poets], the speech of even a single one who possesses every kind of noble wonder becomes uniquely capable of bestowing the desired object.
The meaning is that [this quality] is noble and preeminent compared to all others; it belongs to one who possesses such wonder (*camatkṛti*), but the implication is that not everyone is like this.
He says to Śrī Rāma:
"O Prince, in whom else but you does wisdom—bearing the fruit of discernment—thus attain its full bloom, like a forest creeper?"
This is clear.
That man is considered truly wise in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom dwells in the heart, blazing brightly like that of Rāma and providing illumination.
This is clear.
Numerous and extremely widespread machines made of blood, flesh, and bone remove objects; there is no sentient being among them.
There have been many past machines of blood, flesh, and bone—meaning bodies inhabited by persons. Of what nature were they?

They drew things away through their dullness and were conquerors [of others]. However, among them, not even a single machine of blood, flesh, and bone was endowed with consciousness or possessed of discernment. The meaning is that there was no person whatsoever who was conscious.
Bound by delusion, these cattle of saṃsāra do not reflect upon it; they undergo again and again the suffering of birth, death, and old age.
Regarding the phrase "they reflect," here too, the very suffering of birth, death, and old age constitutes their activity; these ignorant ones are the cattle of saṃsāra.
Only rarely and in some place is one person seen whose disposition is pure and who is worthy of reflection upon his past and future, such as this destroyer of enemies.
Worthy of investigation as to what precedes and follows; fit for correct inquiry.
Those who possess auspicious forms and yield the fruit of unsurpassed wonder are indeed rare in this world, like mango trees.
Those who are capable are endowed with discernment.
Right view regarding the birth of the world is the wonder of one's own discernment; within this noble intention, it appears as if something entirely different.

O Bhavyamati, within this child-form Śrī Rāma, we perceive this wondrous flash of our own discernment— the marvel of self-discrimination— as if it were a new vision, distinct from our previous perceptions regarding the birth and existence of the world. It is seen as a true insight, the very nature of right vision.
Worlds that are easily accessible and full of fortune abound with trees possessing fruit and foliage; however, sandalwood trees do not grow in every land.
They are fortunate, captivating the mind by their mere appearance.
It is true that there are trees in every forest possessing fine fruits and foliage; yet the clove tree, with its unprecedented wonder, is not always easily found.
This is clear.
Like the cool moonlight from the moon, like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree, or like a trail of fragrance from a flower—such was the wonder beheld from Rāma.
The meaning is that "wonder" (*camatkṛti*) takes the form of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

O best of the twice-born, from this burnt-out cycle of existence—which is fashioned by the workings of fate and characterized by unrestrained wickedness—the essence is indeed extremely difficult to obtain.

O best of the twice-born! From what kind of world was he liberated? It was from one whose nature is such that it is produced (*nirmiti*) from the creation (*nirmāṇa*) of Fate (*daiva*), which is the Ordainer (*vidhi*). Fate is that which possesses unrestrained wickedness due to its causing extreme inequality.
One should see the distinction between *nirmāṇa* and *nirmiti* as being that of the general and the particular. This is because of the excellence of his dispassion (*vairāgya*) in this regard.
It should not be suspected otherwise that it is improper to feel resentment toward destiny.
Those who, as repositories of glory, strive with their intellect to attain the essence, are the fortunate ones; they alone are counted among the foremost of the virtuous and are the best of men.
This is clear.
"In these three worlds, there is no one equal to Rāma; it is our conviction that he is discerning, noble-souled, and great-souled. (MU 1.32.42)
This is clear.
He concludes the section on dispassion with a verse at the end of the canto:
"If that which is desired by the mind of Rāghava—which causes wonder even to all the worlds—does not bear fruit, then it is clearly we sages ourselves who are of ruined intellect."
The desired answer to the question just stated has been provided. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the thirty-second canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
May this commentary on the chapter titled "Detachment" grant excellent fruit to those listeners whose hearts are graced by the immersion in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
By the power of its penetration, may there arise a capacity within the sphere of action.
May this effort regarding all phenomena, determined by their nature as effects, succeed;
may the flood of water called dispassion—the expert at uprooting the tree known as the passion-seed of latent tendencies—manifest within my mind. (16–17)
Thus all is auspicious.

Thus ends the chapter titled "Detachment" (*vairāgya*) in the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā*, composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Avatārakaṇṭha, grandson of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha— the great devotee of Maheśvara and worshipful teacher residing within the region of Śrī-Kāśmīra.
